areas.area: Custom Fields (Salesforce) — data-type permanence, API-name immutability, required semantics, unique/external ID, indexing, formula/roll-up limits, field history, deletion & restore, per-object field allocations

practices.practice: In a formula field or validation rule, do NOT divide a Percent field by 100 — the platform already does it. In Flow assignments/record-update values, DO treat the same field as the whole number.
practices.specifics: Official verbatim: "Note that percent fields are expressed divided by 100 in formulas (100% is expressed as 1; 50% is expressed as 0.5)." Salesforce's own sample validation rule for a 0–100% custom field is `OR(Mix_Pct__c > 1.0, Mix_Pct__c < 0.0)`. Flow is the opposite: passing a percent value between sObject variables leaves 100 as 100 (= 100%), but "Reference an sObject variable's percent field into a formula → Divide by 100", so 100 becomes 1 and saving writes 1%.
practices.why_it_matters: The two contexts are inverted relative to each other. An LLM that applies one rule everywhere produces values that are wrong by a factor of 100 — silently, because no error is raised and the number still renders with a % sign.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs uniformly emit `Amount * (Discount_Percent__c / 100)` for formula fields, reasoning from the fact that the UI displays 15 for 15%. Official docs say the formula engine has already divided, so this yields 1/100th of the intended value. The repo's own flow/flow-formula-and-expression-patterns package asserts the LLM version as fact — the anti-pattern has already been absorbed into the corpus.

practices.practice: Treat Activity (Task/Event) custom fields as a hard ceiling tied to record volume, not just edition — and check activity row count before promising an admin another field.
practices.specifics: Up to 300 custom fields on Activities, but only while the org has fewer than 700 million tasks and events. Once the org is past 700 million activities AND already has more than 100 custom activity fields, no further custom fields can be created at all. Existing fields are retained to prevent data loss. The only way back is to archive activities (Salesforce Archive, Data 360, or third-party) and delete the archived rows.
practices.why_it_matters: This is the one object where the field allocation is a function of data volume. Large Sales Cloud orgs hit it and there is no Support case that fixes it — only an archival programme measured in months.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM asked "how many custom fields can I add to Task?" answers with the edition table (500 EE / 800 UE) or says 100, and never mentions that the ceiling collapses at 700 million activity rows. It will confidently tell a 900-million-activity org to just add the field.

practices.practice: Never enable field history tracking on Long Text Area, Rich Text Area, Multi-Select Picklist, or any field longer than 255 characters and then promise an auditor the before/after values.
practices.specifics: For Text Area (Long), Text Area (Rich), Picklist (Multi-Select), and any field with length > 255 characters, the change is recorded as "edited" but OldValue and NewValue are stored as null. You get who and when, never what. Formula, roll-up summary and auto-number fields cannot be tracked at all. Standard tracking caps at 20 fields/object; Field Audit Trail raises it to 60.
practices.why_it_matters: Compliance programmes are built on the assumption that "tracked" means "reconstructable". For these four field classes it does not, and the gap is only discovered during an audit, years after the data is gone.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs answer "enable Field History Tracking on Description__c and you'll see the old and new value in AccountHistory" and even generate `SELECT OldValue, NewValue FROM Account__History WHERE Field = 'Description__c'`. The query runs and returns rows with nulls — no exception, no warning.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Field Audit Trail (Salesforce Shield add-on or standalone) for >20 tracked fields per object, 10-year retention, and the FieldHistoryArchive big object; the RetainFieldHistory user permission is required to set retention policies

practices.practice: Marking a custom field Required at the field definition level (universally required) makes it visible on every edit page even to users whose FLS hides it — so never use it to enforce a field the audience is not allowed to see.
practices.specifics: A universally required field must have a value whenever a record is saved via Salesforce UI, the Lightning Platform API, automated processes such as Web-to-Lead and Web-to-Case. It is required across all record types, and "edit pages always display universally required fields, regardless of field-level security". Field-definition Required is the only one of the three mechanisms (field Required, page-layout Required, validation rule) that the API enforces — page-layout Required is UI-only and is bypassed by every API call, Data Loader job and integration.
practices.why_it_matters: Admins reach for the field-level Required checkbox to enforce data quality and inadvertently punch a hole through FLS on every edit page, and separately assume a page-layout-required field is protecting their integration payloads when it is not.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs treat the three mechanisms as interchangeable ("mark it required on the layout to make it mandatory") and never state that only field-definition Required reaches the API, nor that it overrides FLS on edit pages. They also recommend field-level Required for conditionally-required data, where a validation rule is the only correct tool.
practices.verbatim_error_string: REQUIRED_FIELD_MISSING: Required fields are missing: [Field_Name__c]

practices.practice: A formula field can only be custom-indexed if it is deterministic — and the disqualifying constructs are specific, not intuitive.
practices.specifics: A formula field is indexable only if it: references fields from a single object only (no relationship/lookup traversal), does not reference non-deterministic functions such as SYSDATE/TODAY/NOW, does not reference DATEVALUE() on a Date/Time field, does not reference the record Id, does not use TEXT() on a picklist, and — if it references a lookup field — that lookup must not clear its value when the referenced record is deleted. Deterministic formula indexes must be requested from Salesforce Support; they add maintenance overhead on every DML that touches an underlying field, which slows bulk loads.
practices.why_it_matters: Teams design a filterable "status" formula field, hit a full-table scan on a 5-million-row object, and cannot index their way out because a single TEXT(picklist) call disqualified the field.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs say "formula fields can't be indexed" (too absolute) or "just request a custom index from Support" (too optimistic), and never enumerate DATEVALUE()-on-Date/Time or TEXT()-on-picklist as the specific disqualifiers. They routinely generate exactly those two patterns in the formula they are proposing to index.

practices.practice: Custom indexes exclude null rows by default — a `WHERE Field__c = null` filter is unindexed no matter how selective it is.
practices.specifics: "By default, underlying Force.com field indexes don't include nulls." Null-inclusive indexes must be requested from Salesforce Support, and "even if you already have custom indexes on your custom fields, they need to be explicitly enabled and rebuilt to get the empty-value rows into index tables." The option does not apply to picklists, external IDs, or foreign key fields; for null external-ID queries Support creates a two-column compound index instead.
practices.why_it_matters: "Find the records that were never populated" is the most common backfill query in a data-cleanup project, and it is precisely the query the index cannot serve.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs advise "mark the field as External ID so it's indexed, then query WHERE Field__c = null" — which is doubly wrong, because external IDs are explicitly excluded from null-inclusive indexing. They also fail to mention that an existing index must be rebuilt, so a team that files a Support case still sees no improvement.
practices.verbatim_error_string: Non-selective query against large object type (more than 200000 rows)

practices.practice: External ID fields, Unique fields, and custom indexes draw from the same 25-per-object budget — count all three before designing a multi-source integration key.
practices.specifics: Maximum 25 external ID fields per object; custom fields marked Unique count against the same pool, so (Unique + External ID + custom-indexed) ≤ 25 per object. Soft limit — Salesforce Support can raise it. External ID is only available on Auto Number, Email, Number, and Text field types; marking a field External ID auto-creates the index. Upsert matching on an external ID is case-INSENSITIVE by default ('ABC' matches 'abc') unless the field also has Unique with the case-sensitive option selected.
practices.why_it_matters: An org that gives every source system its own external ID field runs out of indexed-field budget on the object that most needs indexes, and the case-insensitivity default silently merges records that the source system considers distinct.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs treat External ID, Unique, and custom index as three independent knobs and recommend turning on all three "for performance", not realising they consume one shared allocation. They also assume external-ID upsert is case-sensitive, so they design keys like 'cust-001' vs 'CUST-001' expecting two records.
practices.verbatim_error_string: DUPLICATE_VALUE (duplicate keys in the payload) vs DUPLICATE_EXTERNAL_ID (duplicate matches already in the target org) — two different codes for two different root causes

practices.practice: Enabling Advanced Currency Management invalidates every currency roll-up summary field on Account (summarising Opportunities) and Opportunity (summarising custom objects) — delete them first.
practices.specifics: Official guidance: if the org enables advanced currency management, delete the currency roll-up summary fields on accounts that summarize opportunity values and on opportunities that summarize custom object values; "otherwise, the fields continue to display with an invalid roll-up summary icon because their values are no longer calculated." Roll-up summary fields also cannot reference formula fields containing cross-object references or NOW()/TODAY()/DATEVALUE(); long text area, multi-select picklist, and lookup fields cannot be used in a roll-up filter column. Deleting a child record does not always trigger recalculation — the parent field's edit page has a "Force a mass recalculation of this field" option.
practices.why_it_matters: The roll-up keeps displaying its last calculated number forever. Pipeline totals go stale on the day ACM is enabled, and nobody notices because the field still shows a plausible value.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked "should we turn on Advanced Currency Management?", LLMs list dated exchange rates as the trade-off and never mention that existing currency roll-ups silently stop calculating. They also propose roll-ups over formula fields that use TODAY(), which Salesforce rejects at save time.

practices.practice: Roll-up summary allocation is 25 per object by default and 40 is the hard ceiling — design the parent object's aggregate strategy against 40, not against "as many as you need".
practices.specifics: Default 25 roll-up summary fields per object; Salesforce Support can raise it to a maximum of 40, which is hard-coded and cannot be exceeded. Roll-ups require a master-detail relationship on the parent side. A deleted roll-up summary field continues to count against the roll-up allocation until it is erased from the Deleted Fields queue.
practices.why_it_matters: Teams building a financial or scoring parent object plan 60 aggregates and only discover the 40-field wall after the data model is deployed and the master-detail relationships are locked in.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs quote 25 as "the limit" without mentioning the 40 hard ceiling or that it is Support-raisable, so architects either over-engineer an Apex rollup framework they didn't need or plan for unlimited roll-ups they can't have.

practices.practice: When a field type conversion causes data loss, the collateral damage extends past the field: list views built on it are deleted and assignment/escalation rules are affected.
practices.specifics: Official guidance: "To avoid losing data, only convert custom fields that have no data." If data loss does occur, any list view based on the custom field is deleted, and assignment and escalation rules can be affected. Data loss occurs when changing to or from Date or Date/Time, to Number, to Percent, or to Currency from any other type, from Checkbox to any other type, or from Multi-Select Picklist to any other type. When converting Picklist → Multi-Select Picklist, defined values are retained but any record holding a value that is not in the picklist definition has that value deleted. You cannot change the data type of a custom field mapped for lead conversion, or one referenced by Apex/Visualforce. Auto Number ↔ Text is the only safe round trip, and Auto Number caps at 30 characters.
practices.why_it_matters: Losing the field data is recoverable from a backup; losing the shared list views the sales team runs their day on is a separate, unannounced outage.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs say "you can change Text to Number, just back up the data first" and stop there. They never mention that list views on the field are deleted, that assignment and escalation rules are affected, or that lead-conversion mapping blocks the change outright.

practices.practice: Salesforce blocks a field's API-name rename when Apex references it, silently auto-fixes validation rules / workflows / email templates, and leaves Flows to fail at run time — plan the rename as three separate workstreams.
practices.specifics: Apex classes and triggers block the rename (Salesforce refuses the change). Validation rules, workflow rules and email templates auto-update to the new API name. Flow and Process Builder references do not auto-update in every case and surface at run time as an "Error Occurred During Flow" fault, not at save time. Reports, list-view filters, integrations, Data Loader mappings and external systems (Marketo, MuleSoft, ETL) hold the old string and break on the next run.
practices.why_it_matters: The rename appears to succeed. The failures land hours or days later, in the automation nobody deployed that week, and the field name that would let you find them no longer exists.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs say either "you can't rename an API name" (false — you can) or "Salesforce updates all references automatically" (false for Flow, reports, and everything outside the org). Neither answer tells the admin that Apex will hard-block the change while Flow will let it through and fail later.
practices.verbatim_error_string: This custom field is referenced elsewhere in salesforce.com. : Flow Version - <version_number>

practices.practice: Long Text Area is unfilterable in SOQL and only its first 255 characters participate in report filters — do not choose it for anything you will need to query.
practices.specifics: Long Text Area holds 256–131,072 characters and cannot appear in a SOQL WHERE clause at all (the field's `filterable` attribute is false). Reports can apply `contains` to a Long Text Area, but only the first 255 characters are used as the filter value. Long Text Area cannot be custom-indexed, cannot be used in a roll-up summary filter column, and its field history records no old/new value. The standard workaround is a companion 255-character Text field holding the searchable prefix or keyword.
practices.why_it_matters: The choice between Text(255) and Long Text Area looks like a display decision and is actually a permanent queryability decision, made once, at field-creation time.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs generate `SELECT Id FROM Case WHERE Long_Notes__c LIKE '%refund%'` without hesitation, and they recommend Long Text Area for "description" fields as a safe default because it holds more characters — trading away filterability, indexing and history for headroom the business rarely uses.
practices.verbatim_error_string: field cannot be filtered in a query call

practices.practice: Multi-Select Picklist has three separate ceilings and one silent truncation — 500 values in the set, 100 selectable per record (hard), 40 characters per value.
practices.specifics: Total values in a multi-select set: 500 (Support can raise a lower org limit up to 500, never beyond). Maximum values selectable at one time on a record: 100, and this "cannot be increased" under any circumstances. Each value is limited to 40 characters and longer values are truncated without notice. Stored as a semicolon-delimited string; SOQL requires INCLUDES/EXCLUDES rather than `=`; reports cannot use `equals` and can only group rows whose selected combination is byte-identical; TEXT() does not work on the field in formulas (INCLUDES() does).
practices.why_it_matters: The 40-character truncation happens on save with no error, so the picklist value in Setup and the value on the record differ, and every downstream `INCLUDES('...')` filter misses.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs recommend Multi-Select Picklist whenever the requirement contains the word "multiple", then write `WHERE Interests__c = 'Golf'` or `TEXT(Interests__c)` in a formula. They also quote the single-select 255-character value limit for multi-select values, missing the 40-character truncation entirely.
practices.already_covered_by: skills/admin/picklist-and-value-sets (states 1,000 values / 255 chars — the single-select numbers)

practices.practice: Rich Text Area images are file storage, not data storage, and are capped at 1 MB per image in three formats.
practices.specifics: Maximum uploaded image size in a Rich Text Area is 1 MB; only .gif, .jpg and .png are accepted. Images in rich text area fields count toward file storage for the object that contains them and are extracted into the org's weekly export. When a Rich Text Area is referenced in a formula the HTML tags are stripped before the formula runs. Reports can filter and summarise the field, but HTML tags and formatting are not included in report output.
practices.why_it_matters: A Knowledge or Case-comment design that embeds screenshots in Rich Text quietly consumes file storage at a rate nobody forecast, and the formula that was supposed to read the text gets a tag-stripped variant.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs treat Rich Text Area as "Long Text Area with formatting" and never mention the 1 MB / gif-jpg-png image constraint or that images bill against file storage. They also write formulas like `CONTAINS(Rich_Notes__c, '<b>')` that can never match, because tags are stripped first.

practices.practice: Field count is not a storage argument — every record costs a flat 2 KB regardless of how many fields it has.
practices.specifics: Salesforce charges 2 KB per record for all standard and custom objects except Person Accounts (4 KB) and Campaigns (8 KB), "regardless of the number of columns". A record with 2 populated columns and a record with 200 populated columns consume the same 2 KB of data storage. Rich Text Area images are the exception — they bill against file storage separately.
practices.why_it_matters: It reframes the whole field-proliferation conversation: the real cost of 400 fields is page-layout complexity, FLS surface area, deployment time and the 500/800 allocation — not data storage.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked to justify field cleanup, LLMs lead with "reduce storage costs" and produce a fabricated per-field byte estimate. The correct argument is allocation exhaustion, FLS/permission-set sprawl and query cost — storage is unchanged.

practices.practice: Deleted custom fields keep occupying their allocation for 15 days — Erase them from the Deleted Fields queue if you are deleting to make room.
practices.specifics: Deleted custom fields and their data are stored until the org permanently deletes them or 15 days elapse, whichever comes first. The field counts against the org's custom-field maximum until hard deletion, and against its type-specific allocation too (a deleted roll-up summary still counts against the roll-up allocation). Setup → Object Manager → [Object] → Fields & Relationships → Deleted Fields → Erase reclaims the slot immediately and is irreversible; Undelete restores both the field and its data within the window.
practices.why_it_matters: An admin at the 500-field wall deletes 20 fields, immediately tries to create a new one, and is still blocked — with no message explaining why.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs say "delete the field and the slot is freed" and omit the 15-day queue entirely, so the recovery path (Undelete restores the data too) is never offered to someone who just deleted the wrong field.

practices.practice: Formula fields have two independent size limits — 3,900 characters of source text and 5,000 bytes compiled — and referencing another formula field inlines its entire compiled body.
practices.specifics: Formula text limit is 3,900 characters; compile size limit is 5,000 bytes. A formula well under 3,900 characters can blow the 5,000-byte compile limit. Comments, whitespace and field-name length do not affect compile size. Each reference to another formula field adds that field's full compiled size — referencing the same helper formula three times costs three times. Replacing nested IF() with CASE() reduces compile size; renaming fields or adding helper fields does not.
practices.why_it_matters: The usual instinct — "extract it into a helper formula field" — makes the compile size worse, not better, because the helper is inlined at every reference.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs conflate the two limits into one "5,000 character" number, and their standard remedy for a compile error is "break it into helper formula fields", which is the single most reliable way to make the error worse. The correct moves are CASE() over nested IF(), fewer repeated references, or a workflow/Flow field update writing to a stored field.
practices.verbatim_error_string: Compiled formula is too big to execute (5,001 characters). Maximum size is 5,000 characters.

practices.practice: The 10-unique-relationships cross-object limit is per OBJECT and cumulative across all formula fields, validation rules and lookup filters — not per formula.
practices.specifics: Maximum 10 unique relationships per object referenced from cross-object formulas, counted cumulatively across every formula field, rule and lookup filter on that object. `Owner:User.fieldname` and `Owner:Queue.fieldname` count as two separate relationships against the 10.
practices.why_it_matters: The eleventh formula fails to save on an object where each individual formula looks trivially small, and the failure points at the new formula rather than the accumulated ten.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs report this as "you can span up to 10 relationships in a formula" — a per-formula depth limit. It is a per-object breadth budget, which is why an org can hit it with ten single-hop formulas.

practices.practice: Know the exact list of field types that can never carry a custom index before promising a query-performance fix.
practices.specifics: Cannot be custom-indexed: Text Area (Long), Text Area (Rich), non-deterministic formula fields, Classic Encrypted Text, Multi-Select Picklist, currency fields in a multicurrency org, binary/blob/file fields, and standard fields Owner, auto-number, division, and audit fields other than CreatedDate/CreatedById. Selectivity thresholds once indexed: standard index used when the filter matches under 30% of the first million records and under 15% beyond, capping at 1,000,000 targeted rows; custom index 10% / 5%, capping at 333,333 targeted rows. AND conditions use indexes unless one branch returns over 20%; OR conditions unless all branches return over 10%.
practices.why_it_matters: "Currency fields in a multicurrency org" is the one nobody expects — the same field is indexable in a single-currency org and not in a multicurrency one, so a query that was fast in the sandbox times out in production.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs answer "add a custom index on Amount__c" without checking whether the org is multicurrency, and they list the selectivity threshold as a single "10%" without the 333,333-row absolute cap — which is the binding constraint on any object past ~3.3 million rows.

practices.practice: Summer '26 added a Field Access tab in Object Manager — stop telling admins to click through every profile to audit FLS.
practices.specifics: Setup → Object Manager → [Object] → Field Access shows a single consolidated matrix of how access to each field on that object is granted across every profile, permission set and permission set group. Introduced in Summer '26; it appears as a new tab in the object's sidebar.
practices.why_it_matters: FLS audit was previously an N-profiles × M-fields manual crawl, which is why nobody did it. Advice written before Summer '26 sends people down that path unnecessarily.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs give the pre-Summer-'26 procedure — "open each profile, go to Field-Level Security, check each object" — or point at the per-field Set Field-Level Security page, which shows profiles only and omits permission sets and permission set groups entirely.

practices.practice: Field Audit Trail retention defaults differ between production and sandbox, and the archive lands in a big object you must query differently.
practices.specifics: With Field Audit Trail, data is archived after 18 months in production and after ONE month in a sandbox, and archived data is retained for 10 years. The retention period is configurable from 0 to 18 months. Archived rows move into the FieldHistoryArchive big object rather than being purged. Standard Field History Tracking retains for 18 months (24 months via API) with no archive.
practices.why_it_matters: Testing a retention policy in a sandbox gives you one month of live history and then an archive — behaviour that does not match production and reads as data loss to a tester.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs quote "10 years" as though it applies uniformly and then write `SELECT Field, OldValue FROM AccountHistory WHERE CreatedDate = LAST_N_YEARS:5` — which returns nothing, because anything past the archive threshold is in FieldHistoryArchive and needs a big-object query with the correct index-field order.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Field Audit Trail (Salesforce Shield add-on or standalone SKU); RetainFieldHistory user permission to set retention policies and read archived history; Customize Application to configure tracking

practices.practice: Classic Encrypted Text is a masking feature with a 175-character ceiling that removes the field from formulas, reports, WHERE clauses and indexes — reach for Shield Platform Encryption or a validation-rule mask instead.
practices.specifics: Classic Encrypted Text maximum length is 175 characters. The field cannot be indexed, cannot be referenced in formula fields, cannot appear in workflow or process criteria, cannot be filtered in a SOQL WHERE clause, and cannot be filtered in reports. Shield Platform Encryption encrypts at rest while preserving more platform functionality, at the cost of its own feature restrictions.
practices.why_it_matters: Choosing Classic Encrypted Text for a national ID or account number permanently removes that field from every reporting and automation surface, and the field type cannot be converted afterwards.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs recommend "use an Encrypted Text field" for any PII requirement without distinguishing Classic Encryption from Shield Platform Encryption, and then in the same answer write a validation rule or report filter on that field.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Shield Platform Encryption requires the Salesforce Shield add-on (or the standalone Platform Encryption SKU); Classic Encrypted Text requires no add-on, which is exactly why it gets chosen by mistake

practices.practice: Text length can be increased freely but reducing it fails against existing longer data — and every downstream write hits STRING_TOO_LONG at the boundary.
practices.specifics: A field of length 255 rejects a 256-character write with a STRING_TOO_LONG exception. Reducing a Text field's length requires cleaning or truncating existing data first. The same error surfaces in Flow (as a run-time fault) and in bulk loads (as per-row failures), not as a deployment-time validation.
practices.why_it_matters: Length reduction is one of the few field edits that silently passes in a sandbox with 50 test records and fails in production against real data.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs generate Apex and Flow that concatenates strings into a Text(255) field with no truncation guard, and when asked to shrink a field they say "just change the length in Object Manager" with no pre-flight `SELECT Id FROM Obj WHERE LEN(Field__c) > n` equivalent.
practices.verbatim_error_string: STRING_TOO_LONG: data value too large: <value> (max length=255)

practices.practice: Deleting a field referenced anywhere in metadata is blocked, and the blocker is frequently a deactivated Flow version rather than anything visible.
practices.specifics: The delete/deploy fails with a reference error naming the referencing component. The most common hidden referrer is an OLD, deactivated Flow version — Salesforce counts every stored version, not just the active one. Resolution: create a new Flow version without the reference, delete the prior versions that reference the field, then delete the field. In a deployment pipeline, the referencing Flow versions must be removed from the TARGET environment before the field deletion will validate.
practices.why_it_matters: The admin removes the field from the active Flow, the delete still fails, and there is no UI that lists which version is holding the reference.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs list "check formulas, validation rules, layouts, Apex, reports" and stop. They never mention deactivated Flow versions, which is the actual cause most of the time, and they never mention that the fix has to happen in the target org, not the source.
practices.verbatim_error_string: This custom field is referenced elsewhere in salesforce.com. : Flow Version - <version_number>

stale_or_wrong_found: INVERTED MECHANISM — skills/flow/flow-formula-and-expression-patterns states in four places that "Percent fields are stored as the displayed number (15), NOT as a decimal (0.15). Always divide by 100 before multiplying" (references/examples.md:333, references/gotchas.md:87, references/llm-anti-patterns.md:127-135, references/well-architected.md:69). Official Salesforce doc says the opposite for formula context, verbatim: "Note that percent fields are expressed divided by 100 in formulas (100% is expressed as 1; 50% is expressed as 0.5)" (developer.salesforce.com usefulValidationRules number sample), and Salesforce's own sample rule is OR(Mix_Pct__c > 1.0, Mix_Pct__c < 0.0). Salesforce Help 000380436 draws the line explicitly: in Flow, passing a percent value between sObject variables leaves 100 as 100 (=100%); but "Reference an sObject variable's percent field into a formula → Divide by 100" so 100 becomes 1 and saving writes 1%. The corpus guidance is therefore correct ONLY for plain Flow assignments and wrong for every formula resource / formula field / validation rule — where following it produces a result 100x too small. This needs correcting with the context split made explicit, not deleted.

INCOMPLETE-TO-THE-POINT-OF-MISLEADING — skills/admin/picklist-and-value-sets/SKILL.md:83 states "Standard and custom picklists: up to 1,000 total values ... each value label has a max of 255 characters". Those are the single-select numbers. Multi-select picklists cap at 500 values in the set, 100 values selectable per record (hard, not Support-raisable), and 40 characters per value with silent truncation. A reader designing a multi-select from that line will build values that get truncated on save.

POSSIBLY OVERSTATED — skills/admin/custom-field-creation/references/gotchas.md Gotcha 1 asserts "newly created custom fields default to no FLS access for all profiles" in Enterprise/Performance/Unlimited. The Setup field-creation wizard presents an FLS step where Visible is selectable per profile, and the documented failure mode for hidden-on-arrival fields is Metadata API / change-set deployment that omits Profile or PermissionSet fieldPermissions. I could not find an official source stating that the Setup UI default is hidden-for-all in EE/UE. Worth verifying against help.salesforce.com platform.users_fields_fls.htm before this is repeated in a new package; the creation-method distinction (Setup wizard vs Metadata API deploy) is the load-bearing part and is currently absent.

MISSING RELEASE CONTEXT — several admin packages describe FLS auditing as a per-profile crawl. Summer '26 shipped a Field Access tab in Object Manager giving a single matrix across profiles, permission sets and permission set groups. Any guidance that still routes users through profile-by-profile inspection is now out of date rather than wrong.

areas.area: Profiles, Permission Sets, and Permission Set Groups (Salesforce access control)

practices.practice: State that the Permissions-in-Profiles retirement was CANCELLED (announced 6 Jun 2026). Do not tell anyone they must migrate off profile permissions by Spring '26.
practices.specifics: Salesforce Help article ID 003834041, published Jun 6, 2026: "Salesforce previously announced the retirement of permissions in profiles starting in Spring '26. This enforcement has now been cancelled." Profiles continue to carry object permissions, FLS, user permissions and custom permissions. Salesforce still *recommends* a "permission set-led security model" but there is no enforced end-of-life date.
practices.why_it_matters: Whole migration programmes were scoped against an enforced Spring '26 deadline. Repeating the retired deadline makes an org spend budget on a mandate that no longer exists, and makes the library visibly out of date on the single most-asked question in this territory.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Every model trained before mid-2026 confidently says "Salesforce is retiring permissions on profiles in Spring '26 — you must migrate now." It was cancelled on 2026-06-06 because of customer pushback and remaining feature gaps. The LLM then over-recommends aggressive profile stripping on a false urgency.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE — and worse, skills/admin/permission-sets-vs-profiles/SKILL.md:84 currently asserts the cancelled position

practices.practice: When a user cannot see a field, check the three layers in the order the platform evaluates them: object permission → field-level security → record access. A grant at a lower layer cannot rescue a denial at a higher one.
practices.specifics: View All Data, Modify All Data, and View All Records / Modify All Records for a given object do NOT override field-level security. Per Salesforce: "Users must still have field permissions or the View All Fields object permission to access each field on an object." So a System-Administrator-adjacent user with MAD can still get a blank field.
practices.why_it_matters: The single most common access ticket is "this user has admin-ish permissions but the field is blank." Answering it requires knowing MAD stops at FLS.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: View All Fields (object permission) or explicit FieldPermissions read
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs say "grant Modify All Data and the user will see everything." They conflate record-level bypass with field-level bypass. MAD bypasses sharing and object permissions; it does not bypass FLS.
practices.already_covered_by: skills/security/record-access-troubleshooting (mentions View All Records / Modify All Records)

practices.practice: Offer the View All Fields object permission (Spring '25) as the correct answer to "grant read on every field of this object including future fields" — not View All Data, and not a hand-maintained FLS list.
practices.specifics: View All Fields is an object-level permission introduced in Spring '25 (API 254), set on the Object Settings page of a permission set. "This permission is available for all standard and custom objects that support field permissions" and "users are automatically granted access to any new fields created for the object." It is a READ grant only — it does not confer edit on fields.
practices.why_it_matters: Before Spring '25 the only way to guarantee coverage of future fields was View All Data, which also blows the record-sharing model open. View All Fields gives the same FLS breadth with none of the record-level blast radius.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: View All Fields object permission (per-object, permission-set assignable)
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs are pre-Spring-'25 on this and reach straight for View All Data, or they write a script to bulk-set FieldPermissions rows that then silently goes stale the moment someone adds a field. Neither is needed any more.

practices.practice: Never assume a permission set can subtract. Permissions are strictly additive across profile + every assigned permission set + every permission set group; the ONLY subtractive record-level primitive is a restriction rule.
practices.specifics: Restriction rules: enforcementType=Restrict on the RestrictionRule metadata type; up to 2 active rules per object in Enterprise and Developer editions; supported only on custom objects, Contract, Event, Task, TimeSheet and TimeSheetEntry. Scoping rules (enforcementType=Scoping) change the default filter only and do NOT restrict access.
practices.why_it_matters: An architect who believes a permission set can remove access will design a model that silently over-grants. There is no 'deny' in a permission set.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs propose a "deny permission set" or a "negative permission set" to remove access a user got elsewhere. No such thing exists. They also conflate scoping rules with restriction rules and claim scoping rules secure data — they do not.

practices.practice: Muting only bites inside its own permission set group. If the same permission set is also assigned to the user directly, or lives in a second group, the muted permission is still live.
practices.specifics: Salesforce Help, Muting Permission Sets: "When you mute a permission in a permission set group, the muting affects only users assigned to the permission set group, not users assigned directly to a permission set outside of the permission set group" and "If the user is assigned the same permissions via a profile, permission set, or different permission set group, the user still has these permissions despite the muting permission set." One muting permission set per group maximum. Metadata type: MutingPermissionSet, suffix .mutingpermissionset, directory mutingpermissionsets, API v46.0+.
practices.why_it_matters: Muting is routinely sold as the way to enforce least privilege on a group. Auditors accept it. Then the same permission set is directly assigned somewhere and the control is void with no error and no log entry.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: View Setup and Configuration, Manage Session Permission Set Activations, Assign Permission Sets, or Manage Profiles and Permission Sets
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe muting as an org-wide 'deny' and say "add a muting permission set to remove Modify All Data from this user." It only mutes for members of that one group, and only if the permission is not granted by any other path.

practices.practice: Cap permission set group composition at 100 permission sets and design for the recalculation lifecycle — do not assign users while the group status is Outdated, Updating, or Failed.
practices.specifics: "You can add up to 100 permission sets to a permission set group." Status values are exactly Updated, Outdated, Updating, Failed. In Outdated: editing allowed, user assignment restricted, and assigned users "don't yet have the updated permissions." In Updating: neither assignment nor editing permitted. In Failed: editing allowed, assignment blocked. A documented cause of Failed is View Setup / Edit Setup / Create Setup object permissions on an included permission set (Salesforce Help 002723601). There is a manual Recalculate button on the group detail page.
practices.why_it_matters: A go-live that assigns a PSG mid-recalculation ships users with the pre-change permission set — the access looks granted in Setup and is not live at runtime.
practices.verbatim_error_string: The recalculation for Permission Set Group failed.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs treat PSG assignment as instantaneous and never mention the status field or the 100-permission-set ceiling. They then write deployment runbooks that assign users in the same step as the group edit.
practices.already_covered_by: skills/admin/permission-set-group-composition covers the lifecycle; the 100 limit is NOT present (grep for '100 permission set' returned no permission-domain hits)

practices.practice: Deploy the fields and objects BEFORE the permission set or profile that references them, in a separate deployment. Never bundle a new custom field and the permission set that grants it in one package.
practices.specifics: Salesforce validation emits: "In field: field - no CustomField named <xxx> found" on Profile and PermissionSet metadata types when the referenced field does not yet exist in the target org. Same pattern for other metadata types: "In field: field - no <metadata_type> named <xxx> found".
practices.why_it_matters: This is the single most common CI/CD failure in a permission-set-led model, and the failure message names the field rather than the permission set, so people go looking in the wrong component.
practices.verbatim_error_string: In field: field - no CustomField named <xxx> found
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs generate a single package.xml containing CustomField and PermissionSet together and say "deploy this." The dependency ordering is not expressible inside one package — it needs two deployments.
practices.already_covered_by: skills/devops/permission-set-deployment-ordering covers the ordering rule; grep shows the verbatim error string is absent from the entire skills/ tree

practices.practice: When a permission set will not assign, read the error for a LICENCE cause before touching permissions. Two distinct failures exist and they have different fixes.
practices.specifics: Failure 1 — user licence gate: "The user license doesn't allow the permission: <permission name>". Fix: assign the missing Permission Set License first (User record → Permission Set License Assignments → Edit Assignments). Classic case: a user on the free Salesforce Integration user licence needs the Salesforce API Integration PSL before any permission set will attach. Failure 2 — licensed-object gate: "This permission set contains an object that requires a license. Before continuing, assign the user to the related permission set license." Triggered by CPQ / Advanced Approvals licensed objects (Price Rule, Quote, Approval), and by View All Data / Modify All Data which sweep those licensed objects into scope.
practices.why_it_matters: Both errors read like a permission problem and are actually a licence-entitlement problem. Chasing the permission wastes hours and often ends in someone granting Modify All Data 'to make it work', which makes it worse.
practices.verbatim_error_string: This permission set contains an object that requires a license. Before continuing, assign the user to the related permission set license.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Salesforce API Integration PSL (for Salesforce Integration user licence); Salesforce CPQ License / Advanced Approvals License PSL
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs diagnose this as "the permission set is missing object permissions" and tell the user to add more permissions, when the fix is upstream at the Permission Set License Assignment related list. They also do not know that VAD/MAD in a permission set drags licensed managed-package objects into the licence check.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE for the verbatim strings; skills/admin/integration-user-management/SKILL.md:57 names the Salesforce API Integration licence but not the error

practices.practice: Set a permission set's License field to None unless you have a hard reason not to. A licence-scoped permission set can only ever contain permissions that licence entitles, and can only be assigned to users holding it.
practices.specifics: Salesforce Help, Create Permission Sets: "If the permission set is associated with a specific license, it can only include the permission and settings entitled by that license." With None: "the users must still be entitled to its included permissions via their user license or separately assigned permission set licenses." The License field is set at creation time and is not editable afterwards — the remedy is to recreate the permission set and re-assign every user.
practices.why_it_matters: An admin who picks 'Salesforce' on a permission set that later needs to serve Platform-licence users has to rebuild it from scratch and redo every assignment. Choosing None at creation costs nothing and preserves optionality.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Permission set License field (user licence or permission set licence, or None)
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs' scaffolded permission set metadata routinely sets a specific <license> value (usually Salesforce) because that is what most public examples show. They never flag that the field is a one-way door, and they never recommend None.

practices.practice: Enumerate exactly what still lives ONLY on the profile before promising a profile can be stripped to Minimum Access: login hours, login IP ranges, password policies, session settings, default app, page layout assignment, default record type, and the master record type.
practices.specifics: Official wording: "Page layout assignments are specified in profiles only, not in permission sets." "A user's default record type is specified in the user's profile" and "You can't specify a default record type in permission sets." On record types the split is asymmetric: "You can assign the master record type in profiles, but you can't include custom record types in the profile" vs "You can assign only custom record types in permission sets, not master record types."
practices.why_it_matters: The master/custom record type asymmetry is the part nobody knows. A permission set literally cannot grant Master, and a profile's recordTypeVisibilities node does not carry custom types the way people assume.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs list login hours and IP ranges (well known) but then say "record types can be assigned by permission set" without the Master/custom split, and they omit that the DEFAULT record type has no permission-set equivalent at all. A migration built on that advice silently changes which record type users get on New.
practices.already_covered_by: skills/admin/permission-sets-vs-profiles and skills/admin/permission-set-architecture both list login hours / IP / page layout; the master-vs-custom record type asymmetry and the default-record-type point are absent

practices.practice: Before moving users onto Minimum Access - Salesforce, assign page layouts on that profile for every object in scope. Permission sets restore field access but cannot restore the layout the fields render on.
practices.specifics: The Minimum Access - Salesforce profile ships with no page layout assignments configured. After the switch, users get the default layout for each object — so Account fields and related lists that the permission set grants FLS on simply do not appear. There is no error; the record page renders sparse.
practices.why_it_matters: This is the classic day-one-after-cutover incident in a profile-to-permission-set migration, and it presents as "the permission sets didn't work" when the permission sets worked perfectly.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs produce a clean migration runbook — strip the profile, build permission sets, reassign — and never include a page-layout assignment step, because FLS and layout assignment are separate mechanisms they treat as one. The user then reports missing fields and the LLM re-checks FLS, which is already correct.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — skills/admin/permission-sets-vs-profiles/references/gotchas.md:58 covers the 'cannot log in with no permission sets' variant; the page-layout rendering failure is not present

practices.practice: When bulk-loading or deploying object permissions, satisfy the CRUD dependency chain yourself. The Setup UI auto-enables dependent permissions; the API does not — it fails the row.
practices.specifics: Delete requires both Read and Edit; Edit requires Read; Create requires Read. Cross-object dependencies also exist (Account has many). Verbatim API failure format: "Permission Read for object depends on permission(s): Read Badges" — i.e. "Permission <X> for object depends on permission(s): <Y>".
practices.why_it_matters: A permission-set bulk load that works perfectly when clicked in Setup fails row-by-row through the API, and the error names a dependency object the operator has never heard of.
practices.verbatim_error_string: Permission Read for object depends on permission(s): Read Badges
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs generate ObjectPermissions upsert payloads with PermissionsDelete=true and PermissionsRead=false, or PermissionsEdit without PermissionsRead, because they treat the four flags as independent booleans. In the UI Salesforce silently fixes this; through Data Loader / Metadata API it hard-fails.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE — grep for the error string across skills/ returned nothing

practices.practice: Answer "who can see this field?" with SOQL over FieldPermissions using Parent.IsOwnedByProfile to split profile-sourced from permission-set-sourced grants — a profile's FLS is stored on a hidden PermissionSet record, not on the Profile object.
practices.specifics: Profile-owned FLS appears as FieldPermissions rows whose Parent is a PermissionSet with IsOwnedByProfile = true; Parent.Profile.Name resolves the profile, and is blank for real permission sets. Working queries: SELECT PermissionsRead, PermissionsEdit, Parent.Label, Parent.Id FROM FieldPermissions WHERE Field = 'Account.SLA__c' AND Parent.IsOwnedByProfile = false; and SELECT SObjectType, Field, PermissionsRead, PermissionsEdit, Parent.Profile.Name FROM FieldPermissions WHERE Parent.IsOwnedByProfile = true. Field values are fully qualified ('Account.SLA__c'), not bare API names.
practices.why_it_matters: There is no queryable Profile.FieldPermissions relationship. Without IsOwnedByProfile the answer is silently half the truth — you get permission sets only, or you double-count.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs write SELECT ... FROM FieldPermissions WHERE Field = 'SLA__c' (unqualified — returns nothing) or try to traverse from Profile directly. They also do not know that profile FLS materialises as an IsOwnedByProfile=true PermissionSet, so their audit query reports "no profile grants this field" on an org where profiles grant it everywhere.
practices.already_covered_by: PARTIAL — FieldPermissions is referenced in skills/apex/field-level-security-in-async-contexts and skills/admin/salesforce-object-queryability; the IsOwnedByProfile split and the fully-qualified Field format are not the documented pattern anywhere

practices.practice: Point admins at User Access Summary and its Access Granted By action instead of hand-reconstructing a user's access from profile plus N permission sets.
practices.specifics: Setup → Users → select a user → View Summary. Summer '24 surfaced user permissions, object permissions, field permissions, custom permissions, public groups and queues in one view. Winter '25 added the row-level Access Granted By action, which names the exact Profile / Permission Set / Permission Set Group that granted a specific object, field or permission.
practices.why_it_matters: "Why does this user have this?" is answerable in two clicks with a platform-native, always-current view. Reconstructing it by hand or by SOQL is slower and misses PSG-derived grants.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs answer "why does this user have Modify All Data" with a multi-query SOQL script over PermissionSetAssignment and ObjectPermissions, because they predate the feature. The script also misses the PSG source, which Access Granted By reports directly.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE — grep for 'User Access Summary' and 'Access Granted By' across skills/ returned zero hits

practices.practice: Never put a session-based permission set inside a permission set group. Group membership strips the activation requirement entirely.
practices.specifics: Salesforce Help, Permission Set Group Considerations: "If you include session-based permission sets in a permission set group, the permissions in them do not require session-based activation for users assigned to the group." Activation otherwise requires inserting a SessionPermSetActivation record (Apex or the Flow core action Activate Session-Based Permission Set), and the permission set must already be assigned to the user.
practices.why_it_matters: Session-based permission sets are the mechanism for just-in-time elevation. Folding one into a group to reduce assignment count converts a time-boxed elevation into a standing grant, silently, with the same Setup labels.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Manage Session Permission Set Activations
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs recommend "bundle the session-based permission set into the elevation PSG for cleaner administration." That specific advice destroys the control being implemented.

practices.practice: Use PermissionSetAssignment.ExpirationDate for time-boxed elevation instead of building a scheduled job or Flow that removes assignments.
practices.specifics: ExpirationDate is supported on PermissionSetAssignment for both permission sets and permission set groups. Enabled via the Setup release update 'Enable Permission Set Expiration and Enhanced UI' — voluntary in Summer '22, auto-enforced in Winter '23, now GA. Setup Audit Trail records the expiry.
practices.why_it_matters: Platform-native expiry cannot silently fail the way a scheduled Apex job or Flow can, and it is auditable.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs write a Scheduled Flow or a Schedulable Apex class to delete PermissionSetAssignment rows at a cutoff date, because the ExpirationDate field is not in their default mental model of the object.

practices.practice: Reach for a custom permission plus $Permission, not a hardcoded user/profile ID, whenever a validation rule, formula, Flow or Apex class needs a bypass or a feature gate.
practices.specifics: Validation rule / formula syntax: $Permission.<API_Name> (e.g. NOT($Permission.Approve_Deals)). Apex: FeatureManagement.checkPermission('Delete_Tasks') returns Boolean. Flow: $Permission is a global resource usable in entry criteria formulas, formula resources and Decision elements. Custom permissions are assignable only via permission sets and permission set groups.
practices.why_it_matters: Hardcoded IDs are the classic source of 'works in sandbox, fails in production'. Custom permissions move the bypass list into a permission set an admin can delegate.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Custom permission, assignable only through a permission set
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs write $User.Id = '005xx...' or $Profile.Name = 'System Administrator' in validation rules. They also sometimes claim $Permission is unsupported in Flow, which is false.

practices.practice: Prefer per-object View All Records / Modify All Records over the org-wide View All Data / Modify All Data whenever the requirement is scoped to one object.
practices.specifics: Both families bypass sharing rules and org-wide defaults. View All Data / Modify All Data are system permissions that reach every object and every app in the org; View All Records / Modify All Records are object permissions scoped to one sObject. Salesforce's own guidance: they "can be better alternatives to the View All Data and Modify All Data permissions." Neither family overrides FLS.
practices.why_it_matters: MAD on a permission set also drags licensed managed-package objects into the permission set licence check (the CPQ error above), so the org-wide form causes assignment failures the object-scoped form does not.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: View All Data / Modify All Data (system permission); View All Records / Modify All Records (object permission)
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs use "View All" and "View All Data" interchangeably in the same answer, and default to the org-wide one for a single-object requirement. Since Salesforce renamed the object-level pair to View All Records / Modify All Records, models also emit stale labels.
practices.already_covered_by: skills/security/record-access-troubleshooting (SKILL.md and gotchas.md mention View All Records / Modify All Records)

practices.practice: Retrieve profiles with every dependent metadata type in package.xml, or accept that the retrieved .profile is incomplete — and that deploying it can remove permissions in the target.
practices.specifics: Metadata API retrieve() returns .profile files that "only include security settings for the other metadata types referenced in the retrieve request" — with the exception of user permissions, IP address ranges and login hours, which are always retrieved. On deploy, an omitted node is interpreted as remove-this-permission in the target org. The same overwrite semantics apply to PermissionSet from API v40 onwards.
practices.why_it_matters: A retrieve that names only <types>Profile</types> produces a profile file missing all object and field permissions. Deploying that file strips them from the target with no error and no warning.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs write a package.xml with <name>Profile</name> alone and tell the user to retrieve and diff. The resulting file looks plausible, contains almost nothing, and destroys permissions when deployed. This is a data-loss-class error and the deployment reports Succeeded.
practices.already_covered_by: skills/devops/permission-set-deployment-ordering/references/gotchas.md:7 covers the PermissionSet overwrite; the Profile retrieve-incompleteness rule is not stated

practices.practice: Delegated admins can only assign profiles, roles, permission sets and permission set groups explicitly listed in their delegated group. Assignable Permission Set Groups is a separate related list from Assignable Permission Sets.
practices.specifics: Configure via Setup → Delegated Administration → delegated group → the Assignable Profiles / Assignable Permission Sets / Assignable Permission Set Groups / Roles and Subordinates related lists. Optional 'Enable Group for Login Access' checkbox permits login-as for users in the delegated roles. Profiles carrying Modify All Data cannot be made delegable. Delegated administration requires View Setup and Configuration on the delegated admin.
practices.why_it_matters: Delegated administration is the safe alternative to handing out Manage Users. Getting the boundary wrong either blocks the delegate entirely or hands them an escalation path.
practices.verbatim_error_string: You can't disable "View Setup and configuration" in this profile because it's assigned to a user who is a delegated administrator
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: View Setup and Configuration (required on the delegated admin); Customize Application to configure delegation
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs say delegated admins "can manage users in their role hierarchy" and stop there — they omit that every assignable artefact must be enumerated, and they do not know PSGs became delegable as a separate list. They also cannot explain the View Setup and Configuration lock, which blocks profile edits until the user is removed from the delegated group.
practices.already_covered_by: skills/admin/delegated-administration exists; grep shows the verbatim View Setup and Configuration error string is absent from skills/

practices.practice: Treat Assign Permission Sets and Manage Profiles and Permission Sets as privilege-escalation permissions and never grant them together outside a break-glass, time-boxed permission set.
practices.specifics: A user holding Manage Profiles and Permission Sets can add Modify All Data to a permission set; holding Assign Permission Sets they can then assign it to themselves. Neither action requires Modify All Data to start with. The permission-set-level alternative is delegated administration with an enumerated assignable list.
practices.why_it_matters: This pair is the shortest self-escalation path in the platform and it does not appear in any 'admin permissions' checklist because neither permission is individually alarming.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Assign Permission Sets; Manage Profiles and Permission Sets
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs hand these two permissions to a 'Power User' or 'Support Admin' permission set as a matter of course, describing them as needed for day-to-day user administration. They do not flag the compound escalation.

practices.practice: Grant tab visibility and app assignment deliberately when moving to a permission-set-led model — a permission granted without the tab produces 'I have access but cannot find it' tickets.
practices.specifics: Tabs became editable from the Permission Set summary page in Summer '25, alongside inline editing of object and field permissions from that list. Default assigned apps remain a profile setting.
practices.why_it_matters: Object permissions and tab visibility are separate switches; permission sets carry tab settings but the default app does not move with them.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs generate a permission set with objectPermissions and fieldPermissions and no tabSettings, then cannot explain why the user sees nothing in the app launcher.
practices.already_covered_by: skills/admin/permission-set-group-composition/references/well-architected.md:27 flags the 'have the permission but cannot see the tab' failure

practices.practice: Scope permission set group recalculation cost before composing large groups — complexity, not just count, drives the recalculation window.
practices.specifics: Salesforce names the drivers explicitly: "A large number of included permission sets in the permission set group. Complex included permission sets, which can result from a large number of enabled object permissions, field permissions, Apex classes, Visualforce pages, and other settings." Recalculation "can time out or take a long time to complete" including where included permission sets "don't have a required license."
practices.why_it_matters: A PSG built by piling every micro-permission-set together can exceed the recalculation window and land in Failed on every deployment, blocking all user assignment for that group.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs advocate maximally granular permission sets ('one per capability') and then compose 60-80 of them into a persona PSG, presenting it as best practice. Nothing in their answer accounts for recalculation cost or the 100 ceiling.
practices.already_covered_by: skills/admin/permission-set-group-composition (recalculation lifecycle covered); the named cost drivers and timeout risk are not

practices.practice: Distinguish user licence, feature licence and permission set licence precisely, because only one of the three is assignable per user and only one is assignable in bulk via permission sets.
practices.specifics: User licence: exactly one per user, sets the baseline of accessible features, cannot be exceeded by any permission set. Feature licence: one or more per user, extends beyond the user licence. Permission set licence (PSL, sObject PermissionSetLicense): incremental per-user entitlement, assigned via the Permission Set License Assignments related list on the User record, and often a prerequisite before a permission set can be assigned at all.
practices.why_it_matters: The 'The user license doesn't allow the permission' failure is always a user-licence ceiling or a missing PSL, never a permission set defect. Knowing which of the three is missing determines whether the fix is a click or a purchase order.
practices.verbatim_error_string: The user license doesn't allow the permission: <permission name>
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: PermissionSetLicense assignment on the User record
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs use 'feature license' and 'permission set license' as synonyms, and tell users to 'enable the feature license in the permission set' — which is not a place feature licences live. They also assume a permission set can grant a PSL; assigning a permission set that carries a PSL does grant it, but a permission set with License=None cannot.
practices.already_covered_by: skills/architect/license-optimization-strategy and skills/architect/org-edition-and-feature-licensing exist; the three-way distinction with the verbatim error is not grounded in the permissions-domain skills
