areas.area: Objects, relationships, record types, layouts (custom object design, master-detail vs lookup, junction objects, external objects, record types, page layouts / Dynamic Forms / compact layouts, list views and search layouts, object limits)

practices.practice: Never propose a queue, an ownership-based sharing rule, manual sharing, or an owner-based assignment rule on the detail side of a master-detail relationship — the detail object has no OwnerId field at all.
practices.specifics: Official Object Reference: "Detail records in master-detail relationships cannot have sharing rules, manual sharing, or queues"; the detail record's Owner is automatically the owner of its master. OWD on the detail object is forced to Controlled by Parent and is not editable. Reports grouped by Owner, Assignment Rules, Omni-Channel queue routing, and `OwnerId` in SOQL all fail to compile or return nothing on a master-detail child.
practices.why_it_matters: An entire routing/assignment design silently has no landing surface. The only remedy is converting master-detail → lookup, which requires first deleting AND erasing every roll-up summary on the parent, and existing owner data cannot be recovered because it was never stored.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked to "route Inspection__c records to the Field Ops queue", an LLM happily writes an Assignment Rule / Omni-Channel queue design plus `UPDATE Inspection__c SET OwnerId = :queueId`, without checking that Inspection__c is the detail side of a master-detail to Account. It treats OwnerId as universally present on every sObject.

practices.practice: Set the master-detail field's Sharing Setting deliberately — the default requires Read/Write on the master to create, edit, or delete a detail record, which is stricter than most people assume.
practices.specifics: Metadata API `CustomField.writeRequiresMasterRead`: `false` (the default) = "Requires Read/Write access on the master record"; `true` = "Allows users with Read access to create, edit, or delete child records" (UI label: Sharing Setting → "Read Only" vs "Read/Write"). On a junction object with two masters, "the most restrictive access from the two parents is enforced."
practices.why_it_matters: Users with Read-only access to an Account cannot log a child record against it under the default. Admins chase this as a phantom FLS/profile bug for days because the object permissions and FLS all look correct.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM debugging "user can see the Account but can't create the child record" checks Object CRUD, FLS, OWD, sharing rules and validation rules, and never mentions `writeRequiresMasterRead` / the Sharing Setting on the master-detail field itself. The field is invisible in profile and permission-set metadata, so its own retrieval strategy never surfaces it.

practices.practice: Do not tell anyone they can configure cascade-delete on a lookup relationship in Setup — the option is off by default org-wide, only Salesforce Support can enable it, and it deliberately bypasses sharing.
practices.specifics: Metadata API `deleteConstraint` accepts `SetNull` (default, clears the field), `Restrict`, and `Cascade`. The Setup UI exposes only the first two on a lookup; `Cascade` requires an org preference ("Enable cascade delete on custom lookup relationships") enabled by a Salesforce Support case. Salesforce's own wording: "A cascade-delete bypasses security and sharing settings, which means users can delete records when the target lookup record is deleted even if they don't have access to the records."
practices.why_it_matters: A design that assumes lookup cascade-delete is a checkbox stalls at build time waiting on a Support case; and if it IS enabled, a delete escalates into data loss across records the deleting user could not even read.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked "how do I make child records delete when the parent is deleted, without master-detail?", an LLM writes "set the lookup's delete behavior to 'Delete this record also'" as if it were a third radio button in the field wizard. It never mentions the Support case or the sharing bypass.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Org preference "Enable cascade delete on custom lookup relationships", available only via a Salesforce Support case; not self-serve in any edition.

practices.practice: When a lookup uses Restrict delete, expect and match this exact runtime failure — it surfaces identically in the UI, Data Loader, and sandbox seeding tools, and it names the child object's plural label.
practices.specifics: The platform returns `DELETE_FAILED` with message: "Your attempt to delete <ParentRecordName> could not be completed because it is associated with the following <child object plural label>.: <ChildRecordName>" (real capture: "Your attempt to delete Sample Account for Entitlements could not be completed because it is associated with the following entitlements.: Sample Entitlement"). Only the first few blocking children are named.
practices.why_it_matters: This string is the single most common blocker for sandbox data-seeding and org-cleanup jobs. Recognising it immediately points at a `deleteConstraint=Restrict` lookup rather than a trigger or validation rule.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Given this error, an LLM typically blames a `before delete` Apex trigger or a validation rule and starts grepping Apex. It does not recognise `DELETE_FAILED` + "associated with the following" as the platform's built-in restrict-delete constraint, which lives in field metadata and not in code.
practices.verbatim_error_string: Your attempt to delete Sample Account for Entitlements could not be completed because it is associated with the following entitlements.: Sample Entitlement

practices.practice: Check the master-detail blocklist before designing a parent-child model against a standard object — eight standard objects can never be the master, and no standard object can ever be the detail of a custom object.
practices.specifics: Verbatim from the Object Reference: "you can't create a master-detail relationship where these standard objects are the primary object. BusinessHours, Idea, Lead, OrderItem, PriceBook2, Product2, QuoteLineItem, User". Separately: "the standard object can't be on the detail side of a relationship with a custom object." Consequence: no native roll-up summary is ever possible onto Product2, Lead, User, PriceBook2, OrderItem or QuoteLineItem.
practices.why_it_matters: Data models that put a junction object under Product2 with master-detail (the classic "Account_Product__c" pattern) cannot be built as drawn, and the discovery happens at build time after the ERD is signed off.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs produce the canonical many-to-many recipe as "Account__c (Master-Detail to Account) + Product__c (Master-Detail to Product2)". The second leg is impossible. The corpus itself ships this exact wrong recipe (see stale_or_wrong_found).

practices.practice: Quote the real relationship ceilings: 2 master-detail per object, 40 total relationship fields per object (raisable to a hard maximum of 50 via Salesforce Support), and 3 levels of custom detail.
practices.specifics: Max 2 master-detail relationships per custom object. Relationships (master-detail + lookup combined) default to 40 per object; Salesforce Support can raise this, with a hard-coded ceiling of 50. Master-detail hierarchies support up to 3 levels of custom detail. Salesforce's documented guidance is to not exceed 10,000 child records under a single master-detail parent (ownership-skew / lock-contention threshold).
practices.why_it_matters: "40 is a hard limit" causes teams to redesign around a junction object when a Support case would have bought them ten more slots; conversely, planning for 50 without opening the case blocks the deploy.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs state "40 relationship fields per object, hard limit" with no mention that Support raises it to 50, and never mention the 3-level custom-detail cap or the 10,000-child guidance at all. The corpus repeats the same incomplete framing in four places.
practices.already_covered_by: admin/lookup-and-relationship-design (40 only, wrongly called a hard limit; 50/Support and 3-level cap absent)
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Raising the per-object relationship limit from 40 to a maximum of 50 requires a Salesforce Support case; not self-serve.

practices.practice: Roll-up summary is not "master-detail only" — three standard lookup relationships support it natively, and the per-object ceiling is 25 (raisable via Support).
practices.specifics: Roll-up summary fields are supported on all custom master-detail parents PLUS three standard exceptions: Account ← Opportunity, Opportunity ← OpportunityLineItem (Opportunity Product), and Campaign ← CampaignMember. Default limit is 25 roll-up summary fields per object; Salesforce Support can raise it. Deleted roll-up summary fields still consume the 25 until erased. Campaign roll-ups are not recalculated when a lead or contact is deleted.
practices.why_it_matters: Teams add a managed-package or Apex rollup framework to count Opportunities on Account when a native roll-up summary already works — extra CPU, extra lock contention, extra deployment surface, for nothing.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs assert the absolute rule "native roll-up summary fields require a master-detail relationship" with no exceptions, and immediately recommend DLRS or Apex. The corpus repeats this absolute in apex/cross-object-formula-and-rollup-performance and apex/npsp-custom-rollups.
practices.already_covered_by: architect/sales-cloud-architecture (25-per-object limit on Account only; the three standard lookup exceptions and the Support raise are absent, and two skills state the opposite)
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Raising the 25 roll-up-summary-fields-per-object limit requires a Salesforce Support case.

practices.practice: Before promising a master-detail → lookup conversion, check that every roll-up summary on the parent has been deleted AND erased from Deleted Fields — otherwise the Change Field Type button simply does not render.
practices.specifics: Any roll-up summary field on the master that traverses the relationship blocks conversion. Deleting the roll-up is not enough: a soft-deleted field sits in Setup → Object → Fields → Deleted Fields for 15 days and still counts, so you must click Erase. Only then does "Change Field Type" appear on the relationship field. The reverse conversion (lookup → master-detail) requires every child record to have a non-null value in the lookup, and permanently discards the child's OwnerId, manual shares, and any queue membership.
practices.why_it_matters: The failure mode is a missing button with no error message — pure silent failure. Teams file Support cases believing conversion is blocked by their edition.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM says "delete the roll-up summary fields, then convert." It omits the Erase step entirely, so the user follows the instructions, sees no Change Field Type button, and concludes the guidance was wrong. It also never warns that lookup → master-detail destroys owner and manual-share data.
practices.already_covered_by: admin/lookup-and-relationship-design (states roll-ups block conversion; the Erase step and the OwnerId destruction are absent)

practices.practice: Count deleted fields against your limits — a soft-deleted custom field keeps consuming the 500/800 custom-field cap, the 40-relationship cap, and the 25-roll-up cap for 15 days unless you erase it.
practices.specifics: After deletion a custom field and its data are retained for up to 15 days, then hard-deleted. During that window "the field counts against the maximum number of custom fields allowed in your org until it's permanently deleted", and "a deleted custom roll-up summary field counts against the maximum number of roll-up summary fields". The Erase button on Setup → Object → Fields → Deleted Fields removes it immediately.
practices.why_it_matters: An object-cleanup sprint that deletes 60 fields to make room for a new build finds it still cannot create field 501 for two more weeks. This is a schedule-breaking surprise mid-release.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM asked "we're at the 500-field limit, what do we do?" says "delete unused fields" and stops. It does not know deletion is a soft delete that changes nothing about the limit for 15 days, so the user's remediation appears to do nothing.

practices.practice: Turn on Allow reparenting explicitly at master-detail creation if the child will ever move parents — and price the lock cost, because reparenting write-locks the old parent, the new parent, and the child.
practices.specifics: Metadata API `CustomField.reparentableMasterDetail`, default `false`, available since API v25.0; UI checkbox "Allow reparenting". With it off, the master-detail field is read-only after insert and any attempt to change it fails. With it on, a single reparenting DML takes write locks on old master + new master + child, which in a 3-level chain (LineItem → Opportunity → Account) locks 4+ rows across two object trees.
practices.why_it_matters: Bulk realignment jobs (territory merges, account consolidation) either fail outright because reparenting was never enabled, or succeed and then throw UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW at scale.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs state flatly "master-detail children cannot be reparented" — true only of the default. They miss `reparentableMasterDetail` entirely, so they recommend delete-and-recreate (which loses record Ids, audit fields, Chatter feed, and files) instead of a one-checkbox change.
practices.already_covered_by: flow/flow-record-locking-and-contention (lock-contention side is well covered; the metadata flag name, the default, and the design-time decision are not covered in any object-design skill)

practices.practice: On a junction object, create the master-detail you want to control ownership, sharing and branding FIRST — the first master-detail is the primary and it is not a cosmetic choice.
practices.specifics: The first master-detail relationship created on a junction object is the primary: it supplies the junction record's Owner, its sharing, its Division, and the detail/edit page colour and icon. The second is secondary. If you later delete or convert the primary master-detail to a lookup, the secondary master automatically becomes primary and the junction's ownership and sharing silently re-derive from a different parent. Sharing on a junction enforces the most restrictive access of the two masters.
practices.why_it_matters: Field-creation order — normally irrelevant — permanently determines who owns and who can see every junction record. Re-ordering later means deleting a master-detail relationship, which cascades.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs give the junction recipe as "add two master-detail fields" with no statement that order matters, and no mention of primary vs secondary. Asked "who owns a junction record?", they usually say "the user who created it" — wrong; it is the primary master's owner.

practices.practice: Choose Auto Number for the Record Name only if you accept that the Name can never be an upsert key and can never be written by a data load.
practices.specifics: Auto Number fields are not createable and not updateable, so they are deliberately excluded from Data Loader's External ID picklist for upsert ("Auto-Number not available as external ID in Data Loader", KB 000385426). Loading a CSV with a Name column into an Auto-Number-named object fails or silently ignores the column. The documented workaround is to temporarily change the Record Name data type to Text, load, then change back — during which window NEW records receive no name value at all, and on switching back you must manually set the starting number.
practices.why_it_matters: Migrations that must preserve legacy record numbers (case numbers, work-order numbers, contract numbers) discover mid-cutover that the target Name field is unwritable. The workaround has a live-org blast radius.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM designing a migration maps the legacy identifier straight to `Name` on an object it just told the user to create with an Auto Number record name, and separately suggests upserting on Name. Both are impossible simultaneously. The correct answer is a separate Text field marked External ID + Unique alongside the Auto Number Name.
practices.already_covered_by: admin/object-creation-and-design (covers Auto Number as a design choice and its data-quality upside; the not-createable / not-upsertable / Data-Loader-excluded consequence is absent)

practices.practice: Load master-detail children only after their parents exist, and map the parent Id column — an empty master-detail column produces REQUIRED_FIELD_MISSING even though the field is not marked required anywhere in Setup.
practices.specifics: Every master-detail field is implicitly required on the detail record and cannot be left blank; the API returns `REQUIRED_FIELD_MISSING: Required fields are missing: [Parent__c]`. Salesforce's own guidance: "before you insert child records, you must first insert the parent records." Unlike a lookup, there is no "leave blank and fix later" path, and no validation rule or Setup screen shows the field as required.
practices.why_it_matters: This is the number-one master-detail data-load failure. Because the requiredness is structural rather than declared, pre-flight checks that scan for `required=true` fields do not catch it.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Given `REQUIRED_FIELD_MISSING`, an LLM inspects the object's field metadata for `required: true`, finds the master-detail field reported as `nillable: false` but not `required`, and concludes the error is spurious or blames a validation rule. It also generates load-order plans that insert children and parents in the same batch.
practices.verbatim_error_string: REQUIRED_FIELD_MISSING: Required fields are missing: [Parent__c]

practices.practice: State the custom-field ceiling by edition, not as one number: 100 (Professional), 500 (Enterprise), 800 hard maximum — and remember relationship fields and roll-ups consume it too.
practices.specifics: Custom fields allowed per object: Professional 100, Enterprise 500, with 800 as the hard maximum for most objects across all editions. The 40 relationship fields and 25 roll-up summary fields are sub-limits carved out of that same custom-field allocation, and soft-deleted fields keep consuming all three for 15 days. Custom objects per edition: Contact Manager 5, Group 50, Professional 50, Enterprise 200, Performance/Unlimited 2,000, Developer 400 — including managed-package objects.
practices.why_it_matters: A very wide object is not just a style problem: it is a hard wall that blocks the next release, and "we're on Enterprise so we get 800" is wrong by 300 fields.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs quote a single figure — usually 500 or 800 — with no edition qualifier, and never note that relationship and roll-up fields draw from the same pool.
practices.already_covered_by: admin/custom-field-creation (has a per-edition table); admin/object-creation-and-design (per-edition custom-object table)
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Enterprise Edition is capped at 500 custom fields per object; the 800 ceiling requires Performance/Unlimited (and, for custom objects beyond the edition cap, a Salesforce Support case — KB 000386653).

practices.practice: Treat enabling Person Accounts as a one-way door, and confirm at least one business Account record type exists before enabling it.
practices.specifics: "After Person Accounts is enabled, it can't be disabled." Prerequisite: at least one record type must already exist on Account for business accounts; enabling creates a Person Account record type automatically. From that point Account carries two disjoint record-type families whose picklists, layouts, and Contact behaviour differ, and every downstream Account automation must branch on `IsPersonAccount`.
practices.why_it_matters: This is the most consequential irreversible switch in the object/record-type territory, and it is thrown in a sandbox "just to try it" and then propagated by a refresh policy nobody reviewed.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked "should we use Person Accounts?", LLMs weigh B2C fit versus the Account/Contact model but describe it as a configuration choice that can be revisited. They rarely lead with "it cannot be disabled" or with the record-type prerequisite.
practices.already_covered_by: admin/record-types-and-page-layouts (references/gotchas.md has a dedicated Person Account record-type gotcha); data/person-accounts exists
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Person Accounts must be enabled by Salesforce (Support case / self-service enablement depending on edition) and requires at least one pre-existing business Account record type.

practices.practice: Stop telling clients that record-type and page-layout assignment are moving off Profiles — Salesforce cancelled the Permissions-in-Profiles retirement, and page-layout assignment is explicitly not coming to permission sets.
practices.specifics: The retirement of permissions on Profiles, originally scheduled to begin enforcement in Spring '26, was cancelled indefinitely (Salesforce Help KB 003834041, 2026). Default record type, page layout assignment, login hours, IP ranges, and default app remain on Profiles. Salesforce has stated it will not invest in bringing page layout assignment to permission sets because the forward path is Lightning App Builder + Dynamic Forms.
practices.why_it_matters: Migration roadmaps written against the announced Spring '26 deadline are now planning work that will never be forced, and the specific assumption "record type assignment will live in permission sets" is false.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Models trained before mid-2026 confidently state that permissions on Profiles retire in Spring '26 and advise moving record-type assignment into permission sets now. That is a retired plan being described as current, and it drives real migration budgets.
practices.already_covered_by: admin/permission-sets-vs-profiles and admin/permission-set-architecture mention profile retirement — verify whether they describe it as active or cancelled before absorbing anything else

practices.practice: Size a Dynamic Forms migration against the component caps: 100 fields per Field Section column and 100 sections per region — anything past that is silently dropped during import.
practices.specifics: "You are limited to 100 fields in a Field Section component column and to only 100 sections for each region. If you exceed these numbers, the remaining fields and sections are excluded when importing fields from a dynamic page layout." No warning, no error, no diff report — the fields simply do not arrive on the new page.
practices.why_it_matters: On the very wide objects that most motivate a Dynamic Forms migration (400+ field Accounts), the migration wizard is exactly where fields go missing, and the loss is discovered by users, not by the admin.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe the "Upgrade Now / Migrate to Dynamic Forms" wizard as a lossless one-click conversion and produce a migration checklist with no field-count reconciliation step. They do not know the caps exist, so they never tell the admin to diff the field list before and after.
practices.already_covered_by: admin/dynamic-forms-migration (has the migration workflow and a verification step, but no numeric caps — grep for "100 fields"/"100 sections" returns nothing)

practices.practice: Distinguish field-level from section-level visibility timing in Dynamic Forms: field rules re-evaluate live as the user types, section rules only re-evaluate on Save.
practices.specifics: Field component visibility rules are evaluated continuously during edit, so a field can appear or disappear mid-keystroke. Field Section component visibility rules are evaluated on record save, so a newly-qualifying section does not appear until after the user saves. Separately, dependent picklists ignore visibility rules and still appear in the View All Dependencies list.
practices.why_it_matters: A "show the Approval section when Status = Submitted" rule appears broken to the business because the section stays hidden while the user is still on the page. Admins rebuild the rule repeatedly instead of redesigning around the save boundary.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs treat field and section visibility rules as interchangeable and recommend section-level rules for progressive-disclosure UX ("reveal the shipping section once Type = Physical"), which is precisely the pattern that does not work until save.

practices.practice: Order compact-layout fields by priority: Lightning uses only the first 7, mobile up to 10, and any field the user cannot access is skipped with the next field promoted in its place.
practices.specifics: A compact layout accepts a maximum of 10 fields. The Lightning Experience highlights panel renders the first 7; the Salesforce mobile app renders up to 10, varying by screen width, record page, and user permissions. "If a user doesn't have access to one of the fields that you assign to a compact layout, the next field on the layout is used." The first field becomes the record title.
practices.why_it_matters: The FLS-skip rule means two users on the same record see different highlight fields — a support-ticket generator that has nothing to do with the layout being wrong.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs pack 10 fields in and assume all render on desktop. Even when they know the cap, they miss the FLS-substitution behaviour, so they cannot explain why one user sees Amount in the highlights panel and another sees Close Date.
practices.already_covered_by: admin/list-views-and-compact-layouts (references/llm-anti-patterns.md already states the 7-desktop / 10-maximum split correctly; the FLS-substitution rule is absent)

practices.practice: Grant Manage Shared List Views, not Manage Public List Views, when a user only needs to share their own list views — the granular permission shipped in Summer '26.
practices.specifics: New user permission "Manage Shared List Views" (Summer '26 / release 262) lets a user share their personal list views with roles, public groups, and territories they are a member of. Previously the only option was "Manage Public List Views", which grants the ability to edit or delete ANY public list view in the org. Assign either via permission set or profile. A separate org setting, User Interface Settings → "Shared list view editing", lets users without the permission edit filters and names on views shared with them.
practices.why_it_matters: Orgs have been over-granting Manage Public List Views to power users for a decade precisely because there was no alternative — that is now an avoidable least-privilege violation with a named replacement.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked "how do I let a team lead share a list view with their team without making them an admin?", an LLM answers "grant Manage Public List Views" — the exact over-grant Salesforce just shipped a fix for — or says it is impossible and suggests the admin create the view instead.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: "Manage Shared List Views" user permission (Summer '26, release 262), assignable via permission set or profile; the legacy alternative is the much broader "Manage Public List Views".

practices.practice: Say plainly that sharing a list view grants zero record access — the recipient sees the view and an empty or partial result set.
practices.specifics: List view visibility (Private / shared with groups, roles, territories / visible to all users) is UI metadata only. Rows returned are still filtered by OWD, role hierarchy, sharing rules, and manual shares. A user granted a list view over Private-OWD records they do not own sees the view in the picker and zero rows, with no message explaining why.
practices.why_it_matters: This is a pure silent-failure mode: the configuration succeeded, the user has the view, and the data is missing. It is routinely misdiagnosed as a filter bug.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked "give the EMEA team visibility of EMEA opportunities", an LLM creates a filtered list view and shares it with the EMEA public group, and reports the requirement as met. Nobody in EMEA can see a single row until a sharing rule is added.
practices.already_covered_by: admin/list-views-and-compact-layouts (SKILL.md line 68 states UX configuration does not change record access — the empty-list-view symptom and the sharing-rule remedy are not spelled out)

practices.practice: When a lookup field shows the wrong secondary value, check the Lookup Dialogs search layout column order and the field type of column 2 — some field types silently fall through to column 3.
practices.specifics: The Lightning lookup field displays the record Name plus the second column of the object's Lookup Dialogs search layout. Not every field type renders as that secondary value: an Email field placed in column 2 is not displayed and the third column is used instead. Encrypted, formula, lookup, and roll-up summary fields cannot be added to search layouts at all. Separately, Search Filter Fields on the parent's search layout govern which fields the lookup dialog can be searched by.
practices.why_it_matters: Users cannot disambiguate two identically-named records, and admins configure the field they wanted into column 2 and watch nothing change — with no error at any point.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs conflate the Search Results layout with the Lookup Dialogs layout, and tell the admin to "add the field to the search layout" without specifying which of the several search layouts, which column position matters, or that certain field types are silently skipped.
practices.already_covered_by: admin/related-list-configuration (SKILL.md line 97 covers Search Filter Fields governing lookup-dialog searchability — the display-column behaviour and the field-type fall-through are absent)

practices.practice: Bound an external-object design by the org ceiling of 100 external objects and the OData callout budget before promising a Salesforce Connect solution.
practices.specifics: Maximum 100 external objects per org. Salesforce Connect is a paid add-on licence, not a platform feature. OData callouts are capped at 10,000 per hour for Enterprise, Performance and Unlimited Editions (higher on request); a High Data Volume option on the External Data Source skips row-count rate limits. A report including an external object fetches at most 2,000 records for the primary object.
practices.why_it_matters: A virtualisation design that mirrors 150 tables from an ERP cannot be built at all, and the 2,000-row report cap makes external objects unusable for the analytics use case they are most often proposed for.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs present Salesforce Connect as included platform functionality and never mention the add-on licence, the 100-object ceiling, or the 2,000-row reporting cap. They then recommend it as the reporting layer over an external warehouse — the one thing it is worst at.
practices.already_covered_by: data/external-data-and-big-objects and data/data-virtualization-patterns cover the 100-callout-per-transaction limit well; grep shows no hit for "10,000 OData" or the 100-external-objects-per-org ceiling anywhere in the corpus
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Salesforce Connect is a separately purchased add-on licence; without it External Data Sources of type OData/cross-org cannot be created.

practices.practice: Never model an external object with master-detail — the only legal relationship types are Lookup, External Lookup, and Indirect Lookup, and Indirect Lookup requires the Salesforce-side key field to be both External ID and Unique.
practices.specifics: Per the Object Reference: external objects support "only lookup, external lookup, and indirect lookup relationships". Indirect Lookup (external object → Salesforce object) matches an external field value against a Salesforce field that must be marked External ID and Unique. External Lookup points a Salesforce object at an external object via its External ID standard field. External objects additionally support no roll-up summary fields, no formula fields, no triggers, no validation rules, no field history tracking, and no Notes & Attachments.
practices.why_it_matters: The whole point of an external-object model is the relationship back into Salesforce data; getting the direction or the key-field requirement wrong means the related list never populates and the cause is not surfaced.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs propose "a standard Lookup from Contact to the external object" or a master-detail for cascade behaviour, and omit the External ID + Unique prerequisite on the matching field, so the Indirect Lookup cannot even be saved.
practices.already_covered_by: integration/salesforce-connect-external-objects/references/llm-anti-patterns.md (Anti-Pattern 3 covers the indirect-lookup requirement and the three relationship types); the External ID + Unique prerequisite is not stated
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Salesforce Connect add-on licence.

skills/admin/object-creation-and-design/SKILL.md:80 — 'The **Record Name** field type is also permanent after save: either **Text** ... or **Auto Number**'. False. The Record Name data type is editable at any time via Setup → Object Manager → <Object> → Fields & Relationships → Name → Edit; switching Auto Number → Text is in fact Salesforce's own documented technique for overriding auto-number values (help.salesforce.com sf.modifying_standard_auto-number_fields.htm). The same line is echoed in the Review Checklist at :215 ('Record Name type (Text vs Auto Number) chosen intentionally — cannot be changed after save.'). Note the real caveats worth keeping: while the field is Text no new record receives a number, and on switching back the starting number must be reset manually.

skills/admin/object-creation-and-design/SKILL.md:89 — 'Track Field History | ... | History records are retained for 18 months. Cannot be turned off.' This sentence is garbled and the sharing claim is unsupported: the Hierarchical relationship type is a self-lookup on User used for manager chains and for approval-process/manager-visibility features; it does not drive `CustomField__c` sharing.

areas.area: Validation rules, picklists, duplicate management, approvals, assignment/auto-response rules, and the full record-save Order of Execution

practices.practice: State the record-save Order of Execution as 20 documented steps, and place before-save record-triggered flows at step 3 and all Apex before triggers at step 4 — they are separately ordered, not interleaved.
practices.specifics: Official sequence: 3 = 'Executes record-triggered flows that are configured to run before the record is saved'; 4 = 'Executes all before triggers'; 5 = system validation + custom validation rules; 6 = duplicate rules; 7 = save (no commit); 8 = after triggers; 9 = assignment rules; 10 = auto-response rules; 11 = workflow rules; 12 = escalation rules; 13 = Process Builder / workflow-launched flows (no guaranteed order); 14 = after-save record-triggered flows; 15 = entitlement rules; 16 = parent roll-up summary; 17 = grandparent roll-up summary; 18 = Criteria Based Sharing evaluation; 19 = commit; 20 = post-commit (email, async Apex, asynchronous paths in record-triggered flows).
practices.why_it_matters: Almost every 'my field got overwritten' / 'my flow saw stale data' declarative bug is resolved by naming the exact step. Getting steps 3 vs 4 wrong sends the fix to the wrong tool.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs (and this repo's current skill) say before-save flows and before triggers 'run at the same step in undefined relative order.' The docs give them distinct, ordered steps: the flow runs first, then the trigger. So a before trigger CAN deterministically overwrite a before-save flow's value, and an admin told 'the order is undefined' will build a fragile workaround instead of the correct one. LLMs also routinely produce a '16-step' or '18-step' list that drops Criteria Based Sharing evaluation entirely.

practices.practice: When a workflow field update fires, do NOT assume validation rules, flows, duplicate rules, Process Builder processes, or escalation rules re-run. Only system validation and before/after update triggers run again.
practices.specifics: Step 11 of the order of execution. Verbatim doc text: 'Custom validation rules, flows, duplicate rules, processes built with Process Builder, and escalation rules aren't run again.' Before update triggers and after update triggers execute one more time.
practices.why_it_matters: This is the single most common source of 'the workflow field update wrote a value my validation rule should have rejected'. It is also why Apex triggers must be idempotent but validation logic in a flow is not a second line of defence here.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs assert the inverse — that the workflow field-update re-fire 'reruns validation rules, duplicate rules, and the save step.' That inverted claim leads an engineer to trust validation rules as a guard against workflow-written data, which silently does not hold. It also makes them over-engineer recursion guards for automations that never re-enter.
practices.verbatim_error_string: Custom validation rules, flows, duplicate rules, processes built with Process Builder, and escalation rules aren't run again.

practices.practice: On a recursive save (a save triggered from inside another save, e.g. a roll-up cascading to a parent, or trigger DML on the same object), Salesforce skips steps 9 through 17 — assignment rules, auto-response rules, workflow rules, escalation rules, processes, after-save flows, entitlement rules and roll-ups do not run.
practices.specifics: Verbatim: 'During a recursive save, Salesforce skips steps 9 (assignment rules) through 17 (roll-up summary field in the grandparent record).' Before/after triggers, validation rules, duplicate rules and the save itself DO still run.
practices.why_it_matters: Explains the classic 'my after-save flow fires when a user edits the Case, but not when Apex updates it from the Account trigger' report. Without this rule the admin concludes the flow is broken and adds a duplicate automation.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe cascading parent updates as going through 'the complete order of execution' / 'the full save procedure', so they tell you an after-save flow on the parent will fire from a roll-up-driven parent update. It will not — steps 9–17 are skipped. The wrong answer produces an automation design that silently never executes in production.
practices.verbatim_error_string: During a recursive save, Salesforce skips steps 9 (assignment rules) through 17 (roll-up summary field in the grandparent record).

practices.practice: Name the API-layer error code a validation rule produces, not just the friendly message: integrations see FIELD_CUSTOM_VALIDATION_EXCEPTION with the rule's error message text appended, and the response identifies the field only when the rule's Error Location is a field.
practices.specifics: SOAP/REST/Bulk statusCode = FIELD_CUSTOM_VALIDATION_EXCEPTION. The `fields` array in the error is populated only when Error Location = 'Field'; when Error Location = 'Top of Page' the array is empty and middleware has nothing to map to a source column.
practices.why_it_matters: Integration teams filter on statusCode, not message text. A validation rule with Error Location = Top of Page returns an unattributed failure that a middleware retry handler cannot route.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs write validation-rule guidance entirely in UI terms ('the user sees an error at the top of the page') and never surface the API status code, so the resulting skill is useless to the person actually debugging a Bulk API job whose only artefact is a CSV of `FIELD_CUSTOM_VALIDATION_EXCEPTION` rows. They also never mention that Error Location determines whether the field name is machine-readable.
practices.verbatim_error_string: FIELD_CUSTOM_VALIDATION_EXCEPTION
practices.already_covered_by: NONE (skills/admin/validation-rules covers bypass patterns thoroughly but never names the status code)

practices.practice: Budget the per-object active validation rule cap before designing a rule-heavy object; it is edition-dependent and is a hard activation blocker, not a soft warning.
practices.specifics: 100 active validation rules per object in Enterprise and Developer Edition; 500 in Unlimited and Performance Edition. The limit is on ACTIVE rules — inactive rules do not count, so deactivating is the emergency valve. Salesforce Support can raise it (help article 000383591).
practices.why_it_matters: Large regulated orgs (insurance, life sciences) routinely hit 100 on Account/Case and then cannot deploy the next rule at all. The fix — consolidating rules into one formula with OR branches — is a refactor, not a config change, and needs planning.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs either state no limit exists or quote a single number ('100 per object') without the edition split, so a Unlimited-Edition customer is told to start consolidating 400 rules early for no reason, and an Enterprise-Edition customer is told nothing until the deployment fails.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Unlimited / Performance Edition raises the active validation rule cap from 100 to 500 per object

practices.practice: Validation rules on Account, Contact, Opportunity and Task are NOT enforced during Lead conversion unless the org explicitly turns it on — a whole class of data-quality rules silently has a hole at the single highest-value moment in the sales process.
practices.specifics: Two distinct controls: (1) Setup > Lead Settings > 'Require Validation for Converted Leads' — turns enforcement on org-wide (may require a Support case to expose in some orgs); (2) the user permission 'Enforce Validation and Triggers from Lead Convert' — which, critically, cannot be referenced in a validation rule or workflow formula, so you cannot write a bypass around it.
practices.why_it_matters: Teams add mandatory-field validation on Opportunity, then discover months later that every converted-lead Opportunity bypassed it. Turning enforcement ON afterwards breaks lead conversion for everyone until the field mappings are fixed.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs state flatly that 'validation rules always fire on every DML including lead conversion'. They do not, by default, on the records created by conversion. The LLM answer produces a compliance design that has an unremarked hole, and the admin only finds it during audit.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: 'Enforce Validation and Triggers from Lead Convert' user permission; 'Require Validation for Converted Leads' org setting under Lead Settings

practices.practice: Do not set a validation rule's Error Location to a compound Address field in Lightning — the error message is not rendered and the save appears to fail for no reason.
practices.specifics: Known Issue: 'Validation Rule Error Message not displayed in Lightning if Error Location is an Address field' (e.g. Error Location = BillingCity / MailingStreet). The save is correctly blocked but no message appears under the address block. Set Error Location to 'Top of Page' for any address-driven rule.
practices.why_it_matters: A silent-failure UX bug: the user clicks Save, the record does not save, and no error text appears anywhere. It generates support tickets that look like a platform outage.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Every LLM recommends 'always use field-level error location so the user sees the error next to the field' as a universal best practice. Applied to an address field in Lightning it produces exactly the invisible-error failure. The correct rule is field-level EXCEPT for compound (Address, Geolocation, Name) fields.
practices.verbatim_error_string: Validation Rule Error Message not displayed in Lightning if Error Location is an Address field.

practices.practice: Offer the hierarchy Custom Setting bypass ($Setup) alongside the Custom Permission bypass, and pick between them on runtime-changeability, not preference.
practices.specifics: Custom Permission bypass: `NOT($Permission.Bypass_Validation_Rules)` — auditable, assignable per permission set, but changing who is bypassed is a permission-set edit. Hierarchy Custom Setting bypass: `NOT($Setup.Automation_Bypass__c.Skip_Validation__c)` — evaluable at Org / Profile / User level and toggleable mid-migration by a data-loading admin with no metadata deploy. Both must be the LAST AND clause so the rule short-circuits.
practices.why_it_matters: During a cutover weekend you need to flip the bypass on and off within minutes for one integration user. A permission-set change is auditable but slower and needs the right admin; a hierarchy custom setting row is a single record edit.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs present Custom Permission as the only correct bypass and dismiss custom settings as 'legacy, use Custom Metadata Types instead'. That advice is wrong specifically here: Custom Metadata Types have NO per-user hierarchy resolution and cannot be referenced as `$Setup` in a validation-rule formula the way a hierarchy custom setting can. Recommending CMDT for a per-user validation bypass produces a formula that will not compile.
practices.already_covered_by: skills/admin/validation-rules (Custom Permission path is covered in depth; $Setup hierarchy path is not — grep for '$Setup' in that package returns nothing)

practices.practice: Before applying a Global Value Set to a large number of objects, know that past 13 objects you permanently lose the ability to replace or delete values in that value set — only deactivate remains.
practices.specifics: 'If you apply a global picklist value set to more than 13 different objects, you can deactivate values from the picklist value set, but you can't replace any picklist values or delete values from the set.' Related caps: 500 global value sets per org; 1,000 combined active + inactive values per global value set; no limit on how many picklist fields consume a set.
practices.why_it_matters: This is a one-way door. An enterprise standardising 'Country' or 'Region' across 20 objects with one GVS is choosing, permanently, to never be able to rename or remove a value — only deactivate and add. That is a data-governance decision, not a config detail.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs universally recommend 'use a Global Value Set everywhere for consistency' with no counterweight. They never mention the 13-object threshold, so the recommendation actively walks the customer into an irreversible state where value cleanup is impossible. The correct guidance is: use GVS broadly, but if the set will span >13 objects, design the value list as append-and-deactivate-only from day one.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE (skills/admin/picklist-and-value-sets covers 500 GVS/org and 1,000 values/GVS at SKILL.md:85 but not the 13-object threshold)

practices.practice: State the active-rule arithmetic for Duplicate Management before designing matching logic: 5 active duplicate rules per object, up to 3 matching rules referenced per duplicate rule, and 5 active matching rules per object.
practices.specifics: Up to five active duplicate rules per object; up to three matching rules in each duplicate rule; across all duplicate rules on an object, up to five active matching rules. You can create more than five of each — only activation is capped.
practices.why_it_matters: A dedupe design with one rule per business scenario (7 lead sources, 4 account types) is unbuildable and has to be collapsed into composite match formulas. Discovering the cap after the design workshop costs a redesign.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe duplicate rules as if unlimited, and produce a design deck with 8–10 named duplicate rules per object. None of it can be activated. They also conflate 'duplicate rule' and 'matching rule' as one artefact, so the 3-per-rule and 5-per-object matching caps never appear at all.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE (skills/admin/duplicate-management contains no numeric limits at all — grep for 'five active|5 active|three matching' returns nothing)

practices.practice: Duplicate rules with the Alert action do not alert on API, Data Loader or Data Import Wizard inserts — the records save. Only the Block action produces a failure over the API.
practices.specifics: Alert is a UI-only interaction (the 'possible duplicates' card). With Alert, an API insert saves the duplicate. With Block, the API insert fails with statusCode DUPLICATES_DETECTED and, if includeRecordDetails=true, returns the matched record IDs, the duplicate count, and the duplicate rule name. Duplicates are still logged to DuplicateRecordSet / DuplicateRecordItem under Alert if 'Report' is enabled.
practices.why_it_matters: An org that believes it has duplicate protection because banners appear in the UI has zero protection on the channel that creates most of its records. This is a silent-failure mode with no error, no log entry the admin looks at, and steadily growing duplicate debt.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs say 'duplicate rules run on all DML including the API', which is true of evaluation but misleading about outcome: with Alert the evaluation runs and the record still saves. The LLM answer leads to an architecture where the integration is assumed protected. The right answer is: for API-created records, only Block does anything, and the integration must be prepared to handle DUPLICATES_DETECTED.
practices.verbatim_error_string: DUPLICATES_DETECTED
practices.already_covered_by: NONE (skills/admin/duplicate-management/references/gotchas.md says 'Duplicate Rules Ignore System-Created Data' in prose but names no action mode, no status code, and no mechanism)

practices.practice: To let a legitimate load through a blocking duplicate rule, set the DuplicateRuleHeader rather than deactivating the rule.
practices.specifics: Apex: `Database.DMLOptions dml = new Database.DMLOptions(); dml.duplicateRuleHeader.allowSave = true; Database.insert(records, dml);`. SOAP: `<DuplicateRuleHeader><allowSave>true</allowSave></DuplicateRuleHeader>`. REST: request header `Sforce-Duplicate-Rule-Header: allowSave=true`. Other header fields: `includeRecordDetails` (true = return full fields of the matched duplicates, false = IDs only) and `runAsCurrentUser` (true = enforce the current user's sharing rules when the duplicate rule runs).
practices.why_it_matters: Deactivating a duplicate rule for a migration window leaves the org unprotected for everyone, and reactivating a matching rule triggers an asynchronous index rebuild that can strand the rule in 'Activating'. The header is per-call and leaves the rule live.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked 'how do I bypass a duplicate rule for a data load', LLMs answer 'deactivate the duplicate rule, load, then reactivate.' That advice ignores that reactivation kicks off an async matching-rule activation job that can hang for >24h, during which the org has no duplicate protection and no one notices. LLMs also confuse `allowSave` with the Alert/Block action setting and claim `allowSave=true` bypasses Block rules — it bypasses the alert; the header's purpose is to permit the save.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE (grep for 'allowSave' in skills/admin/duplicate-management and skills/data/large-scale-deduplication returns nothing)

practices.practice: When checking duplicates from Apex, cap the batch at 50 records per Datacloud.FindDuplicates call and handle the no-active-rule exception explicitly.
practices.specifics: 'The input array is limited to 50 elements.' All sObjects in the input array must be the same object type. Only ACTIVE duplicate rules are applied. The method does not return custom fields by default.
practices.why_it_matters: A bulkified trigger that hands 200 records to FindDuplicates throws on every 200-record chunk. The 50-element chunking is not optional and is not inferable from the general 200-record trigger convention.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs write `Datacloud.FindDuplicates.findDuplicates(Trigger.new)` directly — passing up to 200 records — because they pattern-match to the standard bulkification idiom. It throws immediately. They also swallow the no-rules case in a bare catch, turning a config error into a silently duplicate-permitting code path.
practices.verbatim_error_string: Configuration error: The number of records to check is greater than the permitted batch size.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE (grep for 'permitted batch size|No active duplicate rules are defined' across skills/ returns nothing; Datacloud.FindDuplicates is named in skills/data/data-quality-and-governance and skills/data/lead-data-import-and-dedup but without the 50-element cap or the exception strings)

practices.practice: Enumerate the documented cases where duplicate rules do not run at all, and check the org's actual record-creation paths against that list.
practices.specifics: Duplicate rules do not run when: records are created via Quick Create; records are created by Experience Cloud self-registration; leads are converted and 'Use Apex Lead Convert' is not enabled; records are restored with the Undelete button; records are added by Einstein Activity Capture; records are manually merged; a Self-Service user creates records and the rule conditions reference the User object; the rule conditions reference a lookup relationship field with no saved value.
practices.why_it_matters: Undelete and Quick Create are the two that bite hardest — an org that mass-restores from the Recycle Bin after a bad delete reintroduces every duplicate the rules previously blocked, with no alert and no DuplicateRecordSet entry.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs give an unconditional 'duplicate rules run on create and edit for all record sources.' They never surface the undelete or lead-convert exclusions, so a disaster-recovery runbook that says 'restore from Recycle Bin' is signed off without anyone realising duplicate protection is off for that operation.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: 'Use Apex Lead Convert' org setting must be enabled for duplicate rules to run during lead conversion
practices.already_covered_by: NONE for the duplicate-management package (the phrases appear only in skills/data/case-history-migration)

practices.practice: Treat matching rule activation as an asynchronous background job with a real failure mode, not an instant toggle: it builds a match index and can strand in 'Activating'.
practices.specifics: Activation status values include Activating; a rule sitting in 'Activating' for more than 24 hours indicates a stalled background job that will never complete on its own and must be aborted before the rule can be activated again. Activating several matching rules at once increases the chance of a stall. On activation failure Salesforce emails the admin with details.
practices.why_it_matters: A deployment plan that says 'deactivate matching rules, load 2M records, reactivate' can leave the org with no duplicate protection indefinitely, and the deploy log shows success because the metadata deployed fine.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs model matching rule activation as synchronous metadata, so their migration runbooks toggle rules off and on in adjacent steps with no verification gate. They never tell you to re-check activation status after the load, and never mention the 24-hour stall signature or that batching activations makes it worse.

practices.practice: Approval.lock() / Approval.unlock() in Apex are inert unless an org-level switch is turned on — and it is off by default in every org type including scratch orgs and sandboxes.
practices.specifics: Setup > Process Automation Settings > 'Enable record locking and unlocking in Apex'. Locks and unlocks are treated as DML: they count toward DML statement limits, they are blocked after a callout in the same transaction, and they roll back with the transaction on failure.
practices.why_it_matters: An Apex unlock utility deployed to production without the setting fails at runtime in an org where nobody thought a Setup checkbox was part of the release. Because it is not metadata that ships in a package, it is invisible in the deployment manifest.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs happily generate `Approval.unlock(recordIds);` as the answer to 'how do I unlock records stuck in approval' and never mention the org setting. The code compiles and deploys; it fails only at execution, in whichever org forgot the checkbox — which is every fresh scratch org used for CI, so the test suite fails mysteriously in the pipeline and passes locally.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Org setting: Setup > Process Automation Settings > 'Enable record locking and unlocking in Apex' (off by default in all orgs, including scratch orgs and sandboxes)
practices.already_covered_by: NONE (grep for 'Enable record locking and unlocking in Apex' across skills/ returns nothing; Approval.lock appears only in skills/apex/salesforce-debug-log-analysis)

practices.practice: Name ENTITY_IS_LOCKED as the approval-process failure signature and note precisely what it blocks and what it does not.
practices.specifics: statusCode ENTITY_IS_LOCKED. A record locked by a pending approval blocks update, delete and undelete; inserting new records is unaffected. Salesforce admins can always edit locked records; assigned approvers can only if the approval process step has record editability configured for approvers. Critically, changing an approval process to allow the current approver to edit locked records applies ONLY to records submitted after the change is saved — records already in flight stay locked to their old rule.
practices.why_it_matters: A middleware sync that updates records nightly starts failing on exactly the records currently awaiting approval, and the failure looks like an intermittent permission problem. The 'change applies only to future submissions' detail means the obvious fix appears not to work.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs tell you to flip the approval step's record-editability setting and say the problem is solved. It is not solved for any record already pending — those must be recalled and resubmitted, or unlocked. The LLM answer looks like it works in a sandbox test (new submission) and does nothing in production (in-flight backlog).
practices.verbatim_error_string: ENTITY_IS_LOCKED
practices.already_covered_by: NONE for the approval packages (grep for 'ENTITY_IS_LOCKED' in skills/admin/approval-processes and skills/admin/approval-process-apex-patterns returns nothing; the code appears only in skills/apex/record-locking-and-contention and unrelated packages)

practices.practice: A record can be in only one classic approval process at a time; on submission Salesforce walks active processes in Process Order and starts the first one whose entry criteria evaluate true.
practices.specifics: Entry criteria are evaluated once, at submission. They are not re-evaluated as the record changes mid-approval. Process Order is a manual ordering on the approval process list — reordering it changes routing for every future submission with no other visible change. Classic approval processes support up to 30 steps.
practices.why_it_matters: Two overlapping approval processes (e.g. 'Discount > 20%' and 'Amount > $1M') do not both run; the higher-ordered one wins and the other never fires. Teams design for parallel approvals that the platform cannot deliver.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs design multi-track approval architectures with several concurrent approval processes on one object, because nothing in their training says only one can be active per record. They also assume entry criteria are continuously re-evaluated, so they propose 'the record drops out of approval automatically when the amount changes' — it does not; it stays in, locked, until approved, rejected or recalled.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE (skills/admin/approval-processes SKILL.md mentions entry criteria only as consulting advice; grep for 'Process Order|one process at a time' returns nothing)

practices.practice: To clear a backlog of records stuck in approval — after a rule change, a bad load, or a deleted approver — use Setup > Mass Transfer Approval Requests > 'Mass remove records from an approval process', not Apex or record deletion.
practices.specifics: Setup Quick Find: 'Mass Transfer Approval Requests'. The same screen transfers pending requests to a different approver. Comments entered during the removal are written to the record's Approval History related list, so the action is auditable.
practices.why_it_matters: When an approver leaves the company, every pending request assigned to them is orphaned and the records stay locked. This is the only supported bulk remediation, and it preserves the audit trail that a delete-and-recreate does not.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs answer 'query ProcessInstanceWorkitem and delete the records' or 'write a batch calling Approval.unlock'. Deleting workitems does not remove the record from the process and leaves ProcessInstance orphaned; unlocking removes the lock but leaves the record still pending, so it can never be resubmitted. Neither writes anything to Approval History.

practices.practice: Configure delegated approvers on the approver's User record with an explicit window, and know the two things that silently defeat it.
practices.specifics: Delegation Information section on the User record: Delegated Approver (lookup to a User), Delegation Start (begins 12:00 AM on the start date), Delegation End (ends 11:59 PM on the end date). Two defeaters: (1) the approval STEP must have the 'the approver's delegate may also approve this request' checkbox selected — delegation set on the user does nothing otherwise; (2) you cannot assign a Group or a Queue as a delegated approver, only a single User.
practices.why_it_matters: Delegation configured on the user record with the step checkbox unset is the classic 'my out-of-office approver setup doesn't work' ticket, and the approver is already on holiday when it surfaces.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe delegation as purely a User-record setting and omit the per-step checkbox entirely, so the instructions produce a configuration that appears complete and does nothing. They also frequently suggest delegating to a queue for team coverage, which the platform does not allow.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE (grep for 'Delegated Approver' in skills/admin/approval-processes returns nothing)

practices.practice: For new approval work, default to Approval Orchestration in Flow (the current strategic path) and name the exact flow types and permissions — but check the one capability it still lacks before committing.
practices.specifics: Flow types: 'Autolaunched Approval Orchestration' and 'Record-Triggered Approval Orchestration', introduced Spring '25. Summer '25 added recall paths and the Approval Process Wizard. Winter '26 added debug mode (runs in rollback mode) plus the delegation model below. Known gap vs classic: manually selecting the next approver at runtime is not supported — all approvers must be resolvable by the flow. Classic Approval Processes are not announced as retired.
practices.why_it_matters: Choosing classic approvals for a greenfield build in 2026 forfeits fault paths, recall paths, debug mode and Flow Builder integration. Choosing Flow approvals for a process that genuinely needs runtime approver selection produces a design that cannot be built.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs still answer approval questions with the classic Setup > Approval Processes wizard, because that is the overwhelming majority of their training data. They do not know Approval Orchestration exists, and when they do mention 'Flow Orchestrator' they describe the pre-Spring-'25 generic orchestration product rather than the approval-specific flow types. They also invent a retirement date for classic Approval Processes; none has been announced.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: End users need Read on the Approval Submission object to participate in Flow approvals
practices.already_covered_by: NONE (grep for 'Approval Orchestration|Approval Designer|View Orchestration in Automation App' across skills/ returns nothing; the lowercase phrase appears once in skills/admin/approval-processes/references/llm-anti-patterns.md)

practices.practice: Delegate approval-process authoring without handing out Manage Flows: grant Approval Designer plus View Orchestration in Automation App, and understand that activation stays with admins.
practices.specifics: Winter '26. 'Approval Designer' system permission + 'View Orchestration in Automation App' user permission let a non-admin create, change and view autolaunched flow approval processes in the Approvals app. Those users do not see an Activate button in Flow Builder — they see 'Submit for Activation'. Actual activation still requires Manage Flow. This is an enforced separation of duties, not a convention.
practices.why_it_matters: Manage Flows is effectively god-mode over org automation. Before Winter '26 the only way to let a business analyst build an approval was to grant it. This is the specific two-permission combination that replaces that.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked 'how do I let a business user build approval processes without full admin rights', LLMs invent a permission like 'Manage Approval Processes' (which does not exist) or fall back to 'you must grant Manage Flows'. The real answer is a specific, named, two-permission pair shipped in Winter '26, and the fact that activation is deliberately withheld is the part that makes the governance story work.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: 'Approval Designer' system permission AND 'View Orchestration in Automation App' user permission (Winter '26); activation still requires the 'Manage Flow' permission

practices.practice: Do not quote the old Flow Orchestration run entitlement — as of Spring '26 orchestration runs are included with no usage-based cap in the applicable editions.
practices.specifics: Previously: usage-based entitlement capped at 600 free orchestration runs per org per year, with flow approvals excepted. As of Spring '26 (week of 16 February 2026), Flow Orchestration runs are included with no usage-based caps in Enterprise, Performance, Unlimited, Einstein 1 and Developer editions.
practices.why_it_matters: The 600-run cap was the single most common reason architects rejected Flow Orchestration for high-volume approvals. Repeating a retired commercial constraint pushes customers back to classic approvals or to custom Apex for no reason.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs trained before 2026 still say 'Flow Orchestration requires a paid add-on' or 'you get 600 free runs per year', which was true and is not any more. This is a licensing claim, so a wrong answer directly changes a purchasing conversation and can lose a customer a design they were entitled to.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Flow Orchestration runs: included with no usage-based caps in Enterprise, Performance, Unlimited, Einstein 1 and Developer editions as of Spring '26 (previously 600 runs/org/year)

practices.practice: Fuzzy matching in matching rules is only available for a fixed, named set of standard fields on Account, Contact and Lead; every custom field can only be matched Exact.
practices.specifics: Fuzzy methods: Fuzzy: First Name, Fuzzy: Last Name, Fuzzy: Company Name, Fuzzy: Phone, Fuzzy: City, Fuzzy: Street, Fuzzy: ZIP, Fuzzy: Title. Fuzzy: Phone and Fuzzy: Street are documented as working best with North American data. Exact works on almost any field including custom fields, and ignores case.
practices.why_it_matters: A dedupe design that plans to fuzzy-match on a custom Legal_Entity_Name__c or a custom address field cannot be built. The workaround — a formula field that normalises the value, matched Exact — has to be designed in from the start because it changes the data model.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe fuzzy matching as a general capability you select per field, and cheerfully propose 'Fuzzy match on your custom Company_Legal_Name__c field'. That option does not exist in the UI. They also miss the North-America tuning caveat and recommend Fuzzy: Phone / Fuzzy: Street for EMEA and APAC data, where it performs badly.
practices.already_covered_by: skills/admin/duplicate-management/references/llm-anti-patterns.md:43-45 and skills/data/duplicate-rule-person-account-edge-cases (SKILL.md:210, references/well-architected.md:21,45, references/gotchas.md:59-63) — the fuzzy method names ARE covered; only the 'custom fields are Exact-only' constraint and the North-America caveat are thin

practices.practice: Assignment rules created via API need TWO headers, not one, if the org expects the owner to be emailed.
practices.specifics: AssignmentRuleHeader with either `useDefaultRule=true` or an explicit `assignmentRuleId` triggers the rule. The assignment notification email additionally requires EmailHeader with `triggerUserEmail=true`. REST equivalent: `Sforce-Auto-Assign: true`. Without the EmailHeader the record is reassigned correctly and the new owner is never notified.
practices.why_it_matters: 'Leads are routing fine but reps say they never hear about them' is a two-header problem that looks like an assignment-rule problem, so teams spend days re-checking rule criteria.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs stop at AssignmentRuleHeader because that is what the question literally asked about, and never mention EmailHeader. The resulting integration silently drops every assignment notification — a pure silent-failure mode with a correctly-owned record as evidence that everything works.
practices.already_covered_by: skills/admin/assignment-rules covers AssignmentRuleHeader, DMLOptions.assignmentRuleHeader, Sforce-Auto-Assign and the one-active-rule-per-object model in depth (SKILL.md:62,84,86,179,208; gotchas.md:13,15; llm-anti-patterns.md:32-48). Only the EmailHeader/triggerUserEmail pairing is uncovered — grep for 'triggerUserEmail|EmailHeader' in that package returns nothing.

stale_or_wrong_found: FACTUALLY WRONG — skills/apex/order-of-execution-deep-dive/SKILL.md step 3: 'Before-save record-triggered Flows also run at this step, interleaved with before triggers in undefined relative order.' The section 'Before-Save Flows Run at Step 3, Not Step 15' and the 'Protecting a Before Trigger from Flow Interference' pattern both build on this. Salesforce documents them as SEPARATE, ORDERED steps: step 3 'Executes record-triggered flows that are configured to run before the record is saved', step 4 'Executes all before triggers'. The whole 'no guaranteed relative order, this is fragile' guidance in that skill is therefore built on an incorrect premise. Source: https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_order_of_execution.htm

FACTUALLY WRONG (inverted mechanism) — skills/apex/order-of-execution-deep-dive/SKILL.md step 12: 'This re-fire also reruns validation rules, duplicate rules, and the save step.' The official documentation states the exact opposite: 'Custom validation rules, flows, duplicate rules, processes built with Process Builder, and escalation rules aren't run again.' Only system validation and before/after update triggers re-run. This is a dangerous inversion — it tells a reader that validation rules will catch bad data written by a workflow field update. They will not. Same source URL as above.

INCOMPLETE / MISLEADING — skills/apex/order-of-execution-deep-dive is presented throughout as 'the 18-step canonical order' (SKILL.md:27, :169, :206) and omits Criteria Based Sharing evaluation entirely. The documented sequence is 20 steps. It also omits the documented recursive-save rule ('During a recursive save, Salesforce skips steps 9 (assignment rules) through 17'), while its own Gotcha #3 asserts that a roll-up-driven parent update runs 'the parent record's own full order of execution' — which contradicts the recursive-save skip. Note step-number drift as a consequence: the skill's own cross-references ('workflow field updates at step 12, roll-up summary updates at step 17') will not line up with any reader who has the official 20-step list open.

BROKEN CITATION — skills/admin/approval-process-apex-patterns/SKILL.md cites 'admin/approval-process-design' twice (in the frontmatter description and in the body 'What this skill is NOT' section). `ls -d skills/admin/approval-process-design` returns 'No such file or directory'. The real package is skills/admin/approval-processes. CLAUDE.md requires every citation to resolve to a real skills/<domain>/<slug>/SKILL.md.

The delete flow actually prompts you to either replace the value with another picklist value or blank it, and the change is applied by a background job with an email on completion — it is not unconditionally an immediate null.
