areas.area: Users, roles, sharing setup, queues, groups

practices.practice: When deploying sharing rules across orgs on different releases, use `roleAndSubordinatesInternal` (Metadata API) / `RoleAndSubordinatesInternal` (SOAP/REST) for internal-only sharing; reserve `roleAndSubordinates` for orgs with Digital Experiences enabled where portal users must be included.
practices.specifics: Renamed group: UI label 'Roles and Subordinates' -> 'Roles and Internal Subordinates'. Metadata API: roleAndSubordinates -> roleAndSubordinatesInternal. SOAP/REST: RoleAndSubordinates -> RoleAndSubordinatesInternal. Rollout: sandboxes Summer '25, production Winter '26. Salesforce dynamically converts remaining references in SOQL and Metadata API deploys, but manual update is still recommended.
practices.why_it_matters: A sharing rule built with roleAndSubordinates in a Digital-Experiences org silently grants record access to external/portal users. This is the exact failure mode Salesforce made the change to prevent.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs emit `<sharedTo><roleAndSubordinates>Sales_Manager</roleAndSubordinates></sharedTo>` in every sharing-rule XML they generate, because that is what all pre-2025 training data contains. Deploying that XML into a Winter '26 production org fails, and if it succeeds (Experience Cloud enabled) it quietly widens access to community users. LLMs also never mention that the two names are not synonyms — they differ in whether portal users are in scope.
practices.verbatim_error_string: sharedTo not allowed:roleAndSubordinates
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: roleAndSubordinates (the portal-inclusive variant) is only selectable when Digital Experiences / Experience Cloud is enabled in the org.

practices.practice: Before deactivating a user, query CronTrigger/AsyncApexJob for jobs they scheduled, delete those jobs, and recreate them as an active service identity. There is no supported way to reassign the running user of an existing scheduled Apex job.
practices.specifics: Scheduled Apex runs in the context of the user who created it. Setup > Environments > Jobs > Scheduled Jobs. Resolution is delete-and-recreate; CronTrigger links to AsyncApexJob via CronTrigger.CronJobDetailId.
practices.why_it_matters: The job does not error at deactivation time — it fails on its next fire, often days later, and the failure email goes to the deactivated user's address.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked 'how do I move a scheduled job to another user', LLMs confidently describe editing the job's owner in Setup or updating CronTrigger.OwnerId. Neither exists — CronTrigger's schedule owner is not writable and there is no reassign UI. The only correct answer is abort/delete and re-schedule while logged in as the new running user.
practices.verbatim_error_string: [INACTIVE_OWNER_OR_USER] owner or user is inactive

practices.practice: Freezing a user does NOT free the user licence; only deactivation does. Use Freeze as the immediate containment action during offboarding, then work through the deactivation blockers, then deactivate to reclaim the licence.
practices.specifics: Salesforce Help, Freeze or Unfreeze User Accounts: 'Freeze user accounts doesn't make their user licenses available for use in your organization. To make their user licenses available, deactivate the accounts.' Users can never be deleted, only deactivated.
practices.why_it_matters: Offboarding runbooks that stop at Freeze leave the org paying for the seat and show a false 'licences available' count in Setup > Company Information.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs routinely state that freezing 'releases the licence' or present Freeze and Deactivate as equivalent security actions. They also frequently claim you can delete a Salesforce user, sometimes inventing a Setup path for it.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Manage Users permission is required to freeze or deactivate.

practices.practice: Enumerate deactivation blockers before the offboarding window, not during it. Salesforce surfaces them one at a time, so a user referenced by six email alerts requires six edit-retry cycles.
practices.specifics: Blockers include: Default Lead Owner, Default Lead Creator (Web-to-Lead), Lead Assignment Rules, Default Case Owner, Automated Case User, Case Assignment Rules, Default Workflow User, the target of a Workflow Field Update, sole recipient of a Workflow Email Alert, dashboard Running User for 'Run as Specified User' dashboards, and the value of any custom hierarchical relationship field on the User object.
practices.why_it_matters: An offboarding scheduled for a 30-minute window turns into a multi-hour hunt because each blocker is discovered serially.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs give a generic 'reassign their records and uncheck Active' answer. They almost never mention the custom hierarchy field on User (the single most common hard blocker) and never mention that the errors are surfaced one at a time, so their checklist reads as a 2-minute task when it is not.
practices.verbatim_error_string: Cannot inactivate user that is the value of a hierarchy field: {Fieldname}

practices.practice: Do not use the Salesforce API Only System Integrations profile for new integration users. Use Minimum Access - API Only Integrations and layer permission sets on top.
practices.specifics: Spring '24: 'Minimum Access - API Only Integrations' replaces 'Salesforce API Only System Integrations'. The old profile incorrectly grants CRUD on custom objects. Since Spring '24 it is not created in newly provisioned orgs; in Summer '24 it was converted to a custom profile in existing orgs so admins can delete it. Both pair with the Salesforce Integration user license.
practices.why_it_matters: The legacy profile silently gives an integration identity create/read/update/delete on every custom object in the org — the opposite of least privilege, on the one identity whose credentials sit in a third-party system.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Because the Salesforce API Only System Integrations profile dominates 2023-era blog content, LLMs still recommend it as *the* profile for integration users, and often instruct the admin to clone it. Cloning propagates the blanket custom-object CRUD into a permanent custom profile.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Salesforce Integration user license, plus the Salesforce API Integration permission set license to extend beyond the base profile.

practices.practice: Budget the five free Salesforce Integration user licenses deliberately — one per integrating system — before buying additional standard Salesforce seats for middleware.
practices.specifics: Five Salesforce Integration user licenses are included per org in Enterprise, Performance and Unlimited editions; one in every Developer Edition org. Additional licenses are $10 each. Available since March 14 2023. Holders cannot log in to the UI at all — API (REST/SOAP/Bulk) only. The Salesforce API Integration permission set license carries the administrative permissions that were lifted out of the System Administrator profile.
practices.why_it_matters: Orgs commonly burn a full Sales Cloud seat on a MuleSoft or ETL identity when a free, strictly-API licence exists.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs advise 'create a dedicated integration user with the System Administrator profile' or 'a Salesforce Platform licence'. They rarely know the five-free allocation exists, and never mention that default record types cannot be set through a permission set — a real blocker when the integration inserts records on objects with multiple record types.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Salesforce Integration user license (5 free per org in EE/PE/UE, 1 in DE, $10 each thereafter); Salesforce API Integration permission set license.

practices.practice: Placing a skewed owner in the role hierarchy is what makes ownership skew expensive — not the record count itself. If a single identity must own >10,000 records, give it no role at all, or a dedicated role at the very top that is never reparented and never added to a sharing-rule source group.
practices.specifics: DRAES: 'Ownership data skew is when a single user owns more than 10,000 records of an object.' The cost is triggered when that user is moved in the hierarchy or in/out of roles or public groups that source sharing rules — Salesforce must adjust a very large number of sharing-table entries.
practices.why_it_matters: Removing a user from a role costs the same as adding them. A one-click role change on an integration user that owns 80,000 accounts can lock group-membership operations org-wide for hours.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs treat ownership skew as a pure record-count problem and prescribe 'redistribute ownership'. They miss that the platform-level mitigation Salesforce actually documents is *removing the role*, and they never say that de-assignment is as expensive as assignment.

practices.practice: Add lookup skew to skew diagnostics alongside ownership and parent-child skew. Distribute the target across multiple lookup values, or replace a low-cardinality lookup with a picklist.
practices.specifics: >10,000 records pointing at the same lookup target constitutes lookup skew. Salesforce locks the target record of every lookup field on insert/update to preserve referential integrity, so concurrent DML against the same lookup target serialises and can throw row-lock errors. Mitigations: spread across multiple lookup values; if the value set is small and fixed, model it as a picklist instead of a lookup.
practices.why_it_matters: Lookup skew produces UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW under parallel Bulk API loads even when ownership and parent-child skew are clean, so teams that only check the two well-known skew types cannot explain the failures.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked about Salesforce data skew, LLMs enumerate exactly two types — account/parent-child and ownership — and stop. Lookup skew is omitted, and when it is mentioned it is described as a query-performance issue rather than a write-time row-lock issue. The picklist-instead-of-lookup remediation is irreversible in practice (field data type change), which LLMs never flag.
practices.verbatim_error_string: UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW

practices.practice: Deferring group membership calculations automatically defers sharing rule calculations too — the reverse is not true. Plan the resume step as a full recalculation, and benchmark it in a sandbox refreshed within the last 30 days at production data volumes.
practices.specifics: DRAES: 'You can choose to only defer sharing rules calculations. However, if you defer group membership calculations, sharing rule calculations are automatically deferred.' After resume, 'the system is in a state that requires a full recalculation of all sharing rules for user access rights to be complete and accurate.' Two caveats: 'Deferring sharing calculations doesn't defer the recalculation of some sharing changes in order to preserve data integrity' and 'Group membership locking can also still occur while sharing calculations are deferred.' The Recalculate button on Sharing Rules related lists is disabled while calculations are deferred.
practices.why_it_matters: Teams schedule a realignment assuming deferral makes the window free, then discover the resume recalculation is the long pole and that lock errors still occur during the deferred period.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs present Defer Sharing Calculations as a self-service checkbox and imply it makes sharing changes free. Two things are wrong: it must be enabled by Salesforce Customer Support before the Setup link appears, and it defers rather than eliminates work — leaving an org in the deferred state indefinitely means access rights are stale, not cheap.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Defer Sharing Calculation must be enabled by Salesforce Customer Support. The Setup link is visible to users with 'View Setup and Configuration'; the Suspend / Resume / Recalculate buttons require the 'Manage Sharing Calculation Deferral' permission.

practices.practice: Treat 'could not acquire lock' and 'Group membership operation already in progress' as concurrency signals, not transient faults: serialise user-provisioning and role-maintenance jobs and add backoff retry, because granular locking does not protect role reparenting.
practices.specifics: DRAES Group Membership Locking: granular locking is enabled by default and 'allows some group maintenance operations to proceed simultaneously if there's no hierarchical or other relationship between the roles or groups involved'. Role reparenting (including customer/partner account ownership changes) is the most restrictive operation and blocks almost all other group updates; role deletion and territory reparenting also block most concurrent activity. Public groups and roles without territories are not blocked by territory operations.
practices.why_it_matters: SCIM/HR-driven provisioning integrations that fire user creates in parallel with an admin doing a role realignment will fail intermittently with no data-quality explanation.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs conflate this org-wide group-membership lock with Apex row-level locking (UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW / FOR UPDATE) and prescribe FOR UPDATE, smaller batch sizes, or Database.Stateful. None of those apply — this lock is held by the sharing subsystem across the whole org, not per record.
practices.verbatim_error_string: could not acquire lock

practices.practice: Grant Access Using Hierarchies can only be unchecked on custom objects. On standard objects it is permanently on, so 'the manager should not see the rep's records' is unachievable for Account/Opportunity/Case through OWD and roles alone.
practices.specifics: Setup > Security > Sharing Settings. The checkbox is greyed out and always selected for standard objects; editable per custom object. Unchecking it means access must come from ownership, sharing rules, teams, manual shares, or Apex managed sharing — it does not suppress View All / Modify All object permissions.
practices.why_it_matters: Confidentiality requirements (HR, comp plans, investigations) on standard objects require restriction rules or a separate custom object, not a hierarchy tweak — a design fork that has to happen before build.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs answer 'uncheck Grant Access Using Hierarchies for Opportunity' when asked to hide records from a manager. The checkbox does not exist for Opportunity. They also claim unchecking it blocks all upward visibility, omitting that View All Data and Modify All Data still cut straight through.

practices.practice: Changing a record's owner deletes every manual share on that record. Sharing rules and Apex managed sharing survive; manual shares and (for Accounts transferred via the wizard) previously granted access do not.
practices.specifics: Manual shares (Share record with RowCause = Manual) are removed on OwnerId change. When transferring accounts and related data, previously granted access from manual sharing, Apex managed sharing, and sharing rules is removed and sharing is re-derived for the new owner.
practices.why_it_matters: A territory realignment that reassigns 40,000 accounts silently destroys years of ad-hoc collaborator access with no audit event and no way to restore it short of a pre-transfer export of the Share tables.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe manual sharing as persistent and never warn that owner change wipes it. Their mass-transfer runbooks omit the single most important pre-step: export AccountShare / <Object>Share WHERE RowCause = 'Manual' before the transfer, because after the transfer the rows are gone.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: The Transfer Record system permission (which subsumes Transfer Case and Transfer Lead) is required in addition to edit access on the records.

practices.practice: Do not plan a mass reassignment around Setup > Data Management > Mass Transfer Records. It handles 250 records per run and supports only Leads, Accounts, and custom objects — use Data Loader or Apex batch for anything else.
practices.specifics: 'You can only transfer ownership of 250 records at a time.' Exceeding the limit transfers only the first 250 silently. Opportunities, Cases, Contacts and Activities are not transferable with this tool. Account transfers offer checkboxes to cascade open opportunities not owned by the existing account owner and closed opportunities; Data Loader and Apex do not cascade at all.
practices.why_it_matters: A go-live cutover plan that budgets the wizard for 50,000 accounts is off by two orders of magnitude, and the silent 250-record truncation means the shortfall is not obvious until reports are wrong.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs recommend the Mass Transfer wizard for bulk offboarding of a departing rep's whole book of business, and list Opportunities and Cases among the supported objects. Both are wrong. They also assume cascade-to-children happens on any OwnerId update, when it only happens via the wizard's checkboxes.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Transfer Record system permission.

practices.practice: Enabling the external sharing model is a one-way door. Once separate internal/external org-wide defaults are turned on, they cannot be turned off.
practices.specifics: Setup > Security > Sharing Settings > Enable External Sharing Model splits each object's OWD into Default Internal Access and Default External Access. Salesforce removed the ability to disable it: 'To better protect your Salesforce org's data, you can no longer disable the external sharing model after it's enabled in your org.'
practices.why_it_matters: This is one of the few genuinely irreversible sharing-setup decisions. Enabling it in production to satisfy a single Experience Cloud pilot permanently changes the OWD model for every object and every future sharing rule.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe external OWD as a reversible convenience toggle and suggest 'try it and turn it off if it doesn't suit you'. There is no off switch. They also fail to note the upside Salesforce documents — separate external defaults reduce the number of sharing rules and improve recalculation performance — so the decision gets framed purely as risk.

practices.practice: Queues are not available on Opportunity, Account, or Contact. If the requirement is 'unassigned opportunities go to a pool', the answer is a placeholder user plus a list view or Omni-Channel, not a queue.
practices.specifics: Queues are supported on Case, Lead, Order, Service Contract, Knowledge Article Version, and custom objects — but not a custom object that is the detail side of a master-detail relationship. QueueSobject maps a queue Group to its supported sObject types. A queue can carry one Queue Email address; ticking 'Send Email to Members' additionally mails every member.
practices.why_it_matters: Queue-based routing designs for Opportunity get to build before the constraint surfaces, forcing a rework of assignment rules and reporting.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs cheerfully write 'create an Opportunity queue and route unassigned deals to it'. They also miss the master-detail exclusion, which is the more subtle trap: a custom object modelled as a detail record can never own a queue, so the queue design has to be settled before the master-detail-vs-lookup decision is locked in.

practices.practice: Size the role hierarchy against the actual ceiling for the org's provisioning date, and keep it shallow. Roles exist to drive record rollup and forecasting, not to mirror the org chart.
practices.specifics: Orgs created in Spring '21 or later: up to 5,000 roles. Orgs created before Spring '21: 500 roles, increasable via Salesforce Customer Support. Salesforce's stated best practice ceilings are 25,000 internal roles and 100,000 external/portal roles. Sharing rules: up to 300 per object including up to 50 criteria-based; recommended practical ceiling is 100 ownership-based and 50 criteria-based per object for recalculation performance.
practices.why_it_matters: Every additional hierarchy level multiplies the sharing-table entries written on each ownership change, and the recommended 100/50 sharing-rule ceiling is far below the hard 300/50 limit — orgs that design to the hard limit hit recalculation timeouts long before they hit it.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs quote '500 roles' as the universal limit (true only for pre-Spring '21 orgs) and recommend building the role hierarchy to match the HR org chart. They also quote the hard sharing-rule limit of 300 as the design target rather than the performance-recommended 100.

practices.practice: Collaborative Forecasts is driven by the forecast hierarchy, which is generated from the user role hierarchy. A user with no role cannot participate in forecasting — so 'give the skewed owner no role' is not available for any identity that must forecast.
practices.specifics: The forecast hierarchy is generated from the user role hierarchy; you enable users and assign forecast managers onto nodes the role hierarchy already provides — you cannot add or remove nodes in the forecast hierarchy directly. Users need the 'View Roles and Role Hierarchy' permission to open the forecasts page in Lightning Experience (assigned to forecast users by default).
practices.why_it_matters: This is the direct constraint that blocks the standard ownership-skew mitigation. It also means role changes made for sharing reasons silently re-shape forecast rollups.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe the forecast hierarchy as an independently editable structure ('add a node for the new region'), and advise removing a heavy-owning sales ops user from the role hierarchy without noting that it drops them out of forecasting entirely.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: 'View Roles and Role Hierarchy' permission to access the forecasts page in Lightning Experience.

practices.practice: Use the User Access Summary and Object Access Summary for access reviews instead of hand-building permission matrices — they answer 'why does this user have this?' with a provenance trail.
practices.specifics: Winter '25. Setup > Users > (user) > User Access Summary shows user permissions, object and field permissions, custom permissions, and public group and queue memberships. The row-level action 'Access Granted From' shows which profile / permission set / permission set group granted each permission. Object Manager > (object) > Object Access is a read-only summary of every permission set, permission set group and profile granting CRUD on that object.
practices.why_it_matters: Access reviews previously required exporting ObjectPermissions and PermissionSetAssignment and joining them offline; the provenance ('Access Granted From') is the part that was hardest to reconstruct.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: For 'how do I audit what this user can see', LLMs still reach for the AppExchange 'User Access and Permissions Assistant' package or hand-rolled SOQL against ObjectPermissions. Both are now second-best: the native summary shipped in Winter '25 and includes group/queue membership, which the SOQL approach usually omits.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: The User object OWD is Private by default; seeing other users' records requires the 'View All Users' permission. 'Manage Users' is required to edit.

practices.practice: Automate joiner/mover access with User Access Policies rather than manual permission-set assignment, but design around the 200-active-policy ceiling and the fact that policies cannot chain.
practices.specifics: Up to 200 active User Access Policies at a time. GA in Summer '24. A policy can assign or remove permission sets, permission set groups, permission set licenses, and package licenses, and add or remove users from public groups and queues. Triggers on user create, user update, or both. Filter logic between conditions is not supported — all criteria must be met (AND only). A policy must be deactivated before it can be edited. One policy cannot trigger another.
practices.why_it_matters: Teams design a policy-per-permutation model (role x region x department) and blow past 200 policies, or assume OR logic and ship a policy that never matches anyone.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs recommend a record-triggered Flow on the User object for automatic permission assignment, which hits MIXED_DML_OPERATION on setup objects and has no native migration mode. They are generally unaware User Access Policies exist, and when they are, they assume OR filter logic and editable-while-active policies.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: 'Manage User Access Policies' permission.

practices.practice: Refer to the territory feature as Sales Territories (formerly Enterprise Territory Management) and size the design against the per-model territory ceiling and the per-edition model count before committing to a territory taxonomy.
practices.specifics: Renamed from Enterprise Territory Management to Sales Territories in Summer '24. Default limit 1,000 territories per territory model. Maximum by edition: Developer 1,000, Enterprise 1,000, Performance 20,000, Unlimited 20,000 — increases require a Salesforce Support limit-increase request. Territory model count: 2 in Enterprise Edition; 4 in Developer, Performance and Unlimited (production and sandbox). API/metadata names are unchanged: Territory2, Territory2Model, Territory2Type, ObjectTerritory2Association.
practices.why_it_matters: A model-per-scenario planning approach (current / proposed / next-FY / archive) exceeds Enterprise Edition's two-model cap, and there is no way to hold an archived model alongside two live ones.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs still call it 'Enterprise Territory Management' and often confuse the per-model territory cap with the model cap. They also frequently repeat the third-party figure of 99,999 territories for Performance/Unlimited; the official article says 20,000.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Sales Territories is available in Performance and Developer Editions, and in Enterprise and Unlimited Editions with Sales Cloud.

practices.practice: Original Territory Management was retired in Summer '21. Do not write guidance that presents it as a live alternative or as something an org might still have enabled — and export territory-derived Share records before any territory migration.
practices.specifics: Original Territory Management retired for all customers as of Summer '21; after retirement users could not access the feature or its underlying data. Migration guidance was to export Share records for Accounts, Opportunities, Contacts and Cases that were generated by territory rule execution, because those shares disappear with the feature.
practices.why_it_matters: Territory-generated shares are the access grant for the whole field organisation. Losing them without an export means rebuilding record access from scratch with no source of truth for what it used to be.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs present 'Territory Management vs Enterprise Territory Management' as a live architectural choice and tell admins to check Setup > Territory Management to see which one is active. In any org today only Sales Territories exists; the comparison is historical.

practices.practice: Setting a child object's OWD to Controlled by Parent removes the implicit-sharing scan that makes parent-child skew expensive — but it also permanently removes the ability to share individual child records, breaking every existing sharing rule and manual share on that object.
practices.specifics: Parent-child skew threshold: >10,000 children under one parent. Implicit sharing grants read on the parent when a user gains access to a child; on access loss Salesforce must scan all siblings of that parent to decide whether the implicit parent share survives. Controlled by Parent eliminates that scan. Trigger: a single-record OwnerId change on one child fires the full sibling scan — this is not a bulk-only problem.
practices.why_it_matters: The OWD change is the cheap fix and the expensive one simultaneously: it fixes the performance problem and silently voids independent child access grants across the whole org.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs recommend Controlled by Parent as a pure performance win and never mention that existing sharing rules and manual shares on the child object stop functioning. They also frame implicit-sharing cost as a data-load concern only, missing that one record edit triggers the same scan.

practices.practice: Manually recalculate sharing rules only when updates have failed or access is demonstrably wrong — the org is effectively locked for the duration, and the duration must be measured on a full-copy sandbox first.
practices.specifics: Setup > Security > Sharing Settings, Recalculate buttons on each object's Sharing Rules related list. Salesforce emails the admin when group membership and sharing rule recalculation completes. Official guidance: 'Manually recalculate sharing rules only if updates have failed or record access isn't working as expected.' The Recalculate button is disabled while group membership or sharing rule calculations are deferred. Benchmark on a full-copy sandbox — elapsed time there approximates production.
practices.why_it_matters: Recalculation on a large org is a multi-hour, org-impacting operation, and admins routinely press Recalculate as a first-line troubleshooting reflex during business hours.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs suggest 'click Recalculate' as a harmless first step when a user reports missing records. It is neither harmless nor usually the fix — the far more common causes are OWD, Grant Access Using Hierarchies being off for a custom object, or the record simply not matching the sharing rule criteria.

practices.practice: Public groups are a sharing/notification construct and cannot own records; queues own records and can be the OwnerId. Nesting public groups deeply is what makes membership changes expensive, so keep group structures flat in large orgs.
practices.specifics: Queues can be assigned as record owner and any member can take ownership; queue members can be individual users, public groups, roles, and roles-and-subordinates. Public groups can contain users, roles, roles-and-subordinates, and other public groups — nested groups multiply the sharing-table rows written on every membership change, and each nesting level participates in the org-wide group membership lock.
practices.why_it_matters: A 'group of groups of groups' regional model looks tidy in a design doc and turns a single user's group addition into a long-running recalculation that blocks concurrent provisioning.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe queues and public groups as near-interchangeable 'ways to group users' and sometimes propose assigning a record's OwnerId to a public group. That is invalid — only a User or a Queue Group can be an OwnerId. They also treat group nesting as free.

practices.practice: Fix the sharing-precedence mental model before touching configuration: OWD sets the floor, then role hierarchy (if Grant Access Using Hierarchies applies), sharing rules, teams, manual shares and Apex managed sharing each only ADD access. Nothing in that chain subtracts.
practices.specifics: Sharing mechanisms are strictly additive — Account Teams 'can only add access, not reduce access'. The only subtractive controls are Restriction Rules and Scoping Rules, which operate on top of, not inside, the sharing chain. Account Team members can be granted Read or Read/Write on the Account and, independently, on related Opportunities, Contacts and Cases — never Create or Delete.
practices.why_it_matters: Every 'how do I take access away from this group' requirement is answered wrongly if the additive model is not understood; the correct answer is restriction rules or a lower OWD, never a narrower sharing rule.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs propose 'create a sharing rule that removes access' or 'set the team member access to Private to revoke'. Neither exists. They also confuse Account Teams (which grant access on related Opportunities/Contacts/Cases as a side effect) with Opportunity Teams, and assume teams work under a Public Read/Write OWD, where they add nothing at all.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Account Teams and Opportunity Teams must be explicitly enabled in Setup; they are off by default.

skills/admin/mass-transfer-ownership/SKILL.md line 57 — the decision table scopes 'Setup -> Data Management -> Mass Transfer Records' to '<50k records on standard objects (Accounts, Leads, Opportunities)'. The tool's documented limit is 250 records per run, and Opportunities are not among the objects it supports (Leads, Accounts and custom objects only). Anyone following this table will plan a 50,000-record transfer around a tool that silently processes the first 250. Sources: https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=platform.admin_transfer.htm&type=5 and https://www.shellblack.com/administration/using-the-mass-transfer-wizards/

skills/admin/data-skew-and-sharing-performance/SKILL.md line 76 — quotes the lock error as 'could not obtain lock'. The DRAES Group Membership Locking page documents the string as 'could not acquire lock'. The skill's own trigger list (line 13) uses the correct 'could not acquire lock', so the body contradicts the frontmatter and half of any string search for the real error will miss. Source: https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_group_membership_locking.htm

skills/admin/enterprise-territory-management/SKILL.md lines 3, 52, 131, 234 — treats Legacy/Original Territory Management as a currently-enableable feature that could be active in an org ('check Setup > Territory Management. If it shows "Enterprise Territory Management", ETM is active. Legacy Territory Management is no longer recommended'). Original Territory Management was retired for all customers in Summer '21; after retirement users could not access the feature or its data. The skill also never uses the current product name, Sales Territories (renamed from Enterprise Territory Management in Summer '24). Sources: https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=release-notes.rn_sales_other_changes_territory_management_retirement.htm&type=5&language=en_US&release=230 and https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000396697&language=en_US&type=1

areas.area: Reports, dashboards, folders, and org-wide reporting governance (report types, filters/formulas, LDV report performance, dashboard running users, folder sharing model, historical trending/reporting snapshots, change control, Setup Audit Trail)

practices.practice: Set a Custom Report Type's Deployment Status to Deployed before telling anyone it exists; while it is 'In Development' only users with 'Manage Custom Report Types' can see it in the report-type picker.
practices.specifics: Setup > Report Types > [type] > Deployment Status = In Development | Deployed. In Development hides the report type from the New Report picker for everyone except users with the 'Manage Custom Report Types' permission (effectively System Administrators). A CRT's status silently flips back from Deployed to In Development if its primary object is a custom or external object whose own Deployment Status changes to In Development.
practices.why_it_matters: The single most common 'the report type isn't there' ticket. Nothing errors — the entry is simply absent from the picker, so the admin who built it (and can see it) cannot reproduce the user's problem.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked 'why can't my users see my custom report type?', an LLM walks through object permissions, profile access, and folder sharing — none of which apply, because report types are not shared by folder and are not FLS-gated. It almost never names Deployment Status, and it never mentions the cascade from the primary object's own deployment status.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Manage Custom Report Types (user permission) — the only permission that can see In Development report types

practices.practice: Never claim a custom report type has a '60-field display limit'. 60 is the cap on OBJECT REFERENCES per report type; the field cap is 1,000; and a separate runtime cap errors any report whose columns span more than 20 different objects.
practices.specifics: Per report type: up to 60 object references (every referenced object counts even if you select no fields from it, and lookup-reachable objects count — 4 object relationships + 56 lookup objects = 60). Up to 1,000 fields per report type. At runtime, a report built on a CRT with columns from more than 20 different objects errors out. Max 4 objects in the primary relationship chain (A-B-C-D).
practices.why_it_matters: Teams building 'kitchen sink' report types blow the 20-object runtime cap long before the 1,000-field cap and get an error that names none of these numbers.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs repeat the folk-wisdom '60 fields' number (it is in this repo too) and never mention the 20-different-objects runtime error, so they advise 'just add fewer fields' when the actual fix is to prune lookup-reached objects.

practices.practice: Turning OFF Historical Trending for an object permanently deletes all of that object's historical data, its historical trending report type, and every report built on it. Treat enabling/disabling it as a one-way door.
practices.specifics: Supported objects: Opportunity, Case, Forecasting Items, plus up to 3 custom objects — Leads are NOT supported. Retention: previous 3 months plus the current month (12 months of Opportunity history only if Historical Trending in Pipeline Inspection is enabled). Up to 5,000,000 rows of historical trending data per object (alert at 70%). Per report: max 100 fields, max 5 historical snapshot dates, max 4 historical filters. Turning trending off for a single field and then deleting the field destroys that field's history even if trending is re-enabled later.
practices.why_it_matters: There is no retroactive backfill and no undelete. An admin who toggles the checkbox to free a custom-object slot destroys the only historical record the business has.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs list Leads and Forecasts as trending-enabled objects, describe the retention as a rolling 3 months, and describe disabling as reversible ('just turn it back on'). They also invent an '8 snapshots per record' limit; the real limit is 5 snapshot dates per report.

practices.practice: Historical trend reports must be Matrix format — request a summary or tabular historical trend report through the API and it is refused outright.
practices.specifics: Historical trend reporting does not support summary format, tabular views in Lightning, row-limit filters, formula fields, dynamic exchange rates, exports, or subscriptions. In Lightning the snapshot date must be the primary row grouping.
practices.why_it_matters: Half the natural requests ('email me the weekly pipeline-change report') are structurally impossible on historical trending, and the platform only tells you at run time.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM will happily design a 'historical trend summary report subscribed weekly to the sales team' — three separately unsupported things in one sentence — because none of them look unusual for ordinary reports.
practices.verbatim_error_string: Historical trend data is unavailable in the report format requested. Change the report format to matrix and try again.

practices.practice: Report and dashboard SUBFOLDERS cannot be shared independently — every subfolder and every report inside it inherits the root folder's sharing. Architect one root folder per distinct audience, not one root folder with per-team subfolders.
practices.specifics: Up to 3 subfolder levels are allowed under a report or dashboard folder. Sharing (Viewer / Editor / Manager) is settable only on the root folder; subfolders inherit and the share panel is not editable on them. Subfolder names must be unique. Creating one requires 'Create Report Folders' (or 'Create Dashboard Folders') plus Manage access on the root folder.
practices.why_it_matters: The obvious folder design — 'Reports' root with 'Sales', 'Service', 'Finance' subfolders — grants everyone with root access to all three. Rebuilding the hierarchy afterwards means moving hundreds of reports and reissuing every share.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs reason from Windows/SharePoint mental models and confidently describe per-subfolder permissions with inheritance-break. They then recommend exactly the folder tree that leaks data.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Create Report Folders / Create Dashboard Folders (user permission) + Manage access on the parent folder

practices.practice: Audit who holds 'Manage Reports in Public Folders' — it grants edit and delete on EVERY public report folder regardless of that folder's sharing, and it is the permission that silently defeats a carefully built folder model.
practices.specifics: Under enhanced folder sharing, 'Manage Reports in Public Folders' replaces the legacy 'Manage Public Reports' + 'View All Data' pair. It confers create-folder rights plus edit on any report in any folder. 'Edit My Reports' is the narrow alternative: edit only reports the user created, in folders they can already save to. Companion perms: 'Create and Customize Reports', 'Run Reports', 'Export Reports', 'Create Report Folders'.
practices.why_it_matters: Standard quarterly access review misses it because it is a report permission, not a data permission — yet it is an org-wide write grant over the reporting layer.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked to design report folder security, an LLM produces a Viewer/Editor/Manager sharing matrix and stops. It does not enumerate the user permissions that bypass the matrix entirely, so the design is audited as compliant while being fully bypassed.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Manage Reports in Public Folders (user permission) — bypasses folder sharing

practices.practice: 'Export Reports' is a separate user permission from 'Run Reports' — revoke it independently when the requirement is 'they can see it but not take it away', and know that Formatted and Details-Only exports have completely different row caps.
practices.specifics: Export requires the 'Export Reports' user permission (Run Reports alone is not enough). Formatted Report export: .xlsx only, up to 100,000 rows and 100 columns for tabular and summary reports, but only 2,000 rows and 100 columns for matrix reports. Details Only export: .xls or .csv, effectively unbounded rows (your spreadsheet's 1,048,576-row ceiling binds first). Long text and rich text fields are truncated to 255 characters in export.
practices.why_it_matters: 'Export to Excel and you'll get everything' is false for matrix reports (2,000 rows) and for any report over 100,000 rows in Formatted mode. Analysts silently lose data.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs state flatly that 'the 2,000-row UI cap does not apply to exports' — true for Details Only, false for Formatted Report on a matrix report, where the cap is still 2,000. This repo currently ships the wrong version.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Export Reports (user permission)

practices.practice: Dynamic dashboards are capped per org by edition, deleted ones in the Recycle Bin still count against the cap, and they cannot live in a private folder, be scheduled, or be subscribed to.
practices.specifics: Enterprise: 5. Unlimited/Performance: 10. Developer: 3. Requires the 'Manage Dynamic Dashboards' user permission to create/edit/delete. Dynamic dashboards refresh manually only — no scheduled refresh, no subscription. Dashboards deleted into the Recycle Bin continue to consume the allowance until purged. Additional allowances are sold per Enablement licence (+1 each), not self-service.
practices.why_it_matters: Orgs hit the cap, delete an old dynamic dashboard to make room, and the error persists — because the deleted one is still counted until the Recycle Bin is emptied.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe the limit as 'maximum simultaneous running users' (it is a count of dashboards), omit the Developer Edition value, and never mention the Recycle Bin behaviour — which is precisely the fact that unblocks the ticket. This repo's fundamentals skill currently uses the 'running users' phrasing.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Manage Dynamic Dashboards (user permission); additional dynamic dashboards require purchased Enablement licences
practices.verbatim_error_string: You reached the limit for dashboards run as the logged-in user.

practices.practice: A 'Run as specified user' dashboard breaks completely when that user is deactivated, and it breaks on deploy when that user does not exist in the target org. Set 'Run as logged-in user' before packaging or deploying, and monitor running users in the deactivation checklist.
practices.specifics: If the running user is inactive, nobody can open the dashboard — reactivate, change the running user, save, deactivate again is the only supported workaround. Deploying a dashboard whose running user is absent in the target org fails validation. A dashboard delivered by a managed package arrives with no 'View dashboard as' user configured at all.
practices.why_it_matters: User deactivation is a routine offboarding step that silently takes out executive dashboards, and the dashboard names no user in its error.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLM offboarding checklists cover record ownership transfer, queue membership, and Apex scheduled jobs — never dashboard running users or reporting-snapshot running users, both of which fail closed and silently on deactivation.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: The running user must hold 'Run Reports' and have folder access to the source reports
practices.verbatim_error_string: Error: The running user for this dashboard doesn't have permission to run reports. Your system administrator should select a different running user for this dashboard.

practices.practice: Do not describe report subscriptions as 'running as the report owner'. Each Lightning subscription has its own running user, defaulting to the subscriber; setting it to someone else needs a named permission and is what actually leaks data to recipients.
practices.specifics: Permissions: 'Subscribe to Reports' (self), 'Subscribe to Reports: Add Recipients' (other users), 'Subscribe to Reports: Send to Groups and Roles' (roles, roles & subordinates, public groups), 'Subscribe to Reports: Set Running User' (choose Another Person; also needs View All Data). Up to 5 conditions can gate whether the email sends. Subscription attachments are capped at 15,000 rows, 30 columns, and 3 MB. Per-user subscription allowance: 15 reports and 15 dashboards on Unlimited Edition, 7 on other editions. Org-wide: 500 report and 500 dashboard subscriptions per hour.
practices.why_it_matters: Recipients see exactly what the running user sees, which may be far more than their own access — the official doc says so explicitly. Getting the mechanism backwards means auditing the wrong thing.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs assert either 'subscriptions run as the report owner' or 'subscriptions run as each recipient' — both wrong, and this repo currently ships BOTH contradictory claims in two different skills. The truth is one running user per subscription, defaulting to the subscription's creator.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Subscribe to Reports: Set Running User (+ View All Data) to run as another person; Subscribe to Reports: Add Recipients to send to anyone else
practices.verbatim_error_string: Recipients see the same report data as the person running the report. It's possible that they see more or less data than they normally see in Salesforce.

practices.practice: A joined report's CHART can go on a dashboard; the joined report itself cannot. And a dashboard containing only joined-report widgets cannot be filtered at all.
practices.specifics: Joined reports support up to 5 blocks, up to 100 columns per block, up to 10 custom summary formulas per block and 50 per report, and up to 10 cross-block formulas. Not supported in joined reports: bucket fields, cross filters, row-level formulas, conditional highlighting, and the Rows to Display filter. You cannot add a dashboard filter to a dashboard whose widgets are all joined reports. Joined report timeout is fixed at 10 minutes and cannot be extended by Support.
practices.why_it_matters: Joined reports are the standard LLM answer to 'combine two objects', and they lose the exact features (buckets, cross filters, dashboard filters) that the rest of the design depends on.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs reach for joined reports whenever two objects are mentioned, then bolt on bucket fields and a dashboard filter — a combination the platform rejects. This repo currently states the dashboard rule inverted (claims charts are unsupported and tables are supported; it is the opposite).

practices.practice: You can put a report with a bucket field on a dashboard, but you cannot use the bucketed field as a dashboard filter — design the bucket as a real formula field if it must be filterable at the dashboard level.
practices.specifics: Bucket limits: 5 bucket fields per report, 20 buckets per bucket field, 20 values per bucket. Dashboard limits: 5 filters per dashboard, 50 values per filter, 25 widgets of which at most 20 are charts and tables, 1,000 groupings per widget. Dashboard filters only bind to a component when the source report has a filterable filter on the same field.
practices.why_it_matters: The failure is silent: the component simply does not respond to the filter, and there is no indicator on the dashboard telling the viewer which components a filter reached.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs design a bucket field precisely so it can become a dashboard filter ('bucket Amount into Small/Mid/Enterprise, then filter the dashboard by tier'). That specific combination is unsupported, and no error is raised.
practices.already_covered_by: admin/reports-and-dashboards-fundamentals (partial — dashboard-filter silent no-op is covered in gotchas.md; the bucket-field-not-filterable rule and the current 25-widget/5-filter numbers are not)

practices.practice: Row-level formulas are capped at 2 per report referencing at most 5 unique fields each, always evaluate in the org's DEFAULT currency regardless of the report's currency setting, and are mutually exclusive with cross filters, bucket columns and 'with or without' report types.
practices.specifics: Max 2 row-level formulas per report; each references up to 5 unique fields. Cannot reference bucket fields, summary formulas, or another row-level formula. Unsupported field types include Boolean, Timeonly, Email, Phone, Multiselect picklist, and some date/text fields (Due Date, Birthdate, Billing Address). Unavailable on joined reports, on historical fields in historical trend reports, in reporting snapshots, in Salesforce Classic, and via the Apex/Analytics API. Must be created from the OUTLINE panel, not the Fields panel.
practices.why_it_matters: The default-currency behaviour is a silent numeric wrongness in every multi-currency org — the report shows converted amounts in the column beside a formula computed on unconverted values.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs treat row-level formulas as a general-purpose formula surface and write four of them referencing bucket fields and other formulas. They never flag the multi-currency behaviour, which produces plausible-looking but wrong money.

practices.practice: A report with 100 or more columns cannot be run at all — the Analytics API refuses it, and detail columns, summaries and custom summary formulas all count toward the 100.
practices.specifics: Also enforced: max 20 field filters in the report builder (10 in the legacy wizard), 3 cross filters per report with up to 5 subfilters each, 5 custom summary formulas per report. Filter logic applies only to field filters, never to cross filters.
practices.why_it_matters: Wide 'export everything' report types are built column by column until one save makes the report permanently unrunnable, and the column count is not displayed anywhere in the builder.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs generate report specs with 120+ columns for 'data extract' use cases and never mention a column cap; they also assume filter logic (1 AND (2 OR 3)) governs cross filters, which it does not.
practices.verbatim_error_string: Only a report with fewer than 100 columns can be run. The columns are fields specified as detail columns, summaries, or custom summary formulas. Remove unneeded columns from the report and try again.

practices.practice: You cannot delete a report that a dashboard component points at — the platform blocks it. Use this as the enforcement point for deprecate-then-delete: rename with a DEPRECATED_ prefix, watch for complaints, then delete.
practices.specifics: Deleting a report referenced by any dashboard returns HTTP 403 from the Analytics API and is blocked in the UI. Deleted reports go to the Recycle Bin. Separately, turning off 'Allow Reports' on a custom object, or changing that object's relationships, makes every report built on it obsolete rather than deleting it.
practices.why_it_matters: It is the one place Salesforce natively enforces dependency-before-delete in the reporting layer, and it is the only signal an admin gets that a report is load-bearing.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLM cleanup plans say 'delete reports not run in 12 months' with no dependency step, and never mention that the platform will refuse — so the plan's own failure mode is presented as an unexpected error rather than the designed guard rail.
practices.verbatim_error_string: The report can't be deleted because there are one or more dashboards referencing it.

practices.practice: Reporting snapshots insert at most 2,000 new records per run and continue on partial field-mapping failure — check Run History after every scheduled run, not just after setup.
practices.specifics: A snapshot run adds up to 2,000 new records to the target object; beyond that the extra rows are silently not recorded. If a field mapping fails the snapshot still runs and Run History records a partial error. A blank Total Row Number in Run History means the run failed before the report completed. Snapshot runs fail when the running user lacks 'Run Reports'/'Create and Customize Reports', lacks folder access to the source report, lacks Create on the target object, or is inactive. Creating snapshots needs the 'Manage Reporting Snapshots' permission.
practices.why_it_matters: A snapshot that silently truncates at 2,000 rows produces a trend line that is wrong in a way nobody can see months later, because each point looks internally consistent.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs recommend reporting snapshots as the general workaround for historical trending's 3-month window without ever mentioning the 2,000-row-per-run ceiling, so the recommendation quietly fails on exactly the large datasets that motivated it.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Manage Reporting Snapshots (user permission); running user needs Run Reports + folder access + Create on the target object

practices.practice: Reports are cancelled at 10 minutes. Before asking Support for the extension, know that it only goes to 20 minutes, only for tabular/summary/matrix, and never for joined reports.
practices.specifics: "If your report takes longer than 10 minutes to complete, Salesforce cancels the report." Support can raise it to 20 minutes for tabular, summary and matrix reports; joined reports stay at 10. Report filtering is fastest on search-optimized fields: Id, Name, OwnerId, CreatedDate, SystemModStamp, RecordType, master-detail fields, lookup fields, and custom fields flagged External ID. Standard indexes are used when the filter matches under 30% of the first million records and under 15% of additional records; custom indexes under 10% and 5% respectively.
practices.why_it_matters: Removing a date filter to 'see everything' converts a selective index range scan into a full scan and makes timeouts certain rather than occasional.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs advise adding a custom index for report performance without stating the selectivity thresholds, so users index a field whose filter matches 40% of rows and see no change — then conclude indexing 'doesn't work' on Salesforce.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Timeout extension to 20 minutes requires a Salesforce Support case
practices.already_covered_by: admin/report-performance-tuning (partial — the 10-minute timeout and selective-filter principle are covered; the 20-minute Support ceiling, the joined-report exclusion, and the 30%/15% and 10%/5% index thresholds are not)

practices.practice: The Analytics API caps concurrent and hourly report runs long before any governor limit fires — budget 500 synchronous runs per hour before designing anything that runs reports programmatically.
practices.specifics: 500 synchronous report runs per hour; 1,200 asynchronous requests per hour; 20 concurrent synchronous requests; 200 concurrent asynchronous requests; 2,000 report instances returned; 200 dashboard refreshes per hour; 5,000 dashboard-results requests per hour. The synchronous GET endpoint still returns only 2,000 rows — use POST /analytics/reports/{id}/instances for full detail.
practices.why_it_matters: Middleware and 'report-to-Slack' automations hit the 500/hour wall in a burst and receive a plain 403 that does not look like a rate limit.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs write Apex/integration code that calls the Analytics API in a loop over accounts, assuming the only relevant limit is the 100-callout governor limit. The binding constraint is 500 report runs per org per hour, shared with every human clicking Run.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Run Reports (user permission) on the integration user
practices.verbatim_error_string: You can't run more than <number> reports synchronously every 60 minutes. Try again later.
practices.already_covered_by: admin/report-performance-tuning (partial — the sync-vs-async 2,000-row trap is covered in gotchas.md; the 500/hr, 1,200/hr and concurrency caps are not)

practices.practice: Reports and dashboards in Private folders, 'Unfiled Public Reports', and the Classic personal folders cannot be deployed at all — move them into a named custom folder before any change set or Metadata API deploy.
practices.specifics: Non-deployable: My Personal Custom Reports, Unfiled Public Reports / Public Reports (Classic), My Personal Dashboards, Private Dashboards. package.xml must reference the folder's API Name (DeveloperName), not its label, and the ReportFolder / DashboardFolder must exist in or be included in the package before the Report / Dashboard member.
practices.why_it_matters: Reports living in private folders are invisible to admins, un-auditable, un-deployable, and lost when the owner is deactivated — a governance failure that only surfaces at deploy time.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs write package.xml with the folder's display name (with spaces) and omit the ReportFolder member entirely, producing a deploy that validates locally and fails in the org with a folder error nobody expected for a 'report-only' change.
practices.verbatim_error_string: Cannot find folder: <folder_name>

practices.practice: A custom object is invisible to the report builder until 'Allow Reports' is ticked on the object definition, and un-ticking it later marks every existing report on that object obsolete rather than deleting it.
practices.specifics: Setup > Object Manager > [object] > Edit > Optional Features > Allow Reports. Without it the object never appears under Other Reports and no custom report type can use it as primary. 'Allow Search' is an independent checkbox, off by default on new custom objects.
practices.why_it_matters: This is a design-time decision made in the object-creation wizard, months before anyone asks for a report; by then the fix requires an edit to a production object definition.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs designing a custom object list Label, Plural, Record Name, and Deployment Status but omit Allow Reports / Allow Search / Allow Activities / Track Field History — the four Optional Features checkboxes that determine whether the object is usable a year later.
practices.verbatim_error_string: The report definition is obsolete. Your administrator has disabled all reports for the custom object, or its relationships have changed.
practices.already_covered_by: admin/object-creation-and-design (mentions 'Allow Reports'; verify whether the obsolete-report error string and the Allow Search default are present)

practices.practice: Setup Audit Trail retains only 180 days, shows only the 20 most recent entries in the UI, and does not record report or dashboard edits at all — schedule a weekly export of SetupAuditTrail to external storage or the evidence is gone.
practices.specifics: 180-day (six month) retention, permanently deleted afterwards with no native extension. The Setup UI lists the 20 most recent entries; Download exports the full 180 days as CSV. The SetupAuditTrail object is queryable via REST, SOAP and Tooling API (available since API v15.0). Viewing requires 'View Setup and Configuration'. It captures setup/metadata configuration changes only — not record data changes, not report runs, not report exports.
practices.why_it_matters: Most compliance frameworks demand 12 months or more of configuration-change evidence; Salesforce gives 180 days by default and the org only discovers the gap during an audit.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe Setup Audit Trail as a complete audit log covering 'all changes' and confuse its 180-day retention with Field Audit Trail's 10-year field-history retention (a different, Shield-licensed feature on a different object).
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: View Setup and Configuration (user permission) to read it; extending retention beyond 180 days is not purchasable — Field Audit Trail (Shield) covers field history, not setup history
practices.already_covered_by: security/security-incident-response (SKILL.md line 65 documents the 180-day SetupAuditTrail retention table); the 20-entry UI cap and the 'does not log report/dashboard edits' gap are NOT covered

practices.practice: The ReportExport event type only captures 'Details Only' exports — Formatted Report and XLSX Detail exports appear under the Report event type instead. Auditing exfiltration on ReportExport alone misses the most common export path.
practices.specifics: EventLogFile ReportExport records Details Only (.csv) exports. Formatted Report and XLSX Detail exports are recorded only under the Report event type. Event log files are available after 24 hours for all customers, hourly for Event Monitoring customers; retention is 1 day without the add-on and 30 days with it.
practices.why_it_matters: An insider-threat investigation that queries only ReportExport concludes 'no data left the org' when the user clicked the default export option in Lightning.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Every LLM answer on tracking report exports names ReportExport and stops. This repo currently states 'ReportExport — records every report exported to CSV/Excel', which is false for the Excel half.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Salesforce Shield or the Event Monitoring add-on licence (Enterprise, Performance, Unlimited, Developer editions) — without it, event log files retain 1 day and hourly generation is unavailable
practices.already_covered_by: security/security-incident-response (references ReportExport and the 30-day Event Monitoring retention); the Details-Only-vs-Formatted split is NOT covered and is stated incorrectly there

practices.practice: Report and dashboard subscriptions do not deliver from a newly created or refreshed sandbox — Email Deliverability defaults to 'System email only', which excludes subscription emails.
practices.specifics: New and refreshed sandboxes default to Access level = System email only under Setup > Deliverability, allowing only automatically generated mail (new user, password reset). Subscription and workflow email requires switching to All email. Separately, sandbox copy appends '.invalid' to every user's email address, so even with All email nothing routes.
practices.why_it_matters: UAT signs off 'subscriptions work' because nobody noticed the emails never arrived, and the first real send happens in production untested.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLM sandbox test plans say 'subscribe to the report and confirm the email arrives' without the two prerequisite steps, so the test is designed to produce a false negative that reads as a false positive.
practices.already_covered_by: admin/sandbox-post-refresh-automation (verify — likely covers .invalid emails and deliverability generally, but not the report-subscription consequence)

practices.practice: Enabling Enhanced Folder Sharing rewrites every existing folder's access model in one shot — legacy 'accessible by all users' folders become View for All Internal Users, and role/group access collapses to View. Model the blast radius before flipping it.
practices.specifics: Enhanced folder sharing gives three levels: View, Edit, Manage. Folders created under it carry no visibility/access type — only a name. On enablement: folders previously readable by all users get View for the All Internal Users group; hidden folders stay unshared; role- and group-scoped access converts to View only. Legacy folder sharing has been retired, so all orgs are on enhanced sharing; orgs created Summer '13 or later were born with it.
practices.why_it_matters: Editors silently become viewers across the whole org at the moment of enablement, and there is no per-folder preview of the conversion.
