areas.area: DevOps and Release Engineering (source tracking, packaging, deployment, test levels, CI/CD auth, sandbox/scratch strategy, rollback)

practices.practice: State the silent test default explicitly: a metadata deploy to a sandbox or Developer Edition org runs ZERO Apex tests unless you pass a testLevel. Only production auto-runs tests, and only when the package contains Apex classes or triggers.
practices.specifics: Metadata API deploy(): default in non-production = no tests at all. Production default = RunLocalTests, and only triggered when the deployment package contains Apex classes or triggers. testLevel enum is exactly: NoTestRun, RunSpecifiedTests, RunRelevantTests (beta), RunLocalTests, RunAllTestsInOrg. Since API 34.0 you can pass RunLocalTests in a sandbox to mirror production. `sf project deploy start --test-level` default is documented as 'Depends on deployment contents'.
practices.why_it_matters: A team validates in a Full sandbox, sees 'Succeeded', then the identical package fails production with a coverage/test failure — because the sandbox deploy never ran a single test. This is the single most common 'it worked in UAT' deployment surprise.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs assert 'Salesforce runs all local tests on every deployment' or 'the default test level is RunLocalTests' without qualifying by org type. They then write a CI sandbox stage with no --test-level flag and call it a gate. It is not a gate — it runs no tests. They also frequently list only four testLevel values, omitting RunRelevantTests (beta), and some invent 'RunAllTests' which is not a valid enum member.

practices.practice: Never set purgeOnDelete / --purge-on-delete in a production pipeline — it is silently unavailable there. The option only works in Developer Edition and sandbox orgs.
practices.specifics: Metadata API deploy() `purgeOnDelete`: 'If true, the deleted components in the destructiveChanges.xml manifest file aren't stored in the Recycle Bin.' Restricted to Developer Edition and sandbox orgs; it does not function in production. CLI equivalent is `--purge-on-delete` on `sf project deploy start`, default false.
practices.why_it_matters: Pipelines that assume purge worked leave deleted components sitting in the production Recycle Bin, where they still consume storage and still block re-creating a component with the same API name until the bin is emptied.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs generate a production destructive-changes step with `--purge-on-delete` on, and describe it as 'permanently removes the components so they can't be restored'. In production the flag is a no-op, so the components ARE recoverable and the API-name collision the user was trying to avoid still happens.

practices.practice: Deleting a roll-up summary field through the Metadata API bypasses the Recycle Bin unconditionally — purgeOnDelete is irrelevant. There is no undelete.
practices.specifics: 'When you delete a roll-up summary field using Metadata API, the field isn't saved in the Recycle Bin.' Applies regardless of the purgeOnDelete setting. Contrast with normal custom fields, which go to the bin and are restorable for 15 days.
practices.why_it_matters: Roll-up summary fields carry historical aggregate values that cannot be reconstructed by re-creating the field — the new field recalculates from current child records only. Deleting one via destructiveChanges is a permanent data loss event dressed as a metadata change.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs treat all custom fields as uniformly recoverable — 'don't worry, deleted fields go to the Recycle Bin and can be undeleted within 15 days' — and apply that reassurance to roll-up summaries. They also suggest 'delete and re-create the roll-up with a different filter' as a routine refactor, not flagging that the old aggregate values are gone.

practices.practice: destructiveChangesPost.xml deletions are applied BEFORE the deployment's Apex tests run. Do not rely on post-destructive ordering to keep code compiling during the test phase.
practices.specifics: 'Post destructive changes are processed before running any tests.' Also: wildcards are not supported in destructiveChanges manifests; a package.xml with a matching API version must sit in the same directory; and 'If you try to delete some components that don't exist in the organization, the rest of the deletions are still attempted' — a partially-wrong manifest does NOT fail the deploy. destructiveChangesPre.xml / destructiveChangesPost.xml require API 33.0+.
practices.why_it_matters: Teams put field deletions in destructiveChangesPost so that new Apex referencing them deploys first — then the test run compiles against an org where those fields are already gone, and every test fails. The wildcard silence is worse: `<members>*</members>` in a destructive manifest is ignored rather than rejected, so the intended deletion just never happens and the deploy reports success.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs routinely emit `<types><members>*</members><name>CustomField</name></types>` inside destructiveChanges.xml to 'delete all fields', which is silently ignored. They also explain post-destructive ordering as 'deletes happen last, after everything including tests', which is the inverted mechanism.

practices.practice: You cannot delete via destructiveChanges anything wired into an ACTIVE Lightning page — the object, the component on the page, or the page itself. Deactivate/reassign the Lightning page first.
practices.specifics: 'You can't use destructiveChanges.xml to delete items that are associated with an active Lightning page, such as a custom object, a component on the page, or the page itself.'
practices.why_it_matters: This is the reason a field-cleanup destructive deploy fails at the last step of a cutover window with no obvious dependency in the metadata diff — the blocker is a FlexiPage assignment, which does not show up in an Apex/Flow dependency scan.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs enumerate dependency blockers as 'Apex, Flows, validation rules, formula fields, page layouts' and stop there. FlexiPage/Lightning-page assignment is almost always omitted, so the generated pre-flight checklist misses the actual failure.

practices.practice: Promoting an unlocked or 2GP package version to released is a one-way door — the same version number can never be promoted again and the promotion cannot be undone.
practices.specifics: 'You can promote and release only once for each package version number, and you can't undo this change.' Command: `sf package version promote --package "Expense Manager@1.3.0-7"`. Success message: 'Successfully promoted the package version, ID: [ID] to released.' Requires the 'Promote a package version to released' user permission in the Dev Hub org.
practices.why_it_matters: A promoted-by-accident version is permanently burned. For 2GP managed you also cannot revert a released version to beta at all (1GP could, via a support case), so the only path forward is a new version number and, if customers installed it, a forced upgrade.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs write CI pipelines that call `sf package version promote` on every successful main-branch build, describing it as 'marking the build as good'. They present it as a reversible label. They also confuse it with `sf package version delete` and claim you can 'un-promote' by deleting — deleting is also permanent and additionally breaks any subscriber that referenced that 04t.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Dev Hub user permission: 'Promote a package version to released'

practices.practice: A 2GP managed package version created with --skip-validation can NEVER be promoted, because code coverage is not computed for it. Do not use --skip-validation on release-candidate builds.
practices.specifics: 2GP managed promotion requires 'a minimum 75% code coverage requirement. And every Apex Trigger in a package needs test coverage.' Coverage is computed at version-create time via `sf package version create --code-coverage`. 'If you skip validation using the --skip-validation parameter, code coverage isn't calculated for that package version.' A beta with no coverage data fails promotion.
practices.why_it_matters: --skip-validation is the standard advice for cutting scratch-org build time (it can halve version-create duration), so teams adopt it globally — then discover at release time that the RC build is unpromotable and has to be rebuilt from scratch, adding hours to a release window.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs recommend `--skip-validation` as a blanket performance optimisation for package builds without distinguishing throwaway CI betas from release candidates, and without mentioning that it silently disables coverage computation. They also state the coverage bar as 'the same 75% as a metadata deploy', missing the extra rule that EVERY Apex trigger in the package needs coverage.

practices.practice: Once a component is in a released 2GP MANAGED package, removing it does not delete it from subscriber orgs — for almost every metadata type it is only marked deprecated and persists forever. Only a short, specific list is hard-deleted.
practices.specifics: Hard deleted upon upgrade: Apex Class (excluding global classes), Apex Trigger, External Client App Header, External Client App Settings, Platform Event Channel, Platform Event Channel Member, Visualforce Component (excluding global components). Everything else — Custom Field, Custom Object, Flow, Permission Set, Record Type, Validation Rule, Lightning Web Component, Page Layout, Custom Label, Static Resource, Report, Dashboard, Custom Metadata Type Records — is marked deprecated and stays in the subscriber org until an admin manually deletes it. Also: 'If any component in the package depends on or references the component you're removing, the package version creation operation fails.'
practices.why_it_matters: An ISV who ships a custom field then removes it has permanently added that field to every subscriber org. Global Apex classes and global Visualforce components cannot be removed at all. This is the highest-cost irreversible decision in Salesforce packaging.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs say 'just remove it from the package directory and cut a new version' as if 2GP managed behaved like an unlocked package. They do not distinguish hard-delete from deprecate-on-upgrade, do not know the seven hard-deletable types, and never mention that the component-removal capability itself is not on by default.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Component removal for 2GP managed packages is gated: 'Request access to this feature, log a case with Salesforce Partner Support.'

practices.practice: Unlocked packages are the opposite of managed on deletion: released unlocked package versions CAN be deleted — permanently — and any org that later tries to install that version fails.
practices.specifics: For Unlocked Packages the docs answer 'Yes' to 'Can I delete released packages and package versions?' (also Yes for beta). 'Deletion is permanent.' 'Attempts to install a deleted package version will fail.' You must delete all package versions before deleting the package itself, and confirm the package/version is not referenced as a dependency. Requires the 'Delete Second-Generation Packages' user permission.
practices.why_it_matters: Deleting an unlocked package version that a downstream package declared as a dependency breaks every future build of that downstream package, and breaks disaster-recovery reinstalls of any org that had it.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs generalise the managed-package rule ('package versions are immutable and can never be deleted') to unlocked packages, so they never warn about the dependency-breakage risk. Conversely, when they do know deletion is possible, they present it as a tidy-up step for old betas without flagging that installs of that 04t then fail forever.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Dev Hub user permission: 'Delete Second-Generation Packages'

practices.practice: A 2GP package's namespace is fixed at package-create time and can never be changed. Decide namespaced vs no-namespace before the first `sf package create`.
practices.specifics: 'A namespace is a 1–15 character alphanumeric identifier.' It 'is assigned to a second-generation managed package at the time that it's created, and can't be changed.' The Developer Edition org where the namespace is registered must be linked to the Dev Hub. Dev Hub + Second-Generation Managed Packaging must be enabled in the Partner Business Org (PBO).
practices.why_it_matters: Namespace choice changes every API name in the package (`ns__Field__c`), every subscriber integration contract, and every SOQL string in customer Apex. Changing it means shipping a new package and a data migration for every subscriber.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs suggest 'you can add a namespace later once you're ready to distribute' — reasoning from unlocked packages, where you can create a no-namespace package. For a 2GP managed package this is simply false and the advice costs a full re-packaging effort.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Dev Hub + Second-Generation Managed Packaging must be enabled in a Partner Business Org; developers need a user license and a permission set granting Dev Hub access (Limited Access License for Package Developers)

practices.practice: Source tracking is not a sandbox-wide feature. Scratch orgs always have it; only Developer and Developer Pro sandboxes can have it; Partial Copy, Full, Developer Edition orgs and production never can.
practices.specifics: Supports source tracking: scratch orgs (always on), Developer and Developer Pro sandboxes (only if the production org has source tracking enabled). Does NOT support it: Developer Edition orgs, production orgs, Partial Copy sandboxes, Full sandboxes. `sf org enable tracking` 'returns an error if the org doesn't support tracking, such as a Full sandbox.' On a non-tracked org, deploy/retrieve still work 'But the commands don't check for conflicts, and you must specify exactly what you want to deploy or retrieve using an appropriate flag' (--source-dir / --metadata / --manifest).
practices.why_it_matters: Teams design a pull-based developer workflow around `sf project retrieve start` with no flags, then move UAT to a Partial Copy sandbox and the whole workflow stops working — with no conflict detection, so two developers silently overwrite each other.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs write 'enable source tracking on your sandbox' as universal advice and give the same pull/push workflow for every sandbox type. They also claim Partial Copy sandboxes support source tracking because they support sandbox templates — the two are unrelated.

practices.practice: Quote Dev Hub scratch org allocations exactly, and distinguish ACTIVE from DAILY. Developer Edition is 3 active / 6 daily — not 6 active.
practices.specifics: Developer Edition or trial: 3 active, 6 daily. Enterprise Edition: 40 active, 80 daily. Unlimited Edition: 100 active, 200 daily. Performance Edition: 100 active, 200 daily. Active allocation = 'the maximum number of scratch orgs you can have at any given time based on the edition type.' Daily allocation = 'the maximum number of successful scratch org creations you can initiate in a rolling (sliding) 24-hour window.'
practices.why_it_matters: The daily limit is a rolling 24-hour window, not a midnight reset, so a CI system that burns its daily allocation at 09:00 is blocked until 09:00 the next day — not until midnight. Scratch org pool sizing that ignores this deadlocks the pipeline mid-sprint.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs conflate the two numbers and quote the daily figure as the active cap (or vice versa), and almost always describe the daily limit as resetting 'each day' / 'at midnight UTC' rather than on a rolling 24-hour sliding window. That single error makes their CI capacity maths wrong.

practices.practice: The scratch org definition `release` key only accepts "preview" or "previous", and only during a Salesforce release transition window. Outside the window either value errors.
practices.specifics: Transition windows: Spring '26 = January 11 – February 21, 2026; Summer '26 = May 10 – June 13, 2026; Winter '27 = August 30 – October 10, 2026. When the Dev Hub is still on GA: `preview` gives the new release, `previous` errors. When the Dev Hub has already upgraded: `preview` errors, `previous` gives the prior release. Omit the key and the scratch org matches the Dev Hub's version. 'Be sure to set the apiVersion to match the scratch org version' — via `sf config set org-api-version` or the SF_ORG_API_VERSION environment variable.
practices.why_it_matters: This is the only supported way to test a package against the next release before your production org upgrades. Miss the window and there is no fallback — you find out about a breaking change when production upgrades.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs write `"release": "Preview"` (capitalised) or invent values like `"next"`, `"winter26"`, or a version number. They also present the key as always available, so a CI job configured with it breaks the moment the transition window closes — with an error the user cannot map back to a calendar window.

practices.practice: An org shape captures edition, features, limits, boolean Metadata API settings, and the LICENCES of installed packages — but not the packages, not integer/string settings, and not metadata or data. Shape-based scratch orgs are not a sandbox substitute.
practices.specifics: 'Features, Metadata API settings, edition, limits, and licenses determine what we refer to as an org's shape.' Included: 'Licenses associated with installed packages, but not the packages themselves.' Explicitly excluded: 'Metadata API settings with integer or string fields', metadata types, and data. Source org editions supported: Developer, Group, Professional, Unlimited, Enterprise. 'The scratch org created from the org shape is the same edition as the source org.' 'Scratch org shapes are associated with a specific Salesforce release' — recreate after the source org upgrades.
practices.why_it_matters: The integer/string settings exclusion is a silent-failure mode: numeric org settings (session timeouts, thresholds, limits expressed as numbers) come back at platform default in the shaped scratch org, so a test that depends on a tuned numeric setting passes locally and fails in the real org. Likewise, package licences without the packages means installs still have to be scripted.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe org shape as 'a snapshot of your production org' and imply installed packages and configuration come along. They never mention the boolean-only settings capture, which is the exact reason shaped scratch orgs quietly diverge from production.

practices.practice: Quote sandbox refresh intervals and storage exactly, and remember the interval is a hard floor — a botched Full sandbox refresh cannot be redone for 29 days.
practices.specifics: Developer: 1 day refresh interval, 200 MB data storage (400 MB upgraded), 200 MB file storage, metadata only. Developer Pro: 1 day, 1 GB data (2 GB upgraded), 1 GB file, metadata only. Partial Copy: 5 days, 5 GB data, production-equivalent file storage, metadata and sample data. Full: 29 days, production-equivalent data and file storage, metadata and all data. Included counts: Professional 10 Developer; Enterprise 25 Developer + 1 Partial Copy; Unlimited/Performance 100 Developer + 5 Developer Pro + 1 Partial Copy + 1 Full. Partial Copy and Full require a sandbox template. New and refreshed sandboxes default Email Deliverability to 'System email only'.
practices.why_it_matters: The 29-day Full sandbox interval is the binding constraint on release-train design: if the staging refresh is fumbled two weeks before go-live, there is no second attempt inside the release window. Teams that plan a 'refresh staging before each release' cadence on a monthly train have zero slack.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs say 'Full sandboxes can be refreshed monthly' (it is 29 days, and the countdown starts at the last refresh, not the calendar month) and routinely give Partial Copy as '30 days' rather than 5. They also state Developer sandboxes hold 'a subset of your data' — Developer and Developer Pro are metadata-only.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Partial Copy and Full sandboxes are not available in Professional Edition; Developer Pro is not included in Professional or Enterprise (add-on purchase only)

practices.practice: Profiles retrieve SPARSELY: a .profile file only contains security settings for metadata types that were in the same retrieve request. Deploying it therefore cannot revoke anything you didn't ask for.
practices.specifics: 'the returned .profile files only include security settings for the other metadata types referenced in the retrieve request.' Always retrieved regardless: user permissions, IP address ranges, and login hours. Retrieving all custom objects with `*` yields object permissions for custom objects but excludes standard objects such as Account unless explicitly listed. The design intent is stated as avoiding 'unintended, high-impact profile changes'. Disabled permissions are not exported by default — you must write an explicit `<value>false</value>` to turn something off on deploy.
practices.why_it_matters: Profile deploys are an overlay, not a replacement. An admin who removes a field permission from the source-controlled .profile and deploys will find the permission still enabled in production. Access is therefore additive-only unless explicitly negated — the exact opposite of what a git diff implies.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs treat .profile files as declarative full-state, saying 'remove the fieldPermissions entry from the profile XML and deploy to revoke access'. That deploy is a no-op. This is arguably the single most dangerous wrong answer in Salesforce access management, because the user believes access was removed when it was not.

practices.practice: For CI JWT auth, the Dev Hub is the exception: you must still use a Connected App, not an External Client App, if that org will create scratch orgs.
practices.specifics: `sf org login jwt --client-id <consumer key> --jwt-key-file server.key --username <user> --alias my-hub-org`. Docs now describe creating an External Client App and uploading the certificate — but: 'If [creating scratch orgs], you must create a connected app instead of an external client app.' Sandbox auth needs `--instance-url` with the My Domain sandbox URL, e.g. `--instance-url https://mydomain--mysandbox.sandbox.my.salesforce.com`. JWT is incompatible with stepped-up / high-assurance authentication: 'you can't use the JWT flow and Salesforce CLI for headless authentication' when that is configured.
practices.why_it_matters: Salesforce is steering everyone from Connected Apps to External Client Apps, so an LLM trained on the new docs will confidently build a Dev Hub External Client App — and every `sf org create scratch` in the pipeline fails. Separately, a security team enabling High Assurance session policy on the CI user's profile silently kills the whole pipeline's auth.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Two failure modes. Older-trained LLMs never mention External Client Apps at all. Newer ones apply External Client Apps universally, including to the Dev Hub, which does not work for scratch org creation. Almost none mention the High Assurance incompatibility, so 'MFA-harden the integration user' advice and 'use JWT for CI' advice get given together despite being mutually exclusive.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Connected App OAuth Policies must be set to Permitted Users = 'Admin approved users are pre-authorized', and the CI user's profile or permission set must be assigned to the app; otherwise JWT returns invalid_grant
practices.verbatim_error_string: user hasn't approved this consumer

practices.practice: Know the real JWT pre-authorization error text. The failure is HTTP 400 `invalid_grant` with description `user hasn't approved this consumer` — not a 'not authorized' or 'not pre-authorized' message.
practices.specifics: Error: `invalid_grant` / 'user hasn't approved this consumer', HTTP 400. Fix path: Setup > Manage Connected Apps > select the app > Edit Policies > OAuth Policies > Permitted Users = 'Admin approved users are pre-authorized' > back to Manage Connected Apps > Manage Profiles (or Manage Permission Sets) > add the CI user's profile.
practices.why_it_matters: `invalid_grant` is the same top-level error code returned for an expired certificate, a wrong consumer key, a username that doesn't exist in the target org, and a clock-skew problem. Only the description string distinguishes them, so grepping pipeline logs for the exact description is the fastest triage in CI.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs invent plausible-sounding error text — 'user is not pre-authorized', 'user not authorized', 'USER_NOT_PREAUTHORIZED' — none of which Salesforce emits. A runbook keyed on a fabricated string never matches the real log line, so the operator concludes the runbook doesn't apply to their situation.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Connected App OAuth Policy: Permitted Users = 'Admin approved users are pre-authorized' plus profile/permission-set assignment on the app
practices.verbatim_error_string: user hasn't approved this consumer

practices.practice: State the two DIFFERENT quick-deploy coverage rules, because which one applies depends on the test level used during validation.
practices.specifics: Quick deploy prerequisites: the components must have validated successfully against the target org within the last 10 days, the Apex tests must have passed as part of that validation, and coverage must be met. Coverage rule splits: with RunLocalTests or RunAllTestsInOrg, org-wide coverage must be at least 75% AND every Apex trigger must have some coverage. With RunSpecifiedTests, each class and trigger being deployed must individually be covered at 75% or more. 'The job ID is valid for 10 days from when you started the validation.' Metadata API equivalent: deployRecentValidation().
practices.why_it_matters: The RunSpecifiedTests rule is per-class, not org-wide — a package containing one new class at 60% coverage fails even when the org sits at 88%. Teams switch to RunSpecifiedTests to shorten validation time and are then blocked by a rule they did not know changed.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs state one universal rule — '75% org-wide coverage' — for every deployment path, and then recommend RunSpecifiedTests as a speed optimisation without warning that it flips the coverage check to per-class. They also frequently claim RunSpecifiedTests is faster AND has a lower bar; it is stricter per component.

practices.practice: Budget deployments against the real hard ceilings, and know they differ by package type: ~39 MB compressed / ~600 MB uncompressed, 10,000 files for unlocked and 2GP, 35,000 files for 1GP managed.
practices.specifics: Maximum compressed .zip: approximately 39 MB. Maximum uncompressed: approximately 600 MB. Maximum files in a deployment / unlocked and second-generation packages: 10,000. Maximum files in first-generation managed packages: 35,000. Default `--wait` on `sf project deploy start` is 33 minutes.
practices.why_it_matters: Static resources and Experience Cloud bundles blow the 600 MB uncompressed ceiling long before the file count matters, and the failure appears as a generic deploy error rather than a limit message. The 33-minute default wait also means a long RunLocalTests validation returns control to CI mid-flight and a naive script reports failure on a deployment that is still running.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs quote 39 MB but omit the 600 MB uncompressed ceiling entirely, which is the limit static-resource-heavy orgs actually hit. They also give '10,000 files' as a universal limit, not knowing 1GP managed packages get 35,000. And they write CI scripts with no --wait or --async handling, so long production validations look like failures.

practices.practice: Never pass --ignore-errors to a production deploy. Salesforce's own documentation calls out that it can leave production inconsistent.
practices.specifics: 'If you specify it, components without errors are deployed and components with errors are skipped, and could result in an inconsistent production org.' Related: `--ignore-warnings` (default false) lets a deploy succeed despite warnings; `--ignore-conflicts` (default false) 'Ignore conflicts and deploy local files, even if they overwrite changes in the org'.
practices.why_it_matters: --ignore-errors converts an atomic deploy into a partial one, so an object deploys without its validation rule, or a trigger deploys without the handler it calls. The org compiles but behaves wrongly, and the deploy result says success.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: When a user says 'my deploy keeps failing on one component', LLMs commonly suggest --ignore-errors or --ignore-warnings as the unblock. For --ignore-conflicts in a source-tracked sandbox this silently destroys another developer's admin-made changes with no record of what was overwritten.

practices.practice: 2GP ancestry: use `"ancestorVersion": "HIGHEST"` rather than a pinned version, and understand that NONE severs the upgrade path for existing customers.
practices.specifics: Three ways to specify: the HIGHEST keyword (recommended), `ancestorVersion` as major.minor.patch, or `ancestorId` as an 04t ID or package version alias. The ancestor must be 'the highest promoted package version number for that package'. Setting ancestor to NONE means 'existing customers can't upgrade to a package version that is created without a specified ancestor' — only valid for versions you will never promote. `--skip-ancestor-check` is required when creating a version with a non-highest ancestor, or when using NONE after previously promoting versions.
practices.why_it_matters: Ancestry is what makes a package version upgradable rather than a fresh install. A version cut with NONE or with a stale pinned ancestor produces a package customers must uninstall and reinstall — which for a managed package means losing all data in packaged objects.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs suggest `--skip-ancestor-check` as the fix whenever `sf package version create` complains about ancestry, framing it as a harmless flag. It is the mechanism that breaks the customer upgrade path. They also apply ancestry concepts to unlocked packages, which do not have the same released-ancestor linear-versioning constraint.

practices.practice: After any destructive deployment involving Apex, run all local tests from the namespace — Salesforce recommends it specifically to surface dangling references the deploy did not catch.
practices.specifics: 'Salesforce recommends that as part of the deployment, you run all local tests from the namespace in order to detect any remaining references.' Combined with the fact that post-destructive changes are processed before tests run, RunLocalTests on a destructive deploy is the only in-deploy mechanism that catches an orphaned reference.
practices.why_it_matters: Deleting an Apex class that another class references does not necessarily fail at deploy time; it can fail later at runtime as an invalid dependent class, in production, on a user-facing transaction. The test run is the only cheap detector.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs pair destructive deploys with --test-level NoTestRun to make the delete 'clean and fast', which is the exact opposite of the documented recommendation and removes the only safety net.

practices.practice: DevOps Center is current as of 2026 but is not universally available — check the operating zone and the Summer '26 PKI change before recommending it.
practices.specifics: 'Available in: Lightning Experience in Enterprise, Performance, Professional, Unlimited, and Developer Editions', plus Government Cloud Plus with data-residency caveats. 'Not available in: EU Operating Zone.' Salesforce documents a mandatory PKI change in Summer '26 and points new implementations at the 'next-generation DevOps Center'.
practices.why_it_matters: Recommending DevOps Center to a customer in the EU Operating Zone is a dead end that only surfaces after the org-level enablement attempt. The Summer '26 PKI change is a mandatory action item, not optional — existing pipelines break if it is not applied.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs either declare DevOps Center dead ('replaced by sfdx / it was a pilot that went nowhere') or recommend it universally as 'the free Salesforce-native change set replacement, available in all editions'. Both are wrong: it is alive, has a next-generation version, and has real availability exclusions.
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Not available in the EU Operating Zone; Government Cloud Plus availability carries data-residency conditions

areas.area: Architecture, Limits and Scale (governor limits as architecture input, LDV/skew/selectivity, multi-org, tenant isolation, Hyperforce/residency, HA/DR, licensing as constraint, Limits API, API allocation)

practices.practice: Never state a single "concurrent long-running" number — Apex and API are two different limits with different thresholds, different counters and different error text. Apex: transactions lasting longer than 5 seconds, allocation = ratio of 100 licences to 1 concurrent long-running Apex transaction, minimum 10, maximum 50. API: requests lasting longer than 20 seconds, 25 per org in production and sandbox, 5 in Developer Edition and Trial.
practices.specifics: Apex Developer Guide, Execution Governors and Limits: "Number of synchronous concurrent transactions for long-running transactions that last longer than 5 seconds for each org. Based on the number of applicable licenses in an org, the limit is calculated as a ratio of 100 licenses to one concurrent long-running Apex transaction. Minimum limit is 10, Maximum limit is 50". API side (Limits and Allocations Quick Reference): Developer/Trial "5" concurrent requests (20+ seconds), Production orgs and Sandboxes "25". A 500-licence org therefore gets 5 concurrent long-running Apex transactions floored to the minimum 10 — not 25.
practices.why_it_matters: Portal and Experience Cloud capacity models are sized against the wrong ceiling. An org sized against "25 at 20 seconds" is actually throttled at 10–50 at 5 seconds, so the wall arrives at roughly a quarter of the modelled concurrency and at a request duration four times shorter.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: A competent LLM emits one blended number: "Salesforce allows 25 concurrent long-running Apex requests org-wide; a request is long-running if it exceeds 20 seconds." That is the API limit's threshold welded onto the Apex limit's name. This exact sentence is already shipping in this repo at skills/architect/omnistudio-scalability-patterns/SKILL.md:90, which proves the failure mode is stable enough to have been written into a skill.
practices.already_covered_by: architect/org-limits-monitoring (Apex side stated correctly at SKILL.md:193-200); the Apex-vs-API conflation itself is NOT covered and is contradicted at architect/omnistudio-scalability-patterns/SKILL.md:88-92
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: The Apex allocation is derived from applicable user licence count — adding licences raises it, up to the hard cap of 50. There is no add-on that raises it further.
practices.verbatim_error_string: Unable to process request. Concurrent requests limit exceeded.

practices.practice: Branch retry logic on the detail string inside REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, not on the code. "TotalRequests Limit exceeded." means the 24-hour allocation is gone and retrying inside the window is futile. "ConcurrentPerOrgLongTxn Limit exceeded." means too many in-flight requests over 20 seconds and it clears in seconds — fail-fast there is a self-inflicted outage.
practices.specifics: Both surface as exception code REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED with HTTP 403. Only the message body distinguishes them: "TotalRequests Limit exceeded." vs "ConcurrentPerOrgLongTxn Limit exceeded." Correct handling: TotalRequests → alert, stop, do not retry until the rolling window advances; ConcurrentPerOrgLongTxn → exponential backoff with jitter starting ~2s, or serialise the offending call.
practices.why_it_matters: The repo currently instructs the opposite for half the cases: skills/security/api-security-and-rate-limiting/references/gotchas.md:31 says "When the error is REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, fail fast, emit an alert, and do not retry until the rolling 24-hour window resets." Applied to the concurrent variant that permanently stops an integration that would have recovered in under a minute.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM asked to handle REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED writes `if error_code == 'REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED': alert_and_stop()` because every blog post equates that code with the daily limit. It never inspects the message body, so the concurrent-limit case — which is the far more common one in bursty middleware — is handled as terminal.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE — grep for both detail strings across all 1,027 skills returns zero hits
practices.verbatim_error_string: ConcurrentPerOrgLongTxn Limit exceeded.

practices.practice: State the custom-index selectivity rule as two tiers, not one percentage. A custom index is used if the filter matches less than 10% of the first million records AND less than 5% of records beyond the first million. The standard-index rule is 30% of the first million and 15% beyond.
practices.specifics: LDV guide verbatim — custom: "Used if the filter matches less than 10% of the first million records and less than 5% of additional records", worked examples "500,000 records: 50,000 or fewer matching records" and "5 million records: 300,000 or fewer matching records". Standard: "Used if the filter matches less than 30% of the first million records and less than 15% of additional records", worked examples "2 million records: 450,000 or fewer" and "5 million records: 900,000 or fewer". Caps still apply above these: 1,000,000 matching rows for standard, 333,333 for custom.
practices.why_it_matters: A flat-10% mental model is wrong in the direction that hurts: on a 20M-row object it predicts 2,000,000 rows is selective when the real ceiling is 100,000 + 5% of 19M = 1,050,000, further capped at 333,333. Architects sign off on filter designs that will never use the index.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs collapse the tiered rule to one number — "custom index selectivity threshold is 10%" — and then compute 10% of the total row count. This exact simplification is live in this repo: skills/architect/large-data-volume-architecture/SKILL.md says "the filter must match less than ten percent of total rows, with an absolute ceiling of 333,333".
practices.already_covered_by: architect/large-data-volume-architecture (present but stated as a single 10%-of-total tier — factually wrong, needs correction not addition)

practices.practice: Know which field types can never be custom-indexed before you design an access path around them. Long text areas, rich text areas, non-deterministic formula fields and encrypted text fields cannot be indexed at all.
practices.specifics: Cannot be custom indexed: text areas (long), text areas (rich), non-deterministic formula fields, encrypted text fields. Can be: deterministic formula fields, and External IDs on Auto Number, Email, Number and Text fields. Platform-maintained indexes exist automatically on RecordTypeId, Division, CreatedDate, SystemModstamp, Name, Email (Contact/Lead), foreign keys and record IDs.
practices.why_it_matters: "Non-deterministic" is the trap: a formula referencing another object across a lookup, or TODAY()/NOW(), or an owner field, makes the formula non-deterministic and permanently unindexable. Teams design a reporting filter on a cross-object formula, discover at 5M rows that Support cannot index it, and have to add and backfill a physical field.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked "how do I speed up this report filtered on my roll-up formula?", an LLM answers "request a custom index on the formula field from Salesforce Support." It does not check determinism, so the recommendation is unactionable for the majority of real-world formula fields — which reference parent records or dates and are therefore non-deterministic.
practices.already_covered_by: data/custom-index-requests and apex/formula-field-performance-and-limits reference indexes and query plans; the explicit deterministic-vs-non-deterministic indexability rule was not found in the architect LDV package
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Custom indexes on most field types are created only by Salesforce Customer Support; External ID is the self-service path.

practices.practice: Skinny tables cannot be created, inspected or version-controlled by the customer, and they do not exist in Developer or Partial Copy sandboxes. Never build a performance test plan that assumes production parity below a Full sandbox.
practices.specifics: LDV guide verbatim: "Skinny tables can contain a maximum of 200 columns." "Skinny tables can be created on custom objects, and on Account, Contact, Opportunity, Lead, and Case objects." "If you want to use skinny tables, contact Salesforce Customer Support. When enabled, skinny tables are created and used automatically where appropriate. You can't create, access, or modify skinny tables yourself." Full sandboxes copy them; other sandbox types require a separate Support request to activate them.
practices.why_it_matters: A report that returns in 3 seconds in production and 90 seconds in a Developer sandbox is not a regression — it is the missing skinny table. Teams chase phantom code problems, or worse, ship a "fix" tuned against the slow path.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe skinny tables as a design choice — "create a skinny table containing the columns your reports need" — implying a Setup screen or metadata type exists. There is none. They also omit the sandbox asymmetry entirely, so the generated performance-test plan is silently invalid.
practices.already_covered_by: architect/large-data-volume-architecture (SKILL.md Core Concepts covers 200 columns, object list, Support-only creation and Full-sandbox-only copy in prose)

practices.practice: The platform event daily allocation is a DELIVERY allocation of 25,000 (Enterprise) / 50,000 (Performance, Unlimited) / 10,000 (Developer). 250,000 is the HOURLY PUBLISH ceiling, a different meter. Sizing an event-driven design against 250,000/day inflates Enterprise headroom by 10x in the wrong direction.
practices.specifics: Platform Events Developer Guide, allocations: high-volume platform events delivered per 24 hours — Performance/Unlimited "50,000", Enterprise "25,000", Developer "10,000". Published per hour — Performance/Unlimited "250,000", Enterprise/Professional with API Add-On "250,000", Developer "50,000". Event message retention is "72 hours". Max event size is "1 MB".
practices.why_it_matters: Delivery is counted per subscriber-delivery, not per publish, so a single published event with four CometD/Pub-Sub subscribers consumes four of the 25,000. An Enterprise org with 4 subscribers exhausts its daily delivery allocation at ~6,250 published events — two orders of magnitude below what the 250,000 figure suggests.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: The LLM sees two numbers in the same doc table and picks the larger one, then attaches the wrong period: "Enterprise supports 250,000 platform events per day." It also never mentions that delivery is multiplied by subscriber count. This is live in the repo at skills/integration/event-driven-architecture-patterns/SKILL.md:70 and repeated in that skill's gotchas.md:19 and well-architected.md:7.
practices.already_covered_by: integration/event-driven-architecture-patterns states it, but with the publish-per-hour number presented as the deliver-per-day allocation — needs correction, not addition

practices.practice: Platform event headroom is purchasable, and the add-on is the answer when a design is 2-5x over allocation. The Platform Event Add-On License adds 100,000 delivered events per day (3 million per month) and 25,000 published events per hour. Enterprise and Professional need the separate API Add-On to reach the 250,000/hour publish ceiling at all.
practices.specifics: Platform Events allocations doc: the Platform Event Add-On License increases the 24-hour delivery allocation by "100,000 per day (3 million a month)" and adds "25,000 events per hour" to publishing. Hourly publish of "250,000" is listed for "Enterprise/Professional (with API Add-On)".
practices.why_it_matters: Architects redesign around a limit that money removes, replacing a clean event-driven design with polling or a middleware queue. Conversely, teams that assume they can just buy their way out do not know the increment size and cannot cost the design.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked "we exceed the platform event limit, what do we do?", an LLM proposes batching multiple business events into one platform event, or falling back to Change Data Capture — never "buy the Platform Event Add-On License, which adds 100,000 deliveries/day." Licensing is invisible in its training distribution because docs and blogs discuss limits, not SKUs.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE — `grep -rn "Platform Event Add-On\|Event Add-On License"` across skills/ returns zero hits
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Platform Event Add-On License; plus API Add-On for Enterprise/Professional to reach 250,000 published events/hour

practices.practice: Calling /services/data/vXX.0/limits requires the View Setup and Configuration permission, and DataStorageMB / FileStorageMB additionally require Manage Users. Grant these to the monitoring integration user explicitly or the monitor silently reports fewer keys than it should.
practices.specifics: REST API Developer Guide, Limits resource: "Required Permission: View Setup and Configuration"; introduced in API version 29.0. DataStorageMB and FileStorageMB are annotated as requiring the Manage Users permission. Storage keys are simply absent from the response for a caller without Manage Users — no 403, no warning.
practices.why_it_matters: The failure is silent and shaped exactly like "the org has no storage pressure." A storage monitor built on a least-privilege integration user reports healthy forever while the org walks into a storage wall.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs write the monitoring script — GET /limits, parse DataStorageMB.Remaining — and never mention a permission prerequisite, because the endpoint returns HTTP 200 with a partial body rather than an error. The generated code has no key-presence check, so a missing key becomes a KeyError in production or, worse, a default of zero used consumed.
practices.already_covered_by: architect/org-limits-monitoring enumerates the keys and correctly gates the Event Monitoring surfaces, but does not state the View Setup and Configuration / Manage Users prerequisites for /limits itself
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: View Setup and Configuration (whole resource); Manage Users (DataStorageMB, FileStorageMB)

practices.practice: Treat OrgLimits and /limits values as advisory, not transactional. Salesforce documents these values as updated asynchronously in near-real-time, so a pre-flight "do we have API headroom" gate can pass and the very next call can still fail.
practices.specifics: Apex Reference, OrgLimits class: "Limit values are updated asynchronously, in near-real-time." OrgLimits.getMap() returns a map keyed by limit name; getAll() returns a list of OrgLimit instances. There is no documented freshness SLA.
practices.why_it_matters: Designs that gate a nightly load on `OrgLimits.getMap().get('DailyApiRequests').getValue() < threshold` are building a race condition into the control plane. Under concurrent integration traffic the read is stale by an unbounded amount.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs generate a "safe" pattern: check OrgLimits before enqueueing, abort if consumption > 90%. They present this as a guarantee. The correct architecture is to treat the reading as a trend signal for alerting and to handle REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED at the call site regardless.
practices.already_covered_by: architect/org-limits-monitoring uses OrgLimits extensively; grep for "near-real-time" in that package finds it only describing dashboard refresh, not the freshness caveat on the limit values themselves

practices.practice: A Full sandbox has 5,000,000 API calls per 24 hours regardless of licence count. Never validate production API headroom in a Full sandbox — the sandbox has 10-50x the production allocation.
practices.specifics: API Request Limits and Allocations: Full Sandbox "5,000,000" calls. Production Enterprise = 100,000 base + 1,000 per Salesforce/Salesforce Platform licence; Unlimited/Performance = 100,000 base + 5,000 per licence; Developer Edition = "15,000" flat. A 200-licence Enterprise production org therefore has 300,000 calls against the sandbox's 5,000,000 — a 16x gap. Calls carrying DebuggingHeader have a separate allocation of "1,000 calls per 24-hour period".
practices.why_it_matters: Integration load tests, migration dry runs and ETL rehearsals all run in Full sandbox by policy. They will never reproduce the production API wall, so the wall is discovered on cutover day.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Two failures. First, LLMs quote "15,000 API calls per day for Enterprise Edition" — that is the Developer Edition number, and this exact error is already catalogued in this repo at skills/admin/api-contract-documentation/references/llm-anti-patterns.md:9. Second, when asked to design an API load test they say "run it in a Full sandbox for production parity" without flagging that API allocation is the one dimension where Full sandbox is deliberately NOT at parity.
practices.already_covered_by: integration/api-governance-and-rate-limits and security/api-security-and-rate-limiting cover the per-edition formula; the 5,000,000 Full-sandbox figure and the sandbox-parity trap were not found (`grep -rn "5,000,000"` returns only unrelated record-count hits)

practices.practice: Salesforce grants a soft grace above the daily API allocation, but only for paid active orgs. Trials, Developer Edition and sandboxes get a hard stop. Do not design a burst tolerance that only exists in production.
practices.specifics: API Request Limits and Allocations: once daily limits are reached "Salesforce still lets the operations proceed by a certain amount, if possible" — and this grace "applies only to paid, active orgs—not trials, Developer Edition, or sandboxes."
practices.why_it_matters: This is the inverse of the sandbox-parity trap: an integration tuned in production against invisible grace will hard-fail the moment it is exercised in a scratch org, DE org or partner trial, and the team will conclude the code changed.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe the daily API limit as an absolute hard stop in all orgs. They therefore over-engineer throttling for production and under-warn for DE/trial, which is where the hard stop actually lives.
practices.already_covered_by: NONE found — the grace-allocation asymmetry did not appear in the api-governance or api-security packages

practices.practice: Bulk API and Bulk API 2.0 share one 15,000-batch-per-rolling-24-hours allocation. They are not separate buckets. Running Bulk 1.0 nightly ETL alongside Bulk 2.0 migration jobs draws from the same well.
practices.specifics: Bulk API limits: "You can submit up to 15,000 batches per rolling 24-hour period. This allocation is shared between Bulk API and Bulk API 2.0." Records per 24 hours: "150,000,000 (15,000 batches x 10,000 records per batch maximum)". Bulk 2.0 job upload cap is "150 MB per job" with data that should "not exceed 100 MB" pre-base64. Ingest results are retrievable "within 7 days of job completion". Max characters per field 131,072; per record 400,000.
practices.why_it_matters: The 7-day results window is the irreversible part: once it lapses, the per-record success/failed/unprocessed detail is gone permanently. A migration that discovers a mapping defect on day 9 cannot reconstruct which records failed.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs present Bulk 1.0 and Bulk 2.0 as independent allocations and tell teams to "fall back to Bulk API 1.0 if you hit the 2.0 limit" — which does nothing, because the batch counter is shared. They also never mention the 7-day results retention, so generated migration runbooks have no step to archive job results.
practices.already_covered_by: data/bulk-api-and-large-data-loads and data/bulk-api-patterns cover 150,000,000 records / 15,000 batches / 150 MB accurately; the word 'shared' between the two APIs and the 7-day results retention were not found in those packages

practices.practice: Big Objects are capped at 100 per org and only the first 1,000,000 records are included in the base edition entitlement. They support neither Platform Encryption nor transactions, and the documented failure protocol is to retry the entire batch rather than reconcile partial success.
practices.specifics: Big Objects Implementation Guide: "You can create up to 100 big objects per org." "Available in: Enterprise, Performance, Unlimited, and Developer Editions for up to 1 million records" — beyond that is a purchased entitlement. "Big objects don't support encryption". "Big objects don't support transactions". "The best practice when writing to a big object is to have a retry mechanism in place" and "Don't try to figure out which records succeeded and which failed. Retry the entire batch."
practices.why_it_matters: Archival designs routinely justify Big Objects as the cheap home for regulated history. Discovering after the design is signed that Shield Platform Encryption cannot follow the data into the archive is a compliance failure, not a performance one. And the 1M-record inclusion means the "free archive" is free only until the first quarter of real volume lands.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs present Big Objects as unlimited-and-free ("billions of records at no storage cost") and pair them with Shield in the same compliance-archive recommendation. Both halves are wrong: there is a purchased entitlement above 1M records, and encryption is unsupported. They also generate insertImmediate error handling that inspects Database.SaveResult per record to retry only failures — the opposite of the documented guidance.
practices.already_covered_by: data/external-data-and-big-objects covers composite-index prefix semantics, insertImmediate silent failure and no-update semantics very well; the 100-per-org cap, the 1M-record entitlement, no-encryption and no-transactions were not found in that package
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Base entitlement is 1,000,000 big object records in Enterprise / Performance / Unlimited / Developer; additional capacity is a purchased add-on. Shield Platform Encryption cannot be applied to big object fields at all.

practices.practice: Cumulative callout time is capped at 120 seconds per transaction and the default per-callout timeout is 10 seconds — so a synchronous transaction can make at most ~12 sequential callouts at default settings before the transaction dies, regardless of the 100-callout limit.
practices.specifics: Apex governor limits: "Maximum cumulative timeout for callouts by a single Apex transaction: 120 seconds" — same for synchronous and asynchronous. "Default timeout of callouts (HTTP requests or Web services calls) in an Apex transaction: 10 seconds". Maximum callouts per transaction is 100. Callout request/response size cap is 6 MB synchronous, 12 MB asynchronous. Maximum settable per-callout timeout is 120,000 ms.
practices.why_it_matters: The 100-callout number is the one everybody quotes and it is almost never the binding constraint. Time is. An orchestration that fans out 30 enrichment callouts is designed against 100 and killed by 120 seconds.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked "how many callouts can I make in a transaction?", an LLM answers "100" and stops. It does not surface the 120-second cumulative ceiling, so the design it validates is arithmetically impossible against any real external service latency.
practices.already_covered_by: apex/callouts-and-http-integrations/references/llm-anti-patterns.md:74 mentions the 120-second total budget in passing; the derived architectural ceiling (~12 sequential callouts at defaults) and the 6MB/12MB payload asymmetry were not found stated together

practices.practice: Batch Apex concurrency is 5, not a queue depth you can tune. Only 5 batch jobs may be queued or active at once; a 6th goes to the Apex flex queue in Holding status, which itself caps at 100. Scheduled Apex classes cap at 100 concurrently (5 in Developer Edition).
practices.specifics: Apex governor limits, 24-hour platform section: "Maximum number of batch Apex jobs queued or active concurrently: 5"; "Maximum number of batch Apex jobs in the Apex flex queue that are in Holding status: 100"; "Maximum number of Apex classes scheduled concurrently: 100. In Developer Edition orgs, the limit is 5." Batch Apex QueryLocator max is 50 million records.
practices.why_it_matters: Nightly-window architectures that assume "we'll just schedule 12 batch jobs at 01:00" silently serialise into 5-wide execution plus a 100-deep holding queue. The window blows out and nobody can see why from the job code.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs know the 5-concurrent number but present the flex queue as unlimited overflow, so they recommend "just enqueue them all, the flex queue will handle it." The 100-Holding cap means the 106th job is rejected outright, and Developer Edition's 5-scheduled-class ceiling makes the whole pattern untestable in a scratch org.
practices.already_covered_by: apex/batch-apex-patterns covers the 250,000-or-licences×200 daily ceiling; the flex queue Holding cap of 100 and the DE-specific 5-scheduled-class limit were not found there

practices.practice: Apex cursors carry their own 24-hour org-wide meters that are invisible to per-transaction thinking: 10,000 cursors per 24 hours, 100 million cumulative cursor rows per 24 hours, 50 million rows per cursor, 100 Cursor.fetch calls per transaction.
practices.specifics: Apex governor limits — per transaction: "Apex cursors (rows): 50 million", "Cursor.fetch calls: 100", "Pagination cursor rows: 100,000", "Pagination cursor instances: 50", "Pagination rows per page: 2,000". Per 24 hours: "Apex cursors: 10,000", "Pagination cursor instances: 200,000", "Cumulative cursor rows: 100 million".
practices.why_it_matters: Cursors are the newer alternative to Batch Apex for large scans, and teams adopt them precisely because they are told cursors avoid batch limits. They do not — they add a distinct set of daily org-wide ceilings that no per-transaction Limits.get* method reveals.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: Asked to replace a Batch Apex job with cursors for a 200M-row scan, an LLM writes the cursor loop and asserts it sidesteps the 50M QueryLocator ceiling. It does not mention the 100-million-cumulative-cursor-rows-per-24-hours org meter, which makes a 200M-row scan impossible in one day regardless of the code.
practices.already_covered_by: apex/governor-limits/references/gotchas.md is the only file in the corpus mentioning Apex cursors; the 24-hour cursor meters were not found

practices.practice: Hyperforce IP ranges are published as a machine-readable feed at https://ip-ranges.salesforce.com/ip-ranges.json with a syncToken and createDate. Automate allowlist reconciliation against that feed; do not copy CIDRs out of a Knowledge article into a firewall rule.
practices.specifics: The feed is live as of createDate "2026-07-06-09-00-00", syncToken "1783342800", with 23 IPv4 region entries (21 AWS, 2 GCP) and 20 IPv6 entries (all AWS). Entries are shaped {region, provider, ip_prefix} e.g. region us-east-1 / aws / 155.226.144.0/22 and 155.226.137.0/24; IPv6 e.g. eu-central-1 / aws / 2a03:5d67:fe48::/45. Salesforce explicitly does not recommend IP allowlisting for Hyperforce integrations because cloud-provider prefixes change outside Salesforce's control.
practices.why_it_matters: The 'we missed an allowlist' failure is the single most common Hyperforce day-1 incident, and it recurs after migration whenever a prefix is added. A one-time manual copy guarantees recurrence; a syncToken-diffed job does not.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs tell you to "check the Salesforce Knowledge article for the current Hyperforce IP ranges and update your firewall" — a manual, point-in-time instruction. They do not know the JSON endpoint exists, so the runbook they produce has no re-validation step and no drift detection.

practices.practice: Heroku AppLink is the current name (formerly Heroku Integration) and it requires a named Salesforce system permission — Manage Heroku AppLink — assigned via a permission set. As of Spring '26 you can no longer create new connected apps, so AppLink authorisations must be built on External Client Apps.
practices.specifics: Heroku Dev Center: "Heroku AppLink (formerly Heroku Integration) exposes your Heroku apps as API services in Salesforce." Setup step verbatim: "In the Find Settings… box, enter and select Manage Heroku AppLink." Release constraint verbatim: "As of the Salesforce Spring '26 release, you can no longer create new connected apps in Salesforce. We're deprecating using connected apps with Heroku AppLink, and replacing them with external client apps." Publishing supports --authorization-permission-set-name to elevate to user-plus authorisation mode.
practices.why_it_matters: Every AppLink tutorial written before Spring '26 begins with 'create a connected app'. Following it now dead-ends. And the Manage Heroku AppLink permission is a system permission with no permission set licence behind it, so it is easy to miss in an access design that only audits PSLs.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: An LLM asked to wire Heroku to Salesforce produces the 2018 recipe — connected app, consumer key/secret, JWT bearer flow, Apex @future callout — or, if it knows AppLink, still opens with 'create a connected app'. It has no knowledge of the Spring '26 creation block and never names the Manage Heroku AppLink permission.
practices.already_covered_by: integration/heroku-salesforce-integration covers AppLink as a pattern and correctly prefers it over @InvocableMethod + callout; the Manage Heroku AppLink permission and the Spring '26 connected-app block were not found in that package (it dates AppLink as '2024+', which is the Heroku Integration era)
practices.gating_licence_or_permission: Manage Heroku AppLink (Salesforce system permission, granted via permission set). External Client App required for new authorisations from Spring '26.

practices.practice: Row lock waits are fixed at 10 seconds and produce two different exception types depending on how you touched the row: QueryException for a blocked FOR UPDATE, DmlException for a blocked update. Neither is configurable.
practices.specifics: Apex Developer Guide, locking statements: "If the wait time exceeds 10 seconds, a QueryException is thrown. Similarly, if you attempt to update a record currently locked by another client and the lock isn't released within a maximum of 10 seconds, a DmlException is thrown." The DmlException carries StatusCode UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW.
practices.why_it_matters: Retry frameworks that catch only DmlException miss the FOR UPDATE path entirely, and the failure looks like a query problem rather than a contention problem. The 10-second ceiling also bounds how long a transaction may hold a lock before it starts failing everyone else.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs write `catch (DmlException e) { if (e.getDmlType(0) == StatusCode.UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW) retry(); }` and call the problem solved. The FOR UPDATE branch throws QueryException and falls through uncaught. They also frequently claim the lock timeout is configurable via a Setup option or a Support case — it is not.
practices.already_covered_by: apex/record-locking-and-contention covers the fixed 10-second timeout, non-configurability and UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW thoroughly (SKILL.md:62, :190, gotchas.md:49, llm-anti-patterns.md:71); the QueryException-vs-DmlException split by access path was not found there

practices.practice: Reserve the QueryException 'non-selective query against large object type' guard for what it actually is: a trigger-context-only guard that fires on objects above 200,000 rows. The same query outside trigger context runs — slowly — without error, which is why the problem is invisible until a trigger touches it.
practices.specifics: Verbatim: System.QueryException: Non-selective query against large object type (more than 200000 rows). Consider an indexed filter or contact salesforce.com about custom indexing. The 200,000 threshold is the object row count, not the result count. A filter can also be rendered non-selective by binding a list containing null, by a leading wildcard, or by != / NOT.
practices.why_it_matters: Diagnosing this as 'my query is slow' leads to index requests; diagnosing it as 'I am doing an unselective scan inside a trigger' leads to moving the work async, which is usually the right architecture and requires no Support ticket.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: The LLM's fix is always 'contact Salesforce Support to request a custom index' — it reads the remediation out of the error string. It does not consider that the query may be unindexable (non-deterministic formula), that the null-in-bind-list case defeats an existing index, or that the correct move is out of trigger context.
practices.already_covered_by: data/soql-query-optimization/references/gotchas.md:63 and llm-anti-patterns.md:182 carry the exact string

practices.practice: Scratch org and packaging allocations are exposed through the same /limits resource as runtime limits — ActiveScratchOrgs, DailyScratchOrgs (a rolling, not calendar, 24-hour window), Package2VersionCreates and Package2VersionCreatesWithoutValidation. Monitor them the same way you monitor DailyApiRequests.
practices.specifics: Limits resource, Salesforce Developer Experience section: ActiveScratchOrgs is "The maximum number of scratch orgs you can have at any given time"; DailyScratchOrgs is "The maximum number of successful scratch org creations you can initiate in a rolling (sliding) 24-hour window"; Package2VersionCreates is "Daily number of package versions that you can create" for second-generation packages.
practices.why_it_matters: CI pipelines that create a scratch org per pull request hit DailyScratchOrgs mid-sprint and the failure looks like a CLI or auth problem. Because the window slides, there is no midnight reset to wait for — the fix is throttling org creation or raising the Dev Hub allocation.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs describe scratch org limits as a Dev Hub setting you view in Setup and treat the daily counter as resetting at midnight. Both are wrong in a way that changes the remediation: the counter slides, and the value is programmatically readable from /limits so it can be pre-flighted in CI.
practices.already_covered_by: architect/org-limits-monitoring enumerates API/storage/PE/async keys but not the Salesforce DX keys; devops packages reference scratch org limits qualitatively

practices.practice: Elastic async Apex changes the failure mode, not just the ceiling. Past the licensed DailyAsyncApexExecutions limit, Queueable and future jobs are throttled rather than rejected — so a monitor alarming at 100% of the licensed key is reporting degraded throughput, not an outage. Batch and Scheduled Apex do not get this and still hit a hard wall.
practices.specifics: DailyAsyncApexExecutions is the licensed daily limit: "250,000 or the number of applicable user licenses in your org multiplied by 200, whichever is greater". DailyAsyncApexElasticExecutions is a separate /limits key covering "Daily number of Queueable Apex and future method executions that can be enqueued, including elastic executions processed at a throttled rate"; the elastic ceiling is the daily async limit plus either the licensed daily async limit or 10 million executions, whichever is less. Elastic limits are Beta and apply only to Queueable Apex and future methods.
practices.why_it_matters: Alert design depends on which key you read. Alarming on the licensed key alone generates a false outage page for a Queueable workload that is merely slow, and generates no page at all for a Batch workload that is genuinely rejected.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs know exactly one async number — 250,000 or licences×200 — and treat it as a uniform hard ceiling for all four async flavours. They do not know DailyAsyncApexElasticExecutions exists, so the monitoring they generate reads the wrong key and misclassifies throttling as failure.
practices.already_covered_by: architect/org-limits-monitoring covers this correctly and in detail at SKILL.md ~line 185; apex/batch-apex-patterns covers the 250,000/licences×200 figure. Recorded here as CONFIRMED-COVERED, not a gap.

practices.practice: Bulk API 2.0 job-status polling consumes the standard daily API allocation. A long-running load polled every 30 seconds spends more API calls on polling than the load itself, and none of it shows up in Bulk API metrics.
practices.specifics: A 9-hour load polled every 30 seconds is 1,080 polls per job; run four jobs in parallel and that is 4,320 calls against DailyApiRequests — on top of the batch allocation, which is a separate meter. Bulk API 2.0 ingest itself does not draw from DailyApiRequests, only the 15,000-batch allocation.
practices.why_it_matters: This is the classic 'we used Bulk API so API limits do not apply' error. The load is exempt; the control plane around it is not. Teams then blame an unrelated integration for the API spike.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs assert flatly that 'Bulk API does not count against the daily API limit' and then generate a polling loop with a 5-second sleep. Both halves are individually defensible and jointly produce an API-limit outage.
practices.already_covered_by: data/data-loader-batch-window-sizing/references/gotchas.md:99 documents exactly this (polling accounts for the 60,000+ calls on a 5M-record load). CONFIRMED-COVERED — do not re-add.

practices.practice: When a feature is gated by a Permission Set Licence, the org-level provisioning and the per-user assignment are two separate acts, and the per-user gap presents as a generic 'feature not available' rather than a licensing error. Always instruct both steps and name Setup > Users > [User] > Permission Set License Assignments as the diagnostic.
practices.specifics: Diagnostic path for org-level provisioning: Setup > Company Information > Permission Set Licenses. Diagnostic path for per-user: Setup > Users > [User] > Permission Set License Assignments. The signature symptom is a feature working for one user and not another in the same org with the same profile.
practices.why_it_matters: This is the single highest-frequency licensing support case shape in Salesforce and it wastes days because the error text points nowhere near the cause.
practices.llm_gets_this_wrong: LLMs give only the org-level enablement step ('Setup > Feature Settings > Enable X') and stop, because that is what enablement docs describe. The PSL assignment step is in a different doc and never makes it into the generated runbook.
practices.already_covered_by: architect/org-edition-and-feature-licensing covers this precisely — SKILL.md:181, gotchas.md:15-19, llm-anti-patterns.md:51-57. CONFIRMED-COVERED; recorded so the corpus is not told this is a gap.

stale_or_wrong_found: FACTUALLY WRONG — skills/architect/omnistudio-scalability-patterns/SKILL.md:90: 'Salesforce enforces a hard limit of 25 concurrent long-running Apex requests across the entire org. A request is "long-running" if it takes more than 20 seconds to complete.' This fuses the API limit's threshold (20s, 25 per org) onto the Apex limit's name. Official: Apex concurrent long-running transactions are those lasting longer than 5 SECONDS, allocated at a ratio of 100 licences to 1, minimum 10, maximum 50. The error is repeated in that skill's llm-anti-patterns.md:63-77 (which ironically presents the wrong number as the thing LLMs miss) and hard-coded into its template at lines 24 and 95 ('Must remain below 25 org-wide', '/ 25'). Official Platform Events allocations: daily DELIVERY is 25,000 on Enterprise, 50,000 on Performance/Unlimited, 10,000 on Developer. 250,000 is the HOURLY PUBLISH ceiling. Enterprise headroom is overstated by 10x. Repeated in that skill's references/gotchas.md:19 ('Platform Events (250,000/day on Enterprise+)') and references/well-architected.md:7 ('Standard Platform Events support 250,000 events/day on Enterprise+').

LIKELY FABRICATED — skills/integration/event-driven-architecture-patterns/SKILL.md:71: 'High-Volume Platform Events bypass the per-org standard allocation and support RetainUntilDate for extended retention beyond 72 hours.' High-volume platform events have their own daily delivery allocation (they do not bypass one), and the Platform Events limits doc states retention as a flat '72 hours' with no customer-settable extension. RetainUntilDate is not a platform-event retention control. Needs verification before it ships further.

WRONG ERROR CODE, three places — EXCEEDED_ID_LIMIT is used as the symptom of exhausting rate/volume allocations. skills/integration/mulesoft-salesforce-connector/SKILL.md:165 ('hit this limit and get EXCEEDED_ID_LIMIT errors'), skills/security/api-security-and-rate-limiting/references/gotchas.md:41 ('Monitor for EXCEEDED_ID_LIMIT or SERVER_UNAVAILABLE errors' for the concurrent limit), skills/agentforce/sf-to-llm-data-pipelines/references/gotchas.md:57 (Bulk quota exhaustion 'causing other integration processes ... to fail with EXCEEDED_ID_LIMIT errors'). EXCEEDED_ID_LIMIT is the too-many-IDs-in-one-request error; allocation exhaustion surfaces as REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED with 'TotalRequests Limit exceeded.'

LIKELY FABRICATED NUMBER — skills/agentforce/sf-to-llm-data-pipelines/references/gotchas.md:57: 'in Enterprise Edition, the base limit is approximately 200 MB of compressed data per 24-hour rolling period.' No such Bulk API 2.0 allocation exists in the limits documentation; the 24-hour meters are 15,000 batches and 150,000,000 records, with a per-job 150 MB upload cap. The hedge '(the exact limit is documented in Salesforce's API limits help article and varies by release)' reads as an LLM covering an invented figure.

SUSPECT NUMBERS — skills/data/bulk-api-and-large-data-loads/SKILL.md:47: 'A batch that cannot process within 5 minutes is retried up to 20 times before the job moves to Failed.' The documented Bulk API behaviour is a 10-minute per-batch limit with up to 10 requeue attempts before permanent failure. I could not re-fetch the exact paragraph (the Bulk API limits page no longer carries it), so this is flagged for verification rather than asserted wrong.

IMPRECISE — skills/data/large-scale-deduplication/SKILL.md:81: 'Bulk API 2.0 supports up to 150 million records per query job.' 150,000,000 is the per-org per-rolling-24-hours ceiling, not a per-job capacity.

IMPRECISE — skills/architect/large-data-volume-architecture/SKILL.md Core Concepts: 'For custom indexed fields, the filter must match less than ten percent of total rows, with an absolute ceiling of 333,333 matching rows.' Official rule is tiered: less than 10% of the FIRST MILLION records and less than 5% of ADDITIONAL records (worked example: 5 million records → 300,000 or fewer). The flat-10%-of-total form overstates selectivity headroom on any object above 1M rows.

SUSPECT ERROR CODE — skills/security/api-security-and-rate-limiting/SKILL.md:71 attributes 'TXN_SECURITY_METERING_ERROR' to the concurrent API request limit. TXN_SECURITY_METERING_ERROR belongs to Transaction Security policy evaluation, not API concurrency. The real distinguishing string is 'ConcurrentPerOrgLongTxn Limit exceeded.' inside a REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED / HTTP 403.
